After more than twenty years of expert
ment fig-raising has become a success in
the United States. The bulk of the figs
produced in this country are grown in CEN
trail California, and more than 100000
pounds of this once solely oriental fruit are
now shipped annually from the great fig
belt" AS figs are the most valuable Of all
wholesale fruits, being worth in the neigh
borhood Of $50 a ton in their crudest state,
the discovery of the secret whereby the
Smyrna fig can be made to thrive was one
of considerable Importance. The first sue
cessful effort to fertiliZe the fruit Of the
fig tree so that it will not become "soured"
was made by George c. Roeding of Fresno
in 1898.


Unless the Smyrna fig is fertilized by
certain wasp, Blastophaga grossorum. the
green fruit Will not mature. To introduce
this wasp from Smyrna, the only country
in which it was found, was the problem
which faced the fruit growers. For many
years attempts had been made to intro
duce the wasp from Asia Minor. The
Blastophaga was brought across the ocean
In glass cases and tenderly packed in cot
ton, but no sooner did 1t reach America
than 1t died, and the expectations of fig
SIOWcIS NdulSu6u.


The Smyrna wasp breeds in the inedible
fruit OF the wild fig, and Smyrna branches
of the wild figs are hung in the orchards
at the proper time. Wild fig trees were
introduced in California and in the season
of polarization their branches were hung
in the orchards. But without exception the
wild figs and the wasps within them
persisted and 1t was not until the DEPART
ment of Agriculture co-operated with Mr.
Roeding that the wild fig tree and the wasp
were successfully imported.


The first trees were carefully wrapped
in cheesecloth and then put into hermet-
1cally sealed glass cases. Even after they
were transplanted the utmost care was
taken to prevent them from being subject
ed to any injury or sudden changes of eli
mate. After the second year the figs were
tried In the open at Niles, Cal. Once ac-
climated they grew with great vigor. Now
they can stand all weathers and are found
throughout the great fruit belt in central
California.


The young wasp emerging from the wild
fig bears upon its wings a heavy pollen
barely discernible through the microscope,
The wasp enters the Smyrna fig at the
open end and the pollen causes the fruit to
develop rapidly and to ripen. The wasp has
three generations each year, which are pro-
duced in three successive crops of the wild
fig, known as the winter, spring and sum-
mer crops. The wasps emerging from the
spring crops fertilize the Smyrna figs


This seasons California fig crop is we'll
over $500,OO0. and If the young trees now
growing bear we'll the ensuing annual crop
Will amount to several times that sum.

after II o'clock New Year night. The diff
ferent operators took turns at the San
Francisco instrument for nineteen consecu-
tive hours yesterday. When the cable was
given over to the contractors last night to
test its qualities and Instruments no less
than 5000 words had passed between San
Francisco and Honoluln Every word so
far sent has been without pay About 500
congratulatory messages went through,
averaging ten words to the message These
We're from the public officials of Hawaii
and the public bodies of the islands from
the different governors of the coast states,
from various chambers of commerce and
boards of trade of the Pacific SLOPE from
several large commercial houses and from
private individuals at both ends of the
wire.


Today and tomorrow the cable will be
open for complimentary MESA ges to pass.

opened for paid messages.

IT EENEY PEARL was the daughter
Of fisherman. Her father lived


in boathouse on the shores OF
the great Missouri River, where It
flowed swiftly by the earth-waIled foun-
dations OF a populous Western town.


Behind Teeney's small frame house
rose the high clay banks, with only here
and there sloping path rising to the
top To the front. and facing the great
level plains which stretched away into
the West, rolled the river. Piles held
the boathouse several feet in the air
above the level OF the waters.


Teeney's little playground beneath the
boat. and in its shadow on the beach
during the afternoon when the sun had
melted the snow and warmed the earth.
was stocked with the simple treasures
that the moving tide had cast upon the
shore.


Teeney's father was Industrious.
Every night he rowed far out into the
river and cast his weighted lines into
the water. Early IN the morning Teeney
stood On the bank and watched him
draw them in and remove the cruel
hooks from the fishes before they were
taken to the market IN the city. IdIing
along the shores and standing by the
side OF the deep places the little girl
gradually came 10 know the playground
OF the f1nny creatures that had their
home in the waters.


Around a little bend not far from her
boathouse home Teeney one day discov-
cred a great catfish IN the bottom OF a
deep pool. II was a cool. shady spot.
and the big fish lay on the bottom when
the day was hot, and Teeney could see
IL move its fms and roll It's long tail
about


At first she was greatly pleased at her
discovery. She thought she would run
and tell her father about the fish. 1t
was much bigger and longer than any
she had ever seen him draw from the
river. But the big fish looked so peace
full and innocent that she resolved to let
IL alone. This determination became
fixed when one day she saw several lit
tie fish swim and circle around the big
fish.


Teeney concluded that they were its
children and that the pool was their
home. She said TO herself:


II Will let the poor fishes live IN their
home down deep In the water"


Every day she carried bread to the
pool and dropped II into the water, and
she laughed with glee as she watched
the big fish bite II and all the little
ones swim around after the crumbs. By
and by the big fish began to watch for
the little girl, and IL would rise TO the
surface 10 take its dinner OF bread from
her hand. Many hours were spent by
lonely Teeney with her strange compan-
ion OF the deep


One morning Teeney's father said he
would take his lines and fish in the pools
along the shore Her heart filled with
dread for the fate of her friend. While
her father was preparing for bis ex-
cursion she ran 10 the pool and hurled
stones into it. The big fish rose TO the
surface and looked az the little girl Its
eyes seemed to wear an expression OF
grief. Teeney shouted:


go away from here. you big nsh. Ny
father is coming 10 catch you on his
hook"


The fish sank from sight and Teeney
went back to her home and watched IN
trembling while her father cast the al
Turing bait into the water. After time
the fisherman gave up and went on TO
another pool. saying as he went that
he did not believe there were any fish
IN that part OF the river.

the hosiery mills in the Kensington district
and one of the Southwark mills resumed
operations today on the old scale of hours
and wages.

however. and the strike leaders and the
officers of the various unions actively iden-

more than 500 of the textile plants in this
city, claim that those who returned to
work today were non-union hands and wo-
men. 4

Officers of the Central Textile Union and
of the executive committee of the strikers
declared today that they do not attach any
Importance to the fact that the hosiery
mills resumed operations. The strike lead
ers had no control over the hosiery work.
ers and do not think that their return to

With this month the snail trade closes

The United States cruiser New York,

class trim for any duty occasion may
require her to perform, sailed yester
day for Panama, where she VIII be
used by Rear Admiral Henry Glass as
his flagship. The final preparations for
sea kept all hands busy during the
early morning and forenoon and steam
cutters and pulling boats loaded with
stores kept UP for several hours an
animated procession between the Clay
street boat landing and the cruiser
BY noon, however. the last of the stores
were on board, boats were hoisted and
secured, the anchor hove short and the
cruiser was ready for sea. She got un-
der way little later and at o'clock
passed out through the Golden Gate


The gunboat Bennington came down
from the navy yard early yesterday
morning and is anchored off Folsom
street, awaiting the arrival from the
East of some belated officers who have
been ordered to join her for The voyage
to the isthmus. 1t is expected that
she will be able to get away to-day.
The Bennington will convoy the tor
pedo-boat destroyers Preble. and Paul
Jones, which are now at Mare Island
ready to start.


The gunboat and her fleet little wards
will call at San Diego, Pichilinoue and
Acapulco to replenish the small boats
coal supply. Other stops may be made.
but if the weather permits the Ben
nington will supply the destroyers with
such coal as they need after leaving
Acapulco in order to save the high
price that would have to be paid at
Corinto and other Central American
ports.

New ORLEANS. March 3l.-Fuller details
OF the capture Of Puerto Cortez and San
Pedro in Honduras by the revolutionists
give some interesting stories Of the revolu-
ton there. Puerto Cortez fell on March
20. San Pedro on March 20, both through
treachery. the troops mutinying and killing
their superior officers,


The revolutionists had been working
among the garrison at Puerto Cortez and
had won over most OF the men. When
Gen Mulla, representing the Bonilla forces
appeared before the barracks with four
aides the soldiers mutinied and killed Major
De Plaza, the second In command and
the staff officer. They were cut to pieces
by the mutineers, but not before three Of
the latter had been killed


Puerto Cortez, upon hearing Of the mutiny
made a dash for the Custom House, seized
the Government money there and, pro-
tected by his son, Capt. Velava. and seventy
five soldiers who remained loyal, succeeded
in escaping with the treasure TO the Sa--
tumbla. a small gunboat, which represented
the entire Honduran Navy: battle took
place between the Satumbla and the revo-
lutionary forces. but when Jamaica negro.
who acted as gunner for the revolutonists,
put ball through the stem OF the Satumbla
the latter sailed away, carrying Comman-
dante Velava and the Honduras treasure.
She landed at Belize, British Honduras.
where the commandante put ashore.


After the departure Of the Satumbla
from Puerto Cotez the small loyal force
which remained there with Capt. Velava
engaged the revolutionists In battle, but
surrendered after losing seven killed and
large number wounded


Capt. Velava would have been murdered
by the revolutionists. as the other officers
were, had he not been rescued by the Ameri-
can marines and brought aboard the Brutus.


Senior Arias, wife of the President OF
Honduras, and her two daughters took
refuge on the American collier Brutlis when
they heard Of the mutiny and were SUBJ
sequently transferred to the United States
gunboat Marietta.


Fearing trouble in Puerto Cortez, Admiral
Coghlan landed the marines from the Olym-
pia and closed all the saloons In the town. A
Frenchman Of the name OF Lefebre pro-
tested, but the marines closed his saloon
and have kept IL closed ever since.


The American Consul at Puerto Cortez
arranged the surrender of San Pedro, which
was taken without firing a shot, but he
Commander-in-C Chief was massacred by
his former troops.


Since Admiral Coghlan's fleet arrived
Americans and their interests have been
unmolested and are respected az they have

From the Sydney (Australia) Telegraph.


The representatives Of the principal Aus
tralian papers were taken out to sea about
fifty miles from Brisbane in the pilot boat
to meet Nine Melba on September 16. She
was travelling from Canada to Australia by
the mail steamship Miowera. While the
pilot boat was waiting for the Mowera the
ships company had remarkable and prob
ably unprecedented experience A great
gray shark, about twelve feet in length, was
hooked on a schnapper line, which broke.
A second time the big fish got on the
schnapper line, and escaped. Then large
shark hook with a chain was thrown out,
and the ravenous brute grabbed it, and was
caught. All hands, pilots, cook and press
men, tugged the shark to the vessels side.
A huge hook on the anchor tackle was put
through his jaw and one eye, and the fish
the crew ripped the monster open from the
head to the tail. The vital organs and en-
trails were thrown overheard, and then
both jaws were hacked out for the sake OF
securing the teeth. Nothing but the shell
lowered overheard. A rush was made to
the side to see him sink, but the company
was astounded to see the fish make Off.
First he swan about fifty yards away, re-
turned to the steamer, then went of on
another tack for about thirty yards, came
back to the vessel and swan astern, and
was still swimming when he was lost sight
Of. That the fish could swim away with
the whole of his interior from head to tail
and the jaw and one eye gone simply raised
the hair Of the pilots and crew, who had
never seen or heard of the like before.

The circumstances of the summary dis
missal of General Dragomiroff have just
leaked out. They strikingly illustrate the
humanitarian ideas Of the Russian ruler.


Dragomiroff, who enjoyed unbounded
favor at court and was the most popular
man in the Russian Army, lost favor and
his office because he did not show modera-
ton in quelling the recent strike riots at
Kieff, which practically involved all the
working people Of the town.


Hearing that the strikers might cause a
repetition of the Kishenev scenes. Drag
omiroff called out the artillery and caused
n wholesale slaughter of the rioters. 1t is
said that several hundred Of them were
killed.


When the Car heard the fact he at once
dismissed Dragomiroff with the words:


'I cannot have that man at Kieff any
longer His hands are stained with human
blood"

The mystery surrounding the disappear
ance of Mrs. N. G. Edridge, which puzzled
the police and her friends for several
weeks, was cleared away yesterday when
the skeleton of the woman was found ly
ing in woods near Lakewood cemetery.
She had evidently been dead for several
weeks as the flesh had fallen off the
bones and the skull had been disconnected
from the trunk. Circumstances seem to
indicate that she died from exposure and
exhaustion, but the police will thoroly
investigate certain ugly rumors before the
case is dropped.


Mrs. Edridge disappeared from her
home, 2601 Thirteenth avenue S, Aug. 10,
and because her mind was unbalanced her
disappearance caused alarm. Her family
reported the matter to the police and
every effort was made to find her. The
river even was dragged.


Yesterday afternoon Oswald Shoemaker,
3434 Harriet avenue, was passing thru the
woods when he caJaea upon the skeleton.
He notified the police and Detectives
Brown and Grumpy were sent to inves-
tigate. They found the woman's hat and
shoes near the remains and in her cloth
ing was found letter from her son at
West Bend, Ind. Her wedding ring, still
on the finger, and her purse containing
slS64 were pc sitlvely identified by Mr..
Ed.idge.


The coroner and police think that the
woman died Of starvation. A mark on her
skull seems to show that she received a
blow Of some kind but a fall against a
stump near which the body was lying
would account for that.

TACOMA, Jan. s-Four days Of steady
downpour of rain following heavy SHOWS
in the mountains caused the railroads of
this State TO be covered last night and
to-day by the greatest bunch of land
slides and snowslides known in North
western railroading. There are not only
few slides but several hundred of them.
They cover the main line tracks of the
Northern Pacific and Great Northern
together with fifteen branch lines.


The only piece of railroad in Western
Washington wholly open to-day is the
Northern Pacific's fortv-niIe branch be-
tween Tacoma and Seattle. Between
Kelso and Castle Rock on the Portland
line there are twenty-five slides within
eighteen miles. Several passenger trains
are being held at Castle Rock.


Commercial travellers aboard them to-
day wired to Kelso for a steamer to come
up the Cowiltz River to Castle Rock and
take them back to the Columbia River
for Portland to spend Sunday. Both the
east and the west bound overland trains
on the Northern Pacific and Great North
ern had transferred its trains to the
Northern Pacific tracks before the latter
road was caught


Division superintendents and train
masters are out with hundreds of men
shoveling off the tracks. The main. lines
will be opened by tomorrow, and prob
ably some of the branches.


Numerous rivers are overf1owing, in
cluding Cowiltz, Chehalis, Puyallup,
Stuck, Duwamish. Sxymonish, Skagit and
Nooksack. They are carrying down large
quantities of logs and stumps. forming
bad jams in many places against railroad
and country bridges. The Cowlitz River
is only four feet below the high water
mark Of June, 1894, when the entire Co
lumbia River Valley was flooded. Many
log booms have been carried away.

Gould interests. The original plan Of

President Yoakum Of the Frisco then

Orleans and Northeastern route. 1t
was decidedly to the interest of the

minals there Without any delay the
matter was carried forward, and the
directors OF the st. Louis and San

Philadelphia, Dec. 27-The Sabbath stiffness
at the League Island Navy Yard was broken
to-day by the hurried fitting out OF the cruiser
Dixie for her trip to Colon and tonight the
vessel lies in the Delaware River ready to sail
tomorrow morning. The activity at the yard
Tesembled the busy scenes there previous to the
Spanish-American War.


Brigadier General Elliott, commanding the
marine corps. who is going to the isthmus on the
Dixie, arrived in the afternoon. Three COM
panies of marines. from Boston and the
others from Washington, also arrived. They
were marched to the barracks. and later were
sent on board the cruiser. Altogether, the Dixie
will take south 600 marines. who will be under
the command of Lieutenant Colonel Waller.


The work Of loading the cruiser continued
until midnight Saturday, and completed this
afternoon. The quantity and character of the
cargo indicate that the government expects a
long campaign at Panama Her holds and decks
are crowded to the limit with stores.


Besides the regular stores and other outfit for
the marines the Dixie will take five wagonloads
of small arms ammunition, larger quantity Of
lumber. camp supplies and number of wagons.

A group of tourists. including several
English and German visitors to Paris. have
Just had an unpleasant experience in the
historic catacombs which undermine the
older portions of the city. The party had,
as usual. entered the catacombs by the
Rue Denfert-Rochereau, and In single file
were proceeding, under the leadership of a
guide. through narrow gallery which runs
toward the Montsouris Plain.


They had been walking for about quar-
ter of an hour when an English gentleman
in the middle of the long Indian file. stop
ped to examine some human remains and
the inscriptions This halt divided the party
into two, and when the Englsman had con-
cluded his examination the latter portion
started on trot to join the leaders. But
in doing SO they took wrong turning, and
only after they had gone some distance did
they discover their error. The first portion
of the little expedition was by this time far
away. and neither the guide nor its menu
bers appear to have taken any notice of
the absence of the remainder of the party
though the guides have orders to count the
number of persons who go down into the
catacombs and the number who come out


For two hours the lost party wandered
from gallery to gallery before they at last
found an outlet. The ladies were much
frightened, and even the men say that the
experiences was not pleasant one.

Fire broke out in the after hold of the navy
yard tug Pontiac while she was carrying one
thousand pounds of black saluting powder to
the cruiser Chicago, off Tompkinsvile, yester-
day. The fire started from some unknown
cause and will be the subject of a special in
vestigation Luckily it some distance away
from the powder, which was contained IN ten
cans. holding one hundred pounds each.


When the fire was discovered the Pontiac was
nearing Tompkinsville, and Tugmaster MCGEE
ordered q full head OF steam in order that the
big fire pump of the cruiser Chicago might be
brought into action as possible


There was much excitement on the Chicago
when they read the signal flying from the swiftly
approaching tug, for it was known that she
was carrying load of powder, and it was con-
jectured that explosion might occur at any
time The officers aboard the cruiser were much
relieved when the Pontiac ran uD alongside
and reported that the fire was not near the
powder. It took only n few minutes for the
large streams of water from the Chicago to
drown out the blaze.


After transferring the powder to the cruiser
and pumping the water out of the after hold, the
Pontiac returned to the yard. Tugmaster MCGEE
reported that he unable to explain the
origin of the blaze. The Pontiac is almost con-
stantly in use carrying ammunition between the
naval magazine at Iona Island, the navy yard
and the ships, and the precautions against fire
are exceptionally thorough.

REPUBLIC SPECIAL,


Springfield, ILL.,, Aug. 29.-Eight hundred
soldiers from Central Illinois, who compose
the Fifth Infantry, entered Camp Lincoln
this morning under command of Colonel
Culver Of Springfield. Every feature of the
weeks encampment of the Fifth will be
held before Tuesday, as Governor Yates
leaves the capital on that day. The Cover
nor's Day ceremonies will be held in the
reservation Monday afternoon. and that
evening the officers of the command Will
be guests of Governor and Mrs. Yates in
the Executive Mansion The customary
banquet to the Governor will be abandoned
this week and social life will drag in camp.


New suits for the Fifth are not available,
and the regiment will wear shabby gar
nents in comparison to the new dress uni
forms donned by the preceding regiments at
the post. Colonel Culver forbade his Hos
ptal Corps occupying the permanent hos
pital building which was built at the res
ervation this summer. and the red cross at
taches are caring for their patients in
tents The Colonies of the seven regiments
which have occupied the camp this summer
have declined to use the brick building, and
militiamen say the hospital is nuisance.


Training OF the candidates for positions
on the State rifle team will begin on the
Lincoln range next Monday under direction
of Captain Benjamin Eick who Will cap
tain the State team in Its defense of the
Washburn trophy in Minnesota next month.
More than sixty candidates, all of whom
wear the silver cross ornament. VIII take
part In the preliminary contests.

Helena, Mont, July 10.-Running Deer,

in the Helena Jail, where she will remain
until the United Staets grand jury in
quireS into her case. She is charged with
the murder Of Kills Twice, a Crow
woman, with whom she lived for many
years at the Pine Ridge agency. She
had a niece, Kills Twice. on the Crow
reservation, and visited and remained
with her for a time.


The old woman was an object OF char
ity, and some Of her new-found friends
arranged benefit dance in her behalf,
and from the proceeds of the dance a
team of horses and a wagon were pur-
chased. The husband of Kills Twice
took care Of the property for the old
woman.


Running Deer finally became possessed
with the idea that her friends had stolen
her team and. Selling a long knife she
plunged it into the stomach Of the young
er woman. At the same time she slashed
another squaw, seriously injuring her.
The bucks We're In another hut and they
ran out. Kills Twice. after being stabbed,
knocked the old woman down with a
club.


A physician was sent for and did all
possible for the wounded woman. but
she died the following day. Running
Deer was placed under arrest and held In
in confinement at the Grow Indian
agency, where she had a preliminary
hearing before United States Commits
sioner Miller, and was bound over to
await the action of the grand jury, and
brought here yesterday for trial.

last mile was pulled in poor form.

this year as it was rowed at a higher
stroke, and the boat spaced well all the
distance. Jordan, who was out Of the
boat Thursday, was not in yesterday and

not feeling well, but was expected to be
in the boat again to-day for the last row
before the crew left for the east. Cap
tain Hetzel of the freshmen boat was also
i'll, and Bodenbach took his place at No. 5.

and this afternoon loaded the boats for
shipment At o'clock they will leave

Glenwood, Mo-, June 5.-Professor Leon
ard NJ. Thompson and his bride Of Lancas-
ter, Mo-, began their bridal tour on n hand
car.


After the ceremony was performed at the
home of the bride. who was Miss Mary r.
Grist, the happy couple started for the de-
pot. Not until they reached the station
did they learn that the night train on the
Keokuk and Western had been abandoned,
owing to the foods. While they were trying
to solve the dilemma. Section Foreman
Charles Daniels of Lancaster sought to
help them out by offering his handcar and
crew. little thinking the bride would hazard
the trip.


Mrs. Thompson. however. leaped at the
suggestion and seemed delighted at the
thought of the innovation. The sky was
overcast with sullen rain clouds. but the
bride was plucky and declared her travelling
suit would weather any storm.


While arrangements were being made for
the trip the word went round the village
and soon big crowd came down to witness
the novel trip. Trunks. of course. had to
be left behind. A few valises were hastily
packed. and the couple set out on the
handcar while their friends cheered wildly
and a band. which had been brought down
to the station. played wedding march.
before midnight, when they caught the
southbound train on the Wabash.


Professor Thompson was principal of the
High School here last year. Mrs. Thomp-
son Is the daughter of George Grist. a WE'LL
known contractor.

road for Trenton, N. j., where they will
serve time in the penitentiary for offenses
committed in this city. 1t has been several
years since District prisoners have been
sent to Trenton, and those who went there
today are the first prisoners sent away since
the authorities decided not to send any
more convicts to Moundsville. Most of
those in the party today expressed them
selves as being sorry that they had not
been sentenced to the West Virginia prison.
At the latter the superintendent has done
away with everything within reason that
will remind the convicts of prison life.
There the lockstep. which prisoners always
regarded as Objectionable, is a thing of the
past, and prisoners are permitted to con-
verse more than they are at most prisons.
In the workshops the men are treated with
consideration, and while on their way
to meals they are permitted to engage in
conversation. Then, too, they are permitted
to visit the library and have reading ma
terial in their rooms. 1t Is said they are
permitted more freedom in Moundsville
than is permitted in any other institution
of its kind In the United States.


The Prisoners and Their Crimes.


Warden Harris arranged yesterday for
the transportation of the prisoners from the
Jail to the train, but by some oversight the
van was late In reaching the prison and
the trip came near having to be postponed.


1t was just about train time when the
fifteen prisoners chained together reached
the station. Leading the party were
Charles Thorn and Robert E. Fennel two
Of the five white prisoners who composed
the party. The former will serve twelve
years for the killing Of his wife, while the
latter will gain his freedom after he has
served a sentence of six years for false
pretenses. Alexander Macgill and James
Reilly, who will spend three years at Tren-
ton for dishonesty, came next E. A. Lei
field who robbed Schmedtie Brothers jew
elTy store, where he was employed brought
up the rear of the white contingent. His
walking companion was a colored prisoner.
Leifield will spend thirty months in the
prison.


The colored prisoners who composed the
party, and the offenses of which they were
convicted, were: Daniel Johnson, assault
with dangerous weapon, two years; James
Quarles, assault with dangerous weapon,
three years; Isaac Laws, rape, twenty
years; George Grimes, housebreaking one
and one-half years; George Corson assault
to kill, eight years; William Ferguson, lar

HAMILTON. Mont, October 14.-Walter
Jackson, the. convicted murderer of Fon
ME Buck, a six-year-old boy was taken
from the county Jail here late last night
by a mob and lynched.


Shortly before midnight seventy-five
masked men, all armed with rifles or shot
guns forced their way through the rear
of the jail and overpowered Jailer Ste
phens. who was able to offer but slight re-
sfstance. Jackson was found cringing in
the darkest portion of his cell. He pleaded
piteously for mercy, but was rushed out
into the street, where the mob had already
provided themselves with a rope This
was quickly thrown over an electric light
pole and the moose placed about Jackson's
neck. He was asked if he had anything to
say, but only pleaded for mercy. The mob
then pulled him into the air, after which
they quietly dispersed. Not shot was
fired.


The identity of the mob leaders is un-
known Thirty-fve minutes after the
lynching Jackson's body was cut down by
the sheriff and coroner and removed to the
morgue.


The murder of little Fonnie Buck was a
peculiarly atrocious crime When the boys
body was found it was horribly mutilated.
Suspicion pointed to Jackson, and when he
was arrested a lynching was narrowly
averted. His trial quickly followed, and
verdict was returned within two hours. He
was sentenced to be hanged, but his attor
neys appealed to the supreme court.

Two little hazel eyes
Five years ago


First saw this strange land
Where the roses grow.
Laughing, liquid, bright eyes,
Fairer than day:
Vying with the silver stars,
Radiant as May.
Dimpled ere the clasped hands,
Falls the flowing hair,
Kneeling at her bedside,
At her evening prayer.
Ev'ry morning early,
Standing on the STAIR
Fresh as the freshest May dawn,
Stands my cherub there.
Patter. patter, sound the feet
On the kitchen floor
Little chubby 'Chin-chin''
Standing at the door.
Fair as the rivers CLEAN
In the breezy morn,
Fresh as the footsteps Of the wind
On the tasseled corn.
Like the gold unfolding
On the leafy throng,
When from every spray-branch
Comes the soul Of song.
Gladdest of the glad joys
Song has ever told,
Beams the love in Maud's eyes
Just five years old.

A Brooklyn elevated train on the Fifth

Flatbush avenue station and the terminal


A coupling broke as the train was pulling
out Of the Flatbush avenue station and the
train parted in the middle. The first half
went ahead three or four blocks before the
motorman got word to hold up. A motor
car in the abandoned half Of the train was
put into commission after ten-minute
delay and dragged the cars along to the
first section. The coupling broke again
at the Fulton street station, and the first
performance was repeated.


The train broke in two once moro just
before reaching the curve between the
Fulton and Bridge street stations. The
first half went of on its own hook then, and
the tail end crept around the curve under
it's own power and hooked onto an over
loaded train from East New York.


But that didn't bring any luck. The
coupling parted twice more, and then tho
East New York train deserted the hoodoo
section, which finished the trip with its
own power.

At first she could do nothing but Iool,

Large and beautiful trees grew about and

thing was fresh and green and vines
twined everywhere. Under one. of the

small seat with tall ferns arching over it


Amy had scarcely noticed these things

Professor Walter z. Magee, director Of

burglars this morning at his residence,
1870 Haste street. He did not get near
enough to grapple with them or take any
chances with his own life, but he stood
by with big pistol and sent the burglars
into flight with stentorian words Of COM
mand.


Professor Magee was awakened at the
very darkest hour this morning by a
noise in the yard just beneath his win
dow. Securing his pistol, he hurried to
the window and looked down upon two
men sitting on the fence. The fence was
near kitchen window and it was evident
the fellows were about to force their way
into the house. But they didn't get that
far for just then Professor Magee leveled
his pistol at them and called upon them
10 explain their presence. The men re-
piled that they had got into the wrong
place by mistake and without any unnec-
essary waste Of time skunk off into the
gloom.


The would-be burglars are supposed to
be the same who have been robbing resi-
dences and business houses around town
lately.

Tlmut for the Federal capital. The New
South Wales members wanted Lyndhurst,

Bombala and Tumut.

LONDON, Dec. H. Political conditions and
religious feuds have hitherto induced the
British Government not to allow the ex-
tension { o Ireland OF the volunteer system,
which has for many years been established
in England and Scotland.


The matter has been often agitated In
the press and in Parliament, but although
the militia has been enrolled for long
time and, like the Irish regulars, proved
among the bravest and most valuable of
Great Britain's troops, successive govern
ments at London would not sanction a
home defence force for Ireland.


The papers this morning state that the
introduction Of the system to Ireland has
been decided upon. Twenty-six battalions
try. Their formation will be provided for
in the forthcoming programme OF army
reform prepared by Mr. ArnoldForster, +,
Secretary of State for War.


The last volunteer force in Ireland was
raised by the great landowners more than
a hundred years ago. when there were fears
Of a French invasion. The British Govern
ment did not support the movement. and
the Viceroy OF Ireland was greatly dis
mayed, although all the volunteers were
Protestants.


The present sanction can be traced to the
splendid services Of the Irish regiments in
South Africa and the improved political
relations.

From the Maryland Medical Journal.


Does sanitation pay? The very best an
swer to this question that can possibly be
given consists Of an unvarntshed citation of
the object lesson afforded by Havana under
American military administration. When
the United States army pushed the shiftless,
thriftless and dirty Spaniards off the island
tumbled them in any old tubs that could
be hired to float them back to their benight-
ed. back-numbered country, they found
city that had practically been a fruitful
focus for the dissemination Of all the infec-
tious diseases that are fostered by tropic
heat in conjunction with human negligence
and want of hygienic decency. There were
no efficient sewers; sewerage ran IN open
the ground throughout the city. Yellow
fever and smallpox were annually epidemic
and the death rate exceeded 5000 every
year


The first step of the army officers on TAX
ing possession was to establish a system of
municipal sanitation. The natives were
harnessed for the work and under compul-
sion and proper supervision soon revolution
lied the situation. Sewers were construct
ed, streets and cesspoolS were cleaned, the
latter being abolished, the water supply was
looked after and, lastly, the perennial crop
of disease-bearing mosquitoes were attacked
right and left-and what is the result? Ma
larial diseases have become much more rare
known in the region; there has not been a
case OF smallpox for more than a year and
half, and yellow fever has been practical
ly abolished.

Boston, Sept. 10.-The fishing schooner
Actor sailed into port yesterday in a badly
leaking condition, the result of an en-
counter with a mammoth sword fish off
the Georges banks.


The big fish met the schooner with ter
rife force in a head-on collision. The
force of the impact shook the schooner
from stem to stern, and at first the crew
thought the vessel had struck a half
sunken wreckage. Shortly afterward the
vessel began to leak. An examination was
made and under the starboard bow about
two feet under the water line there was
found the sword of a. gigantic sword fish.
Further examination showed that the big
sword had penetrated thru the hull of the
vessel, extending several inches within the
hole The vessel was headed for Boston,
and during the voyage it was necessary to
keep the pumps working large part OF
the time,

The residents of Francis street southeast
were aroused from their sumbers about 2
O. clock this morning by a woman's voice
calling for help. By the time number of
the householders reached their front WIN
dows they saw a woman run out Of No.
16O, followed by man, but the calls for
help still continued to come from a room on
the second floor of the house. The man,
after reaching the street, did not follow the
woman, but hurried away in another di-
rection.


In the meantime Policemen Delaney and
Payne, who had been attracted by the
noise arrived on the scene, and, entering
the house. they found Ella Grant. colored,
lying on a bed in room on the second
floor, bleeding from number OF stab
wounds. which she said her husband had
inflicted with knife.


Five Stab Wounds.


The patrol wagon from the fifth precinct
was summoned and the woman was hur-
ried to the Casualty Hospital, where the
physicians found five stab wounds in the
neck back and arms none Of which, how
ever, reached vital spots.


The officers after sending the injured
woman to the hospital. obtained descrip-
ton of Robert L. Grant, the woman's hus-
band and then began search in the i'm
mediate neighborhood for him. Returning
to the house, they saw him entering the
front door.


He was taken into custody and escorted
to the station house. where charge OF as
saulting his wife with dangerous weapon
was preferred against him.


The woman was able to leave the hos
pital this morning, and later in the day she
appeared against her husband when he was
arraigned in the Police Court before Judge
Kimball.


Husband Held for Grand Jury.


She told the court that she gave her hus-
band dollar bill yesterday afternoon, and
he went out and remained until about mid
night, when he returned and threw himself
across the bed with his shoes on. She said
she removed his shoes, and when he awoke
about O'Clock this morning he became
angry with her and threatened to kill her,
and then attacked her with a penknife.


Her cries for help. she said. attracted the
attention of Edith Evans who resides at
the house, and when the latter entered the
room Grant chased her to the street.


The defendant was not permitted to make
a statement and was held under 81 900 real
estate security to await action by the
grand jury.

Some time ago there was a wonderful
story in the European journals about GER
tain grains of ancient Egyptian corn which
had been planted in Germany and had come
to life.

an Egyptian sarcophagus and had been
planted by a Dresden florist Some days

not suppose that there was any life in
grains which were from 1000 to 5000 years
old. The corn. however. was certainly
growing, and even the most incredulous
among them soon became convinced that
grains have lease of life to which there
is practically no limit


Alas! A boy employed by the Dresden
florist has now confessed that he planted
some other grains in the same place where
his master had planted the Egyptian ones
and only few hours after the florist COM
pIeted his work This was sad news for the
scientists and for the numerous Journalists
who had written enthusiastically about the
miraculous qualities of the ancient grains

ROME. August 2S.-A disastrous railway
accident has cut short the festivities and
demonstrations In honor of the king and
queen at Udine. the chief town on the east
ern frontier. sixty miles from Venice, where
the sovereigns had gone to view the grand
army maneuvers.


At 10 o'clock last night, near Udine. a
train overlooking with soldiers collided
with freight train. The force of the col
lisbon was terrific. Those on board were
thrown in all directions and the coaches
were broken up.


Sixteen Killed; Sixty Injured.


Fifteen soldiers and one captain were
killed and over sixty injured. twelve dan
gerously so. The colonel in command of
the soldiers was among the injured.


Darkness rendered the confusion about
the scene of the wreck extreme, while the
terror among those who escaped injury was
increased when the trains took fire a few
minutes after the collision. Fortunately
the flames were Immediately extinguished.


Special Trains fastened.


Special trains were sent hurriedly to the
scene of the disaster. carrying the authori-
ties from the nearest town. who organized
a corps of physicians and ministered to the
wounded


King Victor Emmanuel visited the hos
pital In person later to see lue victims of
the accident.

pairing the Oregon Railroad and Nav

The Greeks were brought here a
short time ago by the corporation and

more than a mile into town. Durin.,
the chase nineteen shots were fired at

to Portland is So.

Here hands now cold have reared a shrine
Where weary frame and throbbing brain
May rest mid garnered sheaves divine
And find a brief surcease from pain.
And cares and penury and toll,
The mills loud whirr and sitting air,
The din the smoke, the dust, the soil
Which vex the workers everywhere.
Meath spells OF the poetic muse,


Or Hers whose stored pages give
The glamour which the Past
And bids vanished Britain live;
Or those which weave for girl and boy
Bright dreams of Life, too fair for truth;
The glow, the flush, the new born joy,
The innocent fantasies of youth;
Or Science with her precious store


Which made and keeps our England great,
Or maxims sage of civic lore


Which bind the Freeman and the State.
Free without price for all who come,
Here new precious mines Of gold
For thoughtful rest denied at home.

WEYMOUTH, England. April 13.-The
Shamrock rs spinnaker boom, which was
carried away by steam yacht which
fouled the old cup challenger during the
race with the Shamrock III off here Satur-
day, has been spliced, but 1t has been de-
cided to postpone further contests under
actual racing conditions between the two
boats until a new spar can be fitted.


A trial spin between the Shamrocks was
arranged for today. but their departure
was delayed while awaiting the moderation
of hard northerly wind.


Most of the forenoon was occupied with
altering the challenger's mainsail which
had stretched considerably.


The two yachts left their anchorage at
about II o'clock this morning. and fetched
out to start a trial race, but the wind,
even inside the breakwater, was harder
and more squally than anything the chal-
lenger had previously experienced. The
boats staggered under their low canvas
alone. Outside the breakwater the condI-
tions were worse, and after a consultation
it was decided to abandon the trial owing

Manila, June 9.-The Philippines Commission
has enacted bill providing for the government
of the Moros. Governor Taft and Major General
Davis Jointly drafted it. The measure prac-
tically makes the Moro Province an autonomous
colony of the Philippines which the Philippine
government closely controls, and creates an ap-
poiltive legislative council to provide local
laws the commission reservtng the right 10
amend or annul them. The council is to be
composed of a governor, secretary. treasurer
engineer attorney and superintendent of schools
Governor Taft will appoint the officials.


The bill will extend the jurisdiction or the
Philippine courts and constabulary to the prov
ince and will recognize Moro laws which do not
conflict with American laws. The measure also
directs the codiicatfon of the tribal laws. ere
ates Moro courts provides that the Philippine
courts Shall try cases between Moros and Chris
tians gives to the province its net customs ana
forestry collections and authorizes the council
to abolish slavery. The province is divided into
five districts-Suu Zamboanga, Lanao, Gotta
bato and Davao


The bill provides for partial military govern
nent and it is thought that General Leonard
Wood may be the first Governor of the Moro
Province

Underwater, Va, September 1.-THE
Smithsonian airship experts were busy
again today with repairs on Prof. Langley 8
flying machine. The accident Wednesday,
when the starboard propeller was wreck
ed, is proving a serious set back to the
plans for a launching. But for that the
machine would probably have been sent off
this morning, as the weather conditions
were good.

morning and were kept actively employed
throughout the day. 1t cannot be said
when the repairs will be finished, but they
will not be delayed any longer than is nee
essary, and with their completion the
launching will be made, providing the ele-
ments permit. Prof Langley has not yet
returned to the houseboat from Washing
ton.

His first greeting that morning had

Of dawn; the grace of spring-tide.
Overhead sang lark; at their feet a
brook whispered; around them .soli-
tude, vast, infinite. He spoke and she
answered.; her reserve became infec-
tious; they ate their oaten cakes and
drank their wine, each strongly con-
scious of the presence of the other.
Then he rose, saddled their horses and
assisted her to mount. She appeared
over-anxious to leave the shepherds
hut; the jester, on the other hand, cast
a backward glance at the poplar, the
hovel, the brook. A crisp, clear CAROL
ing Of birds followed them as they
turned from the lonely spot.

a rustic bridge which spanned a
stream. Both were silent regarding

low mud from Its bed. From the cool
shadows beneath the p1anks where she

text:
BERLIN, December 3.-Chancellor Won
Buelow, as the emperor's representative.
opened the reichstag in the white hall of
the palace today.


The members of the reichstag, in evening
dress, court costume, military uniforms or
clerical coats, stood close together in front
OF the empty throne and did not occupy
much space in the great marble room.


The assemblage was smaller than on the
last occasion, twenty-five of the loyalists
having been turned out by the socialists,
not one of whom ever attends the opening
or the reichstag, which is essentially a
court function, all the members present
wearing royal order.


Company Kept Waiting.


Both the Protestant and Catholic menu
bers were late, each of these bodies had
been detained by services In their respective
churches. The chancellor also kept the
company waiting.


When he appeared with the cabinet min
listers walking two by two behind him, all
present bowed Won Buelow stood on the
left of the throne and read the emperors
message to parliament He said:


His majesty has directed me to express
here his thanks to all those who have sym
pathlZed with his sufferings, and to say
that their sympathy and hopes for his re-
covery have greatly rejoiced him.


Discussed Finance.


The chancellor then passed to the eco
nomic state of the country. which. he said,
still suffered somewhat from the world wide
depression which was unfavorably affecting
the imperial finances.


Emphasizing the ever-increasing necessity
for regulating the financial relations of the
empire with the separate states, the chan
cellor remarked that although a radical set
tlement of the question was not now feast
BILE the government would propose meas
ure introducing the most essential reforms
The government, continued the chancel-
lor, would propose retaining the present
amy footing to April 70, 1905, but it de-
sired to increase the salary list because OF
the growing cost of living.


Social Legislation.


The government further proposes to con-
tinue the development of social legislation
in the interests of the weaker classes. The
Dar-es-Salam- Mrosoro German East Af-
rfca) railroad bill would be reintroduced.
The government also intended prolonging
the present most favored relations with
Great Britain.


The chancellor supplied no informa ton re-
gaTding the progress of the commercial ne
gotiations with other countries.


In congratulating the nembers of the
reichstag on the very friendly relations OF
Germany with all countries, the chancellor
said the imperial government had con-
tributed Its share to the avoidance of serf-
Gus complications in the Balkans.


Hopes Peace May Continue.


He referred to Emperor Williams meet
ings with the great continental rulers, and
to the interchange of views connected
herewith, which had strengthened anew
their desire and hope that peace the great
est boon of the nations, shall continue to
be guarded from dangerous disturbances"
Chancellor Won Buelow then nodded to
DR.. Victor Rintelen, the Oldest member
present, who, stepping forward, proposed
three cheers for the emperor, in which the
few spectators present joined.


The message was favorably commented
upon, emphasis being placed on the fact
that the government had not made any
unusual demands on the taxpayers.


Members Felt Easier.


Although it was announced some time
ago that the government would not de-
nland a large increase for military pur-
poses the members of the reichstag felt
easier after the authoritative declaration
from the throne.


Satisfaction was also expressed at the
fac that the government did not propose
to introduce controversial legislation, SO
that the commercial treaties can be freely
and fully discussed.


After luncheon the members reassembled
In the reichstag TO. the preliminaries OF
organization. All the socialists were then
present

BAR HARBoR, Me-. Aug. 2.-The war
game Of the United States Navy will begin
at sunrise tomorrow morning. and for a
month the enemy" specially prepared
for the manPuvres of the North Atlantic

against the New England coast. The
squadron which will attack the United
States will be under the command OF Rear
Admiral Sands. and it is said here to-day
that his feet will consist of the battleships
Indiana, Massachusetts, and Texas and
three torpedo boat destroyers,


The enemy will have start until Wednes-
day noon and then the defending feet under
to begin the search problem. Admiral
Sands and his feet will try to make land
ing and establish foothold. If they are in
any port for five hours without being dis
covered they will win the victory. IL they
fail the victory will go to the defenders.


Admiral Barker will have his choice OF
the remaining ships and he will probably
take all Of the vessels except those which
have masts.


He will have with him in his feet Rear
Admirals Wise and Coghlan. The command
ing Admiral moved his flag from the Illinois
to the Kearsarge yesterday, and the pride
Of the navy will be the flagship of the fleet
upon which rests the safety Of the coast.

headquarters here at O'Clock tonight
One of the local police force arrested a

able difficulty. There the sailors renewed

volvers. The officers. however. soon de-
cided that discretion was the better part OF
valor and released their prisoner

The extension of the electric railway for interurban
and rural service has produced advantages, of rela

closer to the city and the city is to the woods,

One of the results of rural railway extension is,

frequented the big free recreation place may now be
seen among the hills, in the groves, along the fishing

ban amusement resorts at the termini of electric rail-

are maintained prefer, when they spend care fare
BIZ adieu for the day TO the of work and enjoy
both nature and entertainment.


Conditions multiply to popularize and necessitate
the establishment of small parks in large cities
In the future millions Of dollars will be expended for
small parks against thousands for large parks.
Large parks are, principally, for the wealthy class
while small parks are, owing to their number and To-
cation, for those who need resting places and play
grounds in their immediate environment The small
park is a necessity, the large park luxury


Forest Park, comprising 1872 acres, Carondelet

the divisions sold and the great sum derived there

improving the educational system


Notwithstanding that large parks fail to afford all
OF the conveniences desired expected they are by
common WISH essential features of metropolitan life
Besides being beauty spots for the city, they nculcate
civic pride and stimulate interest in elaborate park
systems. Without them big city would be nearly
as inviting TO the visitor nearly interesting to
tho resident citizen. Without them city would lack
In hne residence districts and there would be less RI
valry in insisting upon the highest type of archtec
ture in mansions and residences.


What the large park does for the rich and for the
whole city indirectly, the small park does for the
poorer people and the middle class, but in greater
degree The small park is useful to the point of neces
sity. Its utlitnriah and moral advantages many
and they constitute the necessity for small parks But
it has also aesthetic virtues that not be over
looked If municipality establishes small parks and
maintains them properly, they will surely develop the
surroundings and ultimately make better and happier
homes The small park is the desderatum of the

which marked the year 1901, and which was
noted in our review OF the situation q year

very small factor in the years business.
Manufacturers have bought woods freely be-

been able to get higher prices for goods and

pronounced especially, in the last three
months of 1902; in fact. there has been a
larger advance in the price of wool this

brought about by natural conditions being

demand.

prices over a year ago. At no time since

of the steamer Maine, which arrived today
from New York.

she went down and her boats were put
overheard to assist boats from the Whit

Booth.

ships and her side crushed in. Being
granite laden, she settled quickly and sank
before the boats could get near her.

captain of the Booth, and one of the
Names boats rescued a sailor named Has
sell, who had jumped from the schooner
and was swimming.

about for nearly an hour, searchlights being
used over the water. e

Hassell says he was one of the deck
watch with the captain at the wheel. The
weather was fairly clear. but the collision.
he says, was entirely unexpected. He be-
heves the lookout was killed when the
steamer crashed into the Booth

From the counties Of the Minnesota valley

Special Cable Despatch to THE SUN.


LONDON, Nov. 17.-Mr. BirchenouRh,
the special commissioner who was sent by
the Government to investigate the position
and prospects of British trade in South
Africa has submitted rosy report.


He says that, excluding war stores. the
imports have increased $50 per cent. in
ten years, the greatest increase by far
being during the past two years.


South Africa is already the second largest
of Great Britains customers. MIR. Birch
enough predicts that the trade with South
Africa will pass that with India during the
current year, and will become the largest


The most serious competitors with British
trade are the United States, Germany.
Belgium and Switzerland. The American
rivalry is concentrated in certain defined
branches, especially agricultural. mining
and electrical machinery. appliances. tools
fencing wire, furniture and other wooden
articles.


This competition s materially aided by
low freights, for which competing British
steamships carry American cargoes from
New York to South Africa. compared with
the freight rates from Great Britain to
South Africa.


Among other causes Of American success
is the presence at the mines OF American
engineers, who favor American machinery,
the superiority Of the American descriptive
catalogues, and the accessibility and bon
homie of the American agents, compared
with the reserve of the British agents.


MIR. Birchenough discusses the compara-
tive merits of the rivals Of the British de-
ducing various facts which show that while
the German and other European compete
ton needs to be watched it is only the
American competition that need really
cause fear.

Asotin, Wash Aug 5.-Despite the efforts of
Sheriff Richards. of Asotin County, father of
the victim who had sworn in twenty-five depu-
ties to guard William Hamilton. a well-to-do
farmer, the self-confessed murderer of Mabel
Richards, Hamilton was taken from the Asotin
County Jail shortly after midnight last night
and lynched by a mob of more than one thou
sand men, who had been congregating all yes
terday from all parts Of the county.


Shortly after l. o'clock a band Of men, with
their faces concealed by. handkerchefs, marched
up the street TO the county jail The officers and
guards were swept aside, the keys taken
from the jailer, and the mob passed into the
Jail. When the cell containing the guilty man
was reached. no key could be found TO fit the
lock. and the door was sawed and hacked open
After about fifteen minutes delay Hamilton was
dragged out OF the cell and down to the yard.


Meanwhile another company of masked men
had marched up the street and taken position
opposite the jail. They kept back the crowd,
which had filled the streets all night waiting for
the lynching. for the entire population OF the
town had turned out and their numbers had
been swelled by people from the surrounding
country. Soon there came procession from the
Jail yard. on each side of the prisoner was
masked man holding his arm, while another
masked man held his hand over the murderers
mouth to prevent an cutlery. other members





group came forward. the men who had been
guarding the entrance to the jail formed
linked chain about captive and captors, and in
this manner they proceeded, keeping the crowd
at respectful distance.


When the lynchers reached First and Fillmore
sts- they halted under guy wire which crosses
the street and connects electric light poles. Here
Hamilton was told that he might confess, and
he did so. speaking in low tone, not audible
more than ten feet away. Afterward he asked
that his jewelry, some trifing trinkets he had
IN his possession and his watch be given to
his father and mother. and it was promised that
this would be done. There was a short wait
then while the manner of Hamilton's death was
discussed. Some of the mob thought hanging
100 good and wanted 10 torture him, but the
original programme prevailed.


A black mask. like that used in a legal hang
3ng, was produced and put over the murderers
head. The rope was placed about his neck and
the other enc thrown over the guy wire. 1t
came within grasping distance of the lynchers
and was seized by many hands. The body was
suspended at a height of about four feet and
the rope tied to one Of the light poles. As soon
2 they were satisfied that Hamilton dead
the crowd quickly melted away, and the streets
were soon deserted.

lived in Apache County for many years.

in a dispute over their respective grazing
permits on the reservation, which are only
issued at certain times in the year, and are
Of considerable value. only limited num-
Der Of cattle being allowed on the reserva-
ton.


A duel with s;x-shooters followed, in

abdomen. from which he died within few
minutes after the shooting. Coleman was
shot through both thighs and was also
badly bruised about the head by blows from

The United States Supreme Court yester-
day rendered, through Justice Harlan, an
opinion affecting the Northern Pacific rail-
road land grant. The case was that OF
Peter and Henry Nelson, who located
upon unsurveyed land within the Northern
Pacific grant, in the then territory OF
Washington, in 1881. This was after the
railroad company had filed its general map
showing its proposed line, but before 1t
had filed its map of definite location.


In the opinion handed down yesterday 1t
was held that the title of the settlers was
better than that Of the railroad company,
and that until the definite map was filed
Congress had control of the lands within
the grant regardless Of the general map.


In dissenting opinion Justice Brewer
said the opinion reverses the judgment or
the court of twenty years ago. by which
the Interior Department had ever since
been controlled in dealing with disputes be-
tween the railroad company and settlers
like the Nelson's.

Bar Harbor, Me. July 2O.-The race feeling
which exists in the navy against the colored
men has been cropping out here since the fleet
of seven United States warships arrived The
white sailors have been making it unpleasant
for the negroes. and the latter have kept aboard
most of the time rather than risk abuse in the
streets.


Last Saturday night number of them came
ashore About midnight several tackles got
into the tent which the naval branch of the
Young Mems Christian Association has erected
in the town park, and drove out the negroes who
were there for a nights lodging.


Two black sailors were knocked down in Main
st by crowd of "jackies,' and, after getting
few kicks and punches, scrambled to their feet
and ran. One negro was thrown over a board
fence into the street Another found his way
to the police station, and was locked up to keep
him away from the angry sailors who had been
chasing him. Still another rushed into drug
store, and put into the cellar to avoid the
mob. He had to make his way across yards
after he went out back door. Since Saturday
night there have been no Colored men ashore
after dark.

the jaw.

to the jaw. Cans directed his blows for the
stomach. and both men We're tired at the

Ell Paso, Tex, yesterday says: Three pas
senger trains of the Rock Island system,
which arrived here last night, were tied up
in the snow nearly one hundred hours on
the plains thirty miles from Santa Rosa,
N. M. and 500 persons on board suffered
intensely for food for twentyfour hours
before the snow ploughs and relief train
arrived


The locomotives were imbedded in drifts
fifteen feet deep. The fires Of one locomo-
tive were extinguished and the cars of that
train were without heat or light. The pas
sengers of the others were not subjected
to that discomfort, but the food supply of
all became short day before the snow
bound people were rescued


The trains were two Golden State Linn
fteds and one local. They were showed in
on Sunday and arrived here late last night.

Helena, Mont. Sept. Lee Sing, the
Chinaman arrested on Friday on a charge
of criminal assault. and William Hughes
and John Broad, arrested at the same
time and charged respectively with Grim
inal assault and procuring young girls for
immoral purposes, were arraigned before
Judge Smith in district court yesterday
afternoon and given until next Satur-
day to plead. All three were remanded
to the custody Of the sheriff.


Before the court opened the two white
prisoners laughed and chatted among
themselves and seemed not to realize the
seriousness Of their alleged offense. Lee
Sing sat apart from the other two. His
stolid face never moved and he said only
two words and those when he told Judge
Smith his name. There was no excite
ment and the law will undoubtedly be
allowed to take its course.

NEW YORK, Dec. A.-The two
mines" fire alarm, summoning more fire
apparatus than any other alarm pro-
vided for in the New York department,
was sounded tonight for a fire which
destroyed the six-story factory build
ing of the Hermann Furniture and
Plumbing Cabinet Works in Mott street
and the four-story varnish factory of
the firm, operated under the name of
the Hermann Lumber Company. A
quarter of a million dollars damage
was done.


Battalion Chief Martin Coleman per-
ished in the fall Of two great walls of
the factory, and a fireman is missing.
There was a frightful panic among the
inmates of the swarmfng front and rear
tenements opposite. and the firemen
and police reserves from three precincts
had the utmost difficulty in getting the
people out TO the street.


DEATH OF CHIEF COLEMAN.


The fire started on the third floor, and
when the flremen arrived the first, sec
ond and third floors were ablaze. The
third, fourth and fifth alarms were sent
in in rapid succession and about ar>hour
after the fire started the 1.-TWO mines"
alarm was sounded.


Battalion Chief Coleman had entered
the building with a number of men, in
Guiding Lieutenant Jones and Father
Smith. the Fire Department chaplain
They were about twenty-five feet in
side when the fire came through the
walls and the building shook The fire
men saw the danger and dashed out.
The chaplain escaped. but a beam fell
and hit Coleman and Jones, pinning
them to the floor.


Father Smith, with three firemen.
turned back to the rescue and dragged
out Jones. who managed to stagger to
his feet. Jones, in pulling himself out.
felt for Coleman He found him so
pinned he could not rescue him. but got
his helmet, which he put on and es-
capped. Within a minute the entire rear
and side walls fell


WON MEDAL FOR BRAVERY.


After the building had been totally
destroyed the body of Chief Coleman
was found wedged under fallen debris
in such position that the fremen were
unable to reach il.


Coleman was made a battalion chief
last August. He won the Bennett medal
for bravery eight years ago for rescu-
ing two women from a clearinghouse
fire in East Tenth street.


Richard Joyce, a fireman, who was
appointed only ten days ago, was re-
ported missing after the fire was extin-
guished. He was last seen in the build
ing just before the walls fell.

All night two hundred officers and citizens

brush was fred in the hope that the con-

learned that they had made their escape

Before the torch was applied the bodies

hiding. The soldiers divided, six remain
ing near the foot of the hill to block the
escape, while the others began to beat the
brush.


The latter party, led by Lieut.. Smith,
had not advanced over 200 yards when they

simultaneously a volley was fired from

southwest. near the Long Bridge, were
blocked for several hours this morning by
an accident. No one was hurt but sew
eral cars were damaged.

long freight train had just come across the
Long bridge from the south and was climb
ing the steep grade up to 10th street south
west, when the coupling holding two ca
boose cars and two freight cars, broke and
the four cars ran backward down the
grade. Fortunately they had clear track,
and they stuck to the rails until the curve
to the bridge was reached. Then they left
the tracks and running along on the ties for
short distance overturned. blocking the
approaches to the bridge. The caboose cars
and a box car were but slightly damaged,
some wood work being broken. but plat
form car loaded with timber spread it's load
across the tracks. wrecking train was at
once sent to the scene and the work of

NEW YORK, March 4.-In heavy fog
which prevailed today two trains on the
9Th avenue elevated line, Brooklyn, col
lided at the oath street Brooklyn station.
Six persons were hurt, two of them ser-
ously. No one was killed. Within few
minutes there was another collision on the
same line at Goth street. The passengers
were badly frightened, but nobody was
hurt.


The fog enveloped the city and covered
the rivers and bay, disrupting the sched-
ules Of the ferry lines and causing COLI
sions both ashore and afloat The ferry
boats Brooklyn and Montauk of the HAM
ilton avenue line collided Just as the Brook
lyn was leaving her slip on the Brooklyn
side. The passengers, who crowded the
Brooklyn, were in a panic. The impact
was severe and the boat was considerably
damaged, although able to continue her
trip to New York. The ferry boats Easton
and Bound Brook of the Central railroad
of New Jersey came together just outside
the Jersey City slip. There were two hum
dred passengers on the Easton, but they
were remarkably cool. Neither boat was
seriously damaged.

occurred at the Chambers street slip of the
Erie railroad, the McCullagh and Ruther-
ford of that line crashing There were eight
hundred passengers on the Rutherford, who
were given a momentary scare. The rail-
fngs Of both boats were carried away but
nobody was injured.

No wonder the oriole and meadow lark
were so busy, twittering and chrping, after
all the other birds were fast asleep.


Dame Natures youngest child, little
Baby Blue Eyes," was to be christened
the next morning at sunrise in the Fairies
Chapel by Jack-in-the-Pulpi


The fairies, the birds and all the flowers
were hidden to the ceremony, and the
meadow lark and oriole had been chosen to
compose and sing the christening hymn.


Morning dawned the sun awoke, yawned
and began to rise.


At the same moment the blue bells in
the Fairies Chapel rang out Sweetly on the
clear morning air, and two by two the
christening party started from the hedge
The Primrose" walked very soberly and
sedately, of course. for she was chaperon-
ing Miss "Larkspur," who was inclined to
be frivolous; the .Maidenhair'' leaned CO.
quettishly toward Mr.. Marigold;" she had
grown worldly from attending SO many
fashionable weddings, and wished a rich
husband, though the gentle Quaker ladies'
told her she might do better than Mari
gold.


After the flowers came the Fairy Queen
and her court, and then every eye was
turned toward Dame Nature, who came
last with the dainty Baby Blue Eyes nes-
tied tenderly in her arms.
Lily-of-the-Valley carried the baptismal
CIldIIce HlleQ Win GeW, ana when Jack-ln-
the-Pulpit asked the baby's name the wee
howerkin's godmamma bent over her and
softly murmured "Forget-Me-Not."


A bevy of "Wold Roses" Scarlet Sages,"
"Nasturtiums' and "Hollyhocks'' pressed
eagerly forward at that moment, to show
their fine clothes I'm afraid. but the ten
der-eyed Pansies," always full of thought,
waved them back and beckoned to the
oriole and meadow lark to commence.
The aeoian harps in the windows of an
old-fashioned homestead played a soft pre-
lude, and this is what the birds sang:
Spring. spring. spring. spring!
All the birds your praises sing,
For to them today you bring


Baby-blue-eyes," dainty thing!
Fom her bed OF eoft green grass
Wakes and smiles on all who pass;
Pass, pass, pass pass!


Mother Nature blue-eyed lass.
Sweet, sweet, sweet. sweet.
Hidden safe from needless feet,


Born Gods message to repeat;
Born, with cheer the world to greet.


Bringing messages Of love,


Down to earth, from realms above,


Love, love- love, love!


List, We mortals, God Is love.


Just then the sun, now wide awake, wink
ed at the Fairy Queen in such a shocking
fashion that she tainted and fell off her
toadstool throne, and in the confusion the
party broke up.


But the little blue-eyed forget-me-not
grew strong and beautiful and lived the
long hot summer through, fulfilling it's mis-
sion, for 1t looked sweetly into the weary
faces of many passers-by and brought, all
unconsciously, balm to many an aching
heart.

WIDE WATER, Va, September 9-Prof.
Langley's flying machine was hoisted to the
superstructure of the houseboat this morn
ing at 1870 preparatory for a prospective
launching this, afternoon. Owing to the
frequent drilling the men have had re-
Gently in handling the machine not more
than twenty minutes was consumed from
the time the aerodrome was moved until 1t
rested on the launching carriage.


Prof Manly personally superintendent the
work. AS soon it became apparent that
the weather was likely to be comparatively
calm and clear throughout the day the ex
perts made ready to elevate the machine.


Photographer Smillie of the Smithsonian.
who has been away from the houseboat for
several weeks, was on hand with his mus
ket camera and other apparatus for max
ing instantaneous photographs.


Prof. Langley was not present this morn
Ing nor did he come down on the noon
train, which the tug Key met at Quantico.
1t was thought that he would arrive early
today.


After getting the machine into position
the propellers were adjusted and the motor
started. 1t did fairly good work The
machine had been top several hours
when this dispatch was sent, but the wings
had not then been fastened into position.
Whether launching will be attempted this
afternoon is uncertain, but the weather
gives promise Of remaining as good as could
be desired.

tremendous volcanic eruption somewhere

cir was close and dry and the light breeze
was charged with fine gray ash which
looked like volcanic dust. There was a
strong smell in the air which the log de-
scribes as mot unlike burning bricks,


These atmospheric conditions Increased
as the vessel neared land, and on Wednes-
day night the smoke pail became 30 thick
that the usual fog precautions. were taken.

all night on deck. On Thursday morning
their fears were increased by the south
ward flight of large numbers OF Wild ducks

Paul Sick reports the case OF young
man who died while being operated upon
for tuberculous peritonitis under chloro-
form. His heart had stopped beating for
forty-dve minutes, his respirations had
ceased and his pupils were widely dilated.
Sick opened the pericardium, massaged
the heart, and applied hot congresses to
1t while respiration was being performed.
In half an hour the heart was beating
strongly and regularly, and life was re-
sumed, the patient living for twenty-seven
hours, when he died in collapse. The
case is illustrative of the extreme value
of direct cardiac massage in cases Of
sudden death.

This was the first accident of the kind

at the Old DAILY, which is located close

The cause of the snowslide was the
heavy storms that had ragged during the
past few days IN this locality, packing
the snow on the mountains so that it had
TO come down. The snow has melted con-
sderably of late around the lower parts
of the mountain and the slush that was
formed in this manner was not strong
enough 10 hold back the tremendous
weight Of the banks above.


II Is feared that more slides will occur
and excitement in the city is great. The
most danger now seems to be to the prop
critics situated in Thayne Canyon, quite
a distance from the Quincy. Here are
located the California, Comstock and
keystone mines. Thayne Canyon is much
deeper than the one where the Quincy
mine is located. All work at the mines
in Thayne Canyon has been abandoned.

Walking into room in the stamp shop

dered the half dozen TRUSTEES" employed
there to lie down. Charles Farmhouse, the
only one who did not obey, was knocked
senseless with hammer. The two men
then compelled one Of the TRUSTEES to carry
the ladder to the wall near by. AS they
were about to scale the wall guards APP
peared, and many shots were exchanged,
but none took effect. MCGOWAN and Grant
were finally taken into custody, and placed
in solitary confinement.

The modern woman does not look after

And with the home garden the home
made bouquet, the parting gift Of every
hostess to the friend who had visited her

Cut flowers from the greenhouse for beau

and mignonette through the house, and
from early spring until late in the fall

OF course, well-trimmed lawn and

mise. and have a little Of each7

the agreement signed at Cologne on Saturday
last by the French Transatlantic Company
with the Morgan shipping combination did not
provide for the former entering the combina-
ton, thereby confirming previous statements on
the subject, but was simply the general traffic
agreement of the North Atlantic steamship
combination, which has been inexistence for
eleven years and which also includes Dutch
and Belgian lines In view of the situation at
present existing, he added, the French line
would not enter the combination, and the lat
ter did not desire it to do so.


In an interview with the Editor of the "Tage
blatt" published to-day Herr Balin said the
German companies regretted the fact that the
British Government had subsidized the Cunard
Line. not because they feared the competition
of that line, but because it a bad example
for other countries, if one country subsidized
lines other countries might do likewise. till
finally all subsidies would have to be abolished
by an international agreement similar to the
Brussels sugar convention. As for the Cunard
Line Herr Ballin did not believe it could sue
cessfuliy compete with the combination, even
with its subsidy, because it did not recognize
that modern conditions compelled working hand
in hand with neghbors. He thought the Cunard
Lines large subsidized steamers were too
extensive to be run at profit, owing to their
enormous consumption of coal The British
Government, Herr Ballin asserted was really
giving to the Cunard Line steamers out
right as it found the capital for building them,
and subsidized the vessels sufficiently to cover
the interest and the amortization of the new
apitaI. Frances experience, he further re-
marked. showed the deadening effects of State
subsidies Herr Ballin would exert influence to
prevent the German Government from initiating
Great Britains example. Means of transporta-
ton created at state expense were always fail
ures when adequate commerce did not exist
The German lines were successful because the
German merchants had the courage to export
German products and buy return freight. Den
mark had created a splendid free port at Copen-
hagen, and the Hamburg American Line had
been induced by Danish friends to establish
line between the United States Gulf ports and
Copenhagen but the freight not there
The only regular commodity offered was oilcake
for cattle feed, but it not in sufficient quan-
tity to maintain the line Hungary trying
to create direct communicate ton between Fiume
and New York, partly by force for Austro-
Hungarian emigrants would be compelled 10
use that line. The Hamburg-American and
North German Lloyd companies, at the request
of the Hungarian Government. sent commits
sion to Hungary year ago to investigate the
possibilities of direct NewYork line but it
was decided that it could not be made profitable,
because the freight not sufficient and pas
sengers preferred seven to ten day voyages to
sixteen and eighteen day passages,


Explaining the Hamburg-k 1erican Lines
present good business in time of depression,
Herr Ballin asserted that it was due to large
exports especially the United States, South

tWinkling of an eye. When on level
with the mans waist the proud cock

lay calmly in its position behind the man.


The stranger was not long in finding

In an instant he beheld the game fowl

squared himself for defense, but the cock

The rooster flew at him with redoubled
fury time and again, always being cum
ming enough to escape the angry grasp
Of the man.


After a hard fight Of few minutes
the that he could not success
fully combat with the determined fowl,
and. turning, he beat hasty retreat.
The cock did not follow. but, tossing his
head high and giving his plump breast q
heaving swell, he tapped his wings de-
family and crowed clear, shrin note
