Mrs. Gilmore Benjamin, handsome
young widow Of l047 Bergen street, Brook
lyn, was assaulted and robbed by a negro
early yesterday morning as she was enter
| ing the vestbule of her home. She made a
gallant fight to retain her jewels and pocket-
book and was badly beaten about the head
with club by the misc-eant who finally
broke away, hatless and with the end of his
thumb bitten off.


Mrs. Benjamin and several friends had
been to the Montauk Theatre. After the per-
formance she accompanied the party to
restaurant, where they tarried until 80
O'Clock in the morning. She refused to
allow her friends to go home with her, say
ing that she could get out of the car at her
door and needed no escort.


When she arrived at the house and was
about to put the latch key in the door
negro jumped out, struck her blow with
short club and attempted to grasp her by
the throat Mrs. Benjamin screamed Justify
for help and, instead of fainting, grappled
with her assailant. She was not strong
enough, however, and the thief succeeded
in dragging diamond ring from her hand,
her watch from her dress and her pocket
book.


Satisfied that the cries OF his victim
would soon bring help the negro tried to
strike a final blow with the club and decamp.
Mrs. Benz was too quick for him, and
grasping him by the arm, she made des-
perate attempt to overpowcr him. In the
struggle she succeeded in getting his right
thumb between her teeth and bit the end
OF it OFF.


With cry of pain, the negro broke away
and ran down the street. lie left his hat
behind him and dropped Mrs. Benjamin's
gold watch. Mrs. Benjamin gave chase,
but lost track of her assailant. On her
return she was met by Patrolmen Sauerbrun
who had heard her cries. They took up
the hunt for the negro. but only succeeded
in learning that he had escaped by way
of the Kings County Elevated Railroad
The ticket agent at the Nostrand avenue
and Fulton street station told the police that
a negro, hatless and with bleeding thumb,
had rushed into the station and asked how
soon he could get a train. He told the
agent that he had been at a negro dance,
got into fight and was anxious to get away.
The negro was traced to the Flat bush avenue
station, where he left the road and went
to the street.

She sent word to the reporters that she
was unable to be seen, but that beyond
few bruises and the shook incident to her

.'pop." and when the whisky turned solid

marsh land quite similar to the tule lands

cayed reed and grass roots. being entirely
Of vegetable mould and quite fertile.
bitches at frequent intervals drain the gar

canal, and thus to the city. Here are

which form one of the principal attractions
to Mexico city. the flower market being a
wonder in the quantity and exquisite beauty

A special train from Cape May, carrying
home a large party of newspaper cor
respondents and ladies of Baltimore and
Washington. ran into a freight train on an
open switch and was wrecked near Will
mington, Del, about 3:15 yesterday after
noon. No one was killed, but the fireman
and engineer were badly injured, the
former by jumping from the engine, the
latter by being pinned beneath the wreck
age.


Saved by Veshbules.


All that prevented the telescoping of the
train was the fact that it was vestibuled,
and even with this protection the cars were
damned together. Windows were smashed
and flying glass cut several people.
The train left Cape May at II o'clock yes
terday morning, and consisted Of nine cars
The passengers were guests of the Pennsyl-
vania railroad on the yearly outing to the
street station, Philadelphia, and there three
of the cars were detached and the train
continued on its way with only the WASH
ington and Baltimore newspaper men
aboard. 1t was going at top speed as 1t ap-
preached Wilmington. There had been
delay in crossing the bridge over the Della
ware before reaching Philadelphia, and
about half an hour was lost. All the way
between Philadelphia and Wilmington
crews are at work making the improve
ments by which the road is to reduce ma
terially the running time between Wash
ington and New York. At this point
switch engine was on a short siding switch
ing some cars. The engine was on the fur
Their side from the rapidly approaching
passenger train, apparently hauling off a
truck loaded with coal and box car.


Struck at Full Speed.


The special was coming along at the rate
of forty miles an hour when suddenly two
shocks were felt, causing great confusion
as the occupants of the seats were shuff1ed
about in the cars and some thrown from
their seats. The train had run at full speed
into an open siding and collided with a
freight car, which had been dropped. The
freight engine. drawing several other cars,
was moving off and the engineer put on
full steam when he saw the special coming,
and was well out of the way when the
crash came.


The engine was crushed beyond SEM
blance of itself and was half buried in the
embankment and the broken timbers of
the box car. The engineer was somewhere
beneath the wrecked locomotive. having
stuck to his post, set the brakes and
versed before the shock came. The distance
from the main track to the cars on the
switch was too short for the train to d.
minish its speed appreciably however, and
1t practically plowed into the freight car at
full speed. For moment the passengers
thought that there must have been heavy
loss of life in the forward cars, but were
soon treasured, and with the assistance of
railroad workmen succeeded in leaving the
train.


All Cars Derailed.


Every one but to rear cars had left
the rails. and fortunately the freight that
caused the damage was unloaded, else the
loss of life would have been appalling. The
scene presented the appearance of a seri
Gus wreck.


The track crews who were on the spot
when the collision occurred ran promptly
to assist in rescuing the engineer and fire.
man, while the passengers made their way
into the open air as quickly as possible to
ascertain the extent of the damage. The
fireman, in leaping from the cab, was cut
about the head. which bled profusely, but
was not dangerously injured. The engineer
was soon extricated. and was not serious
ly hurt. His escape, however, was miracu-
lous. The last two cars of the special had
not left the tracks, and were soon hauled
upon the main track by switch engine and
pushed into Wilmington where surgeons
and officials boarded the train to see If
any of the passengers needed medical at
tention.


The party was brought from Wilmington
at a rapid pace, making the distance from
Baltimore in forty-ive minutes and land
ed at the Pennsylvania station in Washing
ton at $50 1t Is the unanimous opinion OF
the excursionists that only miracle saved
many of them from instant death. One OF
the railroad employees present remarked
that he had seen many railroad accidents,
but this one was the luckieSt he had ever
allayed two of the ladies on board passed
through the cars and in few minutes col
lected hundred dollars for the injured en-
gineer and fireman.

New York. July 1s.-Since the plague Of
mosquitoes has extended over the Bronx.
the girls of that borough have borrowed :,
fad from the girls of New Jersey and have
taken to Joss" sticks as an effective
remedy for the pests. They put the burn
ing sticks in their hair and thus make them
not alone practical. but decorative.


Miss Helen Hills. daughter of George F.
Hills. a paper manufacturer. is one of
those, however. who will not follow the fad
further Miss Hills. who is 10 years old
went out with party of young people
and all the girls had the burning sticks in
their hair. Miss Hills returned to her home
about o'clock. She was tired. and went
to her room to rest.


Forgetting the Joss sticks she lay
down on a couch and was soon asleep She
was awakened about an hour later by heat.
and discovered that the couch and her hair
were afire. She quickly buried her head
in the bed clothing and eXtinguished the
fire in her hair. Then she took rug from
the floor and smothered the flames on the
couch.


She had slept with her arms above her
head. and they were scorched slightly. She
calmly rubbed them with cold cream and
then walked down to the porch and in
formed her parents of her narrow escape


Miss Ellis said: II think I'll let the mos
uuitoes bite next time. The joss sticks are
very good, but they are SO easy to forget,
especially when one is tired"

The California Northwestern Railroad

steam schooner Aberdeen about o'clock

port side about ten feet from the bow,
tearing away her rail and damaging
portion of her deck, but not penetrating

JUred. No one was hurt on either vessel.

the collision and the prompt action of

self the Tiburon made the run into the

Il was on the Tiburon this evening when

The first I knew of the impending danger

BosToN, Dec. 26.-While making her
thirteenth trip to Boston the new Clyde
line steamer Kiowa was Iun down and
sunk by the United Fruit Company's steamer
Admiral Dewey about a mile of Boston
Light, just before noon to-day. The
kiowa carried thirty-one men all told,
and they were taken off the craft by the
city tug CorOmant which was close by at
the time.


The Dewey evidently did not suffer serious
injury, as she continued on her voyage to
the West Indies, having ascertained that
the Kiowa crew was safe.


The collision occurred when thick snow
storm prevailed and, according to all ac-
counts, was unavoidable. The kiowa was
inward bound from Charleston by way
of New York with a large cargo of lumber.
cotton, naval stores, iron and general
merchandise.


She reached the mouth of the entrance
to the channel about II 80, and, encounter
ing the snowstorm, Capt. Chichester
thought it wise to anchor and await clear
weather before entering the harbor.


The Admiral Dewey had sailed an hour
before, bound for Port Antonio and Port
Limon, and was feeling her way cautiously
out to sea through the storm. Neither
captain appears to have seen the other
craft until they were too close to each other
to prevent the collision.


The sharp bow of the Dewey hit the
Kiowa just abaft of the main rigging on
the port side, cutting through the steel
plates and opening up a big hole, through
which the water rush I'd.


The Dewey rebounded from the stricken
craft, which began to settle astern almost
at once, the bow rising high out of the
water. Confusion reigned on the kiowa,
the fremen and engineers rushing up from
below and joining the sailors in getting
the lifeboats cleared away.


The Dewey was on the point OF lowering
away boats when the tug Cormorant came
took off all the men, who left in such hurry
that they lost everything except the clothes
they wore. The city tug was outside with
tow of barges, and transferred the rescued
men to the tug Palas and later the big tug
Storm King brought them to Boston.


After seeing that the crew of the Kiowa
was saved the Dewey headed out to sea
on her voyage. The Clyde liner did not
sink as soon as her crew thought she would.
Her stern settled lower and lower, but finally.
when her bulkhead gave way. the water
filed her hold and down she went like "a
righted when she reached bottom. and at
high water her masts and funnel were
visible.


The Kiowa was the latest addition to the
Clyde Line fleet, having been built by the
Cramp company at Philadelphia early in
the present year. She was 800 fe ct long,
had % feet depth of hold, and her net tom
mage was 2,2t4 She was steel, two
masted, schooner-rigged vessel, having
three decks. Her engines we're of tho
triple expansion type.

NORFOLK, Va, December 31.-The Unit
ed States tugs Peoria and Hercules were
in collision off Currituck inlet on the North
Carolina coast yesterday, and as a result
both vessels were badly damaged The
Hercules, in charge of Lieut.. Douglas, has
returned to the Norfolk navy yard with
her port guard rail forward broken and
splntered. and the boat otherwise injured.
The collision between the two vessels oc-
Cured in heavy sea and was entirely
unavoidable.


The Peoria arrived at Currituck from
this navy yard to relieve the Hercules.
which had been standing by the stranded
submarine boat Moccasin since it went
ashore on December 8. In maneuvering
about the Hercules for the purpose of
shifting the 800 fathoms of hauser attached
to the stranded submarine on the beach,
and the Hercules nearly mile distant, the
Peoria was swept brOadSide with terrific
force against the Hercules. That the blow
was a great one Is evidenced by the splin-
tered condition Of the Hercules guard rail,
which will require some time to repair


Both vessels staggered under the force
of the blow, the Peoria backing off her
starboard guard rail being badly damaged.


Later the Peoria went safely alongside
the Hercules and the hausers attached to
the submarine on the beach were shifted 10
the Peoria, which will await a favorable
wind and tide before attempting to haul
the submarine from her bed in the sand.

Some of the elderly men who are
trudging along at the same gait as
ever in the houses where there are
employed at the same salary they re-
ceived twenty-five years ago, may
benefit by the following incident,
which occurred not long ago in a
downtown store.


A young man who came into the
place less than two years ago was ad-
vanced over a man who had been
there thirty years. The latter went
to the proprietor and complained that
such treatment as he had received
after all his years of service was un-
just. The proprietor, without pre-
tending to notice the complaint,
asked:


"What is that noise in the street :"


The old employee replied that he
did not know and waited.


Better see what it is" said the
proprietor.


The old employee went out and re-
turned with the information that the
noise was made by wagons.


"How many wagons" 7" asked the
proprietor.


The old employee said he hadn't
counted them.


Better find OUT" said the pro-
prietor.


The old employee went out again
and returned with the information
that there were eight.


"What was the cause of the noise"
asked the proprietor.


The old employee said he didn't
know, and the proprietor suggested
that he had better ascertain. The
old employee went out the third time
and returned with the information
that the teamsters were hurrying to
load their wagons with goods.


The proprietor then touched the
bell on the desk, which summoned
the young man who had been ad-
vanced. The proprietor asked him


"What is that noise in the street :"


II will see, replied tile young
man, who went out and returned a
few moments later with the following
report:


"There are eight wagons out there
and the teamsters are hurrying to
load them with goods -


The proprietor turned to the old
employee and said:


do you understand now why this
young man was advanced over you ?"


The old employee understood, but
his knowledge came too late. .-New

the unusual spectacle enjoyed by hun
dreds of Chicagoans last night. Four

alarm being turned in, ,,altho the fire.
men fought the blaze until they were
exhausted. The tract combines al
most virgin forest with carefully cul-

and other small animals abound in

ers were captured and later turned

WASHINGTON, Jan. 3.-The Weather
Bureaus monthly summary of crop condi-
tions is as follows: In the principal win
ter wheat States the month averaged
cold. with more than the usual amount of
precipitation. The temperature condi-
tions were. however, not unfavorable to
winter wheat until. the last decade, when
the States of the Upper Mississippi and
Missouri valleys experienced tenpera-
ture ranging from zero to Is degrees be-
low. During this period the Ohio Valley
States were generally well protected with
snow covering. but in the Central Missis-
sippi and Lower Missouri valleys the crop
was exposed. Only slight damage, how
ever, seems to have resulted, and at the
close of the month the crop appears to be
very promising. Complaints of injury by
fly are not extensive and are largely con-
fined to the Ohio Valley.

There is mourning to-day among the Six Nations
for the death of dearly loved chief Mrs. Harriet
Maxwell Converse or. as she called among the
people of her adoption. ''Ya-re-wah-ro'' ('She
watches for us').


Mrs. Converse the only white woman who
was ever made chief by the Indians. and her in
teTest in the red men and their confidence in her
were both hereditary She born in Indian
village. ard her father and grandfather were both
adopted by Indian tribes. The latter was known
among the red the honest trader" because
of a virtue not very commonly displayed by white
men in their dealings with the Indians.


After she grew up Mrs. Converse spent great
deal of time among her adopted people. and
constantly occupied in promoting their welfare.
She watched their interests in the legislature
thus gaining from them the name Ya-re-wah-no.
and she was the vigant guardian of the Indians
in New-York City. She fed them and clothed them
and sent them back to their homes and all who fel
into the hands OF the police were sure of her inter-
veution and assistance.


Mrs. Converse died yesterday morning from apo
plexy at No 450 West Twentieth-st., and her body
has been removed the Stephen Merritt Burial
Company's headquarters. No. Ill Eighth-ave. Her
Indian friends wish to give her Indian funeral,
with the rites and ceremonies in which Mrs. Con-
verse often took part during her lifetime, and
which she considered very beautiful

The hearing on the Mortgage Tax bill
that occurred in Albany on Tuesday
proved that its hackers were equipped
with no argument that could live for a
moment before the weighty condem-
nation heard from the representatives
of the important interests concerned.
Senator ALLDs, who had been put for
ward to defend the bill, was silenced al
most Immediately. So utterly resource
less and impotent was the defence that
we are constrained to believe that Sena-
tor PLATT spoke the truth yesterday
when in denying that there was anything
but harmony between himself and Gov
ernor ODELL he said that the Governor
agreed with him fully that the measure
in question was bad bill.


The bill was brou yht forward originally
because Governor ODELL, although al
ways a business nan, has become doc
trinaire on the subject of taxation, and
for some inscr.table reason has been
striken with an ambition to abolish the
direct tax. His prejudice for that theory
has led him TO adopt measure which,

PORTLAND Ore, Sept 23.-In an I'M
successful attempt made by four masked
men to hold up and rob the Oregon Rail-
way and Navigation overland train leav-
ing Portland tonight at S:15 o'clock one
of the robbers was shot and instantly
killed and Engineer Ollie Barrett of Port
land was wounded. Express Messenger
Fred Corner fired the shot that killed
the robber and the bullet after passing
through the bandits body. wounded the
engineer.


The men had badly bungled the job
after having successfully stopped the
train and compelled the engineer and fire
man to accompany them in their work.
Instead of attacking the express car they
blew open the door of the baggage car
with dynamite. The noise aroused the
express messenger and he opened his door
and fired at the leading bandit, who stood
at the time but a few feet from him.
The death of the unknown bandit, appar-
emily the leader of the party, disheartened
the others and they abandoned the at
tempt to rob the train. Not a shot was
fired in return and the robbers escaped
before the express messenger could fire
again.


BANDIT IS KILLED.


The holdup was attempted on the curve
west of a tunnel. Two masked men stole
aboard the train at Troutdale, hiding on
the blind end Of the baggage car. Il
short distance out from Troutdale the
men crept over the tender and covering
Engineer Barrett and Fireman Stevenson
with their revolvers, ordered the train to
proceed to a point near mile post q.
When this spot had been reached the ban
dts ordered the engineer to stop.


Two other men joined the bandits at
the mile post and the four ordered the
engineer and fireman to accompany them
back to the express car. The robbers,
apparently ignorant of train formation
and very nervous, attacked the baggage
car When the doors were not opened
they promptly used dynamite and blew
the door open.


Though he had been ordered, with the
fireman, to keep ahead of the party. En-
gineer Barrett managed to slip behind the
leader. AS the door to the express car
was opened and Corners gun was poked
out. Barrett was standing directly behind
the man who was under the door. Cor
ner fired Immediately. the bullet instantly
killing the robber and wounding the en-
gineer. The other bandits. frightened by
the shot. retreated.


BAFFLED ROBBERS ESCAPE.


Engineer Barrett was carried into the
baggage car and the train was run into
Corbetts, where a telephone message was
sent to Portland to notify the railway Of

According to former custom, just re-
yived, the junior and the senior classes at
the state university smoked the pipe Of
peace last night upon the university cam
pus and buried the Ratchet of war. Ih1s
practice, just before commencement,
marks the pa ssing Of hostility that has
previously existed between the juniors
and the seniors.


After an hour of jovial talk beneath
Japanese lanterns, the two classes seated
themselves about a campfire. PRESIDENT
Benjamin Drake Of the senior class took
the ancient pipe-a genuine survival from
many an ancient treaty between the Sioux
and the Ojibways-lighted the kinn1kin-
nick with a coal from the big fire, inhaled
solemn Whit. and passed the pipe to
H. S. Ives, leader of the juniors. Mr..
Ives rose amid loud grunts Of approba-
| ton from the braves seated on the grass.
He told the story of the calumet-how,
moons and moons ago, the bowl of red
stone had fallen from the sky-from the
Great Spirit-into the hands Of HiaWatha:
how the gray feathers along the steam had
been delivered by the west wind into Hia-
wathas lodge as a gift from the chief OF
the war eagles

ahawk from Lake Superior, was buried
deep by two braves accounted the most
! truculent warriors respectively of the jun

New York, Nov 21.-Living in San Fran
cisco has not destroyed the confidence OF
Mrs. Marguerite Tosci in the kindliness
and honesty of human nature. So trust
full Is she that she riskcd having her two
little boys sent all the way from Florence.
Italy, to San Francisco without guar
dian other than such as might be found
among steamship and railroad employees
along tho long journey. And Mrs. Toscfs
confidence has not been misplaced.


The two boys, Guido and Albert vecchi.
and z years old. arrived on the
Sardinia few days ago after their trip
across the water, and they were started
on their journey across the continent.
Neither Of them can speak word Of
English. and all they have to identify
them are tags tied around their necks,
on which are inscribed their names and
destination. They are being shipped"
to No. Montgomery street. San Fran
cisco.


Seated side, by side on one of the bench
they had been escorted by an Italian in
the employ of the steamship company
which brought them from Italy, they were
the center of a crowd of sympathetic men
train left at half past 0. At first shyly,
but after awhile trustfuliy, their big,
black eyes looked out upon those gathered
about them, but they could answer none
of the many questions with which they
were piled.


Whatever may happen to them later,
they certainly started out with their appe-
tites satiated. Taking them by the hand,
kind-hearted woman, escorted by E. II.
Odell, the night stationmaster, took the
youngsters to restaurant and not only
filled them up on coffee and cake, but sup
piled them with a generous basket of
sandwiches and fruit, enough to last them
for at least day. The boys have a little
money with them, and the conductors on
their trains Will undoubtedly see that they
do not go hungry /,


They are both plainly, though neatly.
dressed, and by their appearance indicate
that they have been brought up with con-
siderable care. All the Italians who
brought them to the station know Of them
was that their father, and mother had
come to this country three years ago. and
mother had been able to make and gave
enough to send the money with which to
pay her children's passage and railroad
fare.


The little Italians will be about six days
in reaching their destination. From Buf-
falo they will be transferred to the Lake
Shora Railroad. which will take them to
Chicago. There they will take the Chi
cago. Burlington and Quincy. through
Omaha and Denver, the Colorado Midland
to Grand Junction, the Denver and Rio
Grande to Ogden, and then the Southern
Pacific to San Francisco.

Corps ia divided into three distinct sets
The ENJOYS from Europe form one those
from the Orient another, and the repre-

a third The official relations between

diplomat outranks his colleagues from
the East and the Spanish American coun-

different attitude from that he oxhlpits

The reasons for this distinction are many
and subtle. 1t is due in part doubtless
to the traditions the representatives OF
monarchies inherit and the training they
receive. including a prejudice against
republics generally.


The Spanish countries are re-
sarded by the European statesmen OF to-
day much as their predecessors OF the
latter part Of the eighteenth century re-
Karded the United States They have no
confidence in the stability Of Latin-Amcri-
can governments, and the revolutions that
are constantly taking place give ground
for their doubts. and make it impossible
for the representatives of long established
governments to accept the little republics
OF the Western Hemisphere seriously.

A special cable to the New York Herald
from Port of Spain, Trinidad, yesterday
says: Several persons were killed in seri-
Gus riots. which started here today. Gov
eminent buildings were burned and the
governor of Trinidad was forced to take
refuge on the cruiser Pallas, lying in the
harbor.


The government recently passed an ordi-
nance increasing the cost Of water, follow
ing the building of the new water works.
Public meetings had been held to protest
against the increased rates, and demon
stration was made when the legislative
council met today. 80.


A great crowd surrounded the building,
and when some one threw stone at the
building the crowd became a surging mob.
The place was set fire and burned, and
the mob began looting stores in searching
for firearms.


Then an attack was made on the gov
ernor's house. The governor escaped with
considerable difficulty, his carriage being
destroyed by the mob.


With the director of the waterworks the
governor took refuge on the British cruiser
PallaS.


The police read the riot act and repeatedly
charged upon the mob, but could make lit
tie Roadway, and finally fired into the
crowds. At lease six rioters were killed
and large number We're wounded.


AS rioting continued despite the police,
the commander of the Pallas landed 200
marines and bluejackets with Calling guns.
order. Large numbers of responsible citi-
Zens were sworn in special officers to as
sist in controlling the mob.


The presence of the sailors ready to
sweep the streets with their guns, cowed
the mob and partial order has been re-
stored. Excitement is still very great, how
ever. and it is feared there will be fresh
outbreaks during the night.

One story told of Mrs. Booth-Tucker
when a little girl of thirteen shows her to
have been the true child of her parents.
When walking along the shore at Ports
mouth beside her governess, she saw
donkey cart being driven along furiously
nv a lad who was belaboring the poor beast
sayagely. Breaking away from her COM
pauion, she rushed after it, and pulled the
how from his seat. Catching up his stick
she showered blows upon the lads head
and shoulders with the words, uttered
amid tears. There now, how do you IKE
it?'' Perhaps her pleading proved more
powerful than the blows: but in few
moments the lad was kneeling beside the
donkey asking Gods forgiveness for his
cruelty The climax came with the girl
driving back trimuphantly in the cart be-
side the boy, who promised henceforth to
be kind and to treat his donkey well.

BEATRICE Neb., May 80. - The Blue
river has been rising steadily for thirty-six
hours. 1t is row 20 inches above the high
water mark of last year. Water Is running
over Court street.


Since o'clock yesterday afternoon the
river has risen at the rate of four inches
an hour. The south and west sides are cut
of from the main part of town.


In some places scarcely more than the
roofs Of the houses are to be seen. Many
people moved out of their homes yesterday
and the day before. Some who did not
think the water would reach them were
compelled to move out during the night. in
some instances the escape being made from
second-story windows.


Lights Shut Of.


The electric light plant was shut off yes
terday afternoon, and the water works
plant was stopped at o'clock this morn
ing. the water having flooded the fire
boxes.


The Burlington and the Union Pacific
yards are flooded. The engines were taken
out of the round house last night. The
Burlington passenger station Is flooded and
part Of the platform is washed away


NO trains are expected to be able to get
into town on any road today. All railroad
bridges across Blue river are threatened,
and cannot stand much longer under the
strain.
Thirteen Families Driven From Home.
LINCOLN, Neb.. May 3O.-At o'clock
this morning Salt Creek was within six
inches of the high water mark Of last
year and rising rapidly. The Iowlands
have been flooded and much damage done
Thirty families have been driven from
their homes and taken refuge with friends
Quarters for more homeless victims Of the
flood are being provided in the county
court house.


Risen Nearly Two Feet.


KANSAS CITY. Mo-. May 3O-The flood
situation along the banks Of the Missouri
and Kaw rivers here and west is far more
serious than on yesterday and the predic-
lions of Colonel Common of the local wealth.
er bureau that the disastrous record of
1881 would be exceeded will doubtless be
realized.


Since yesterday afternoon the Missouri
had risen nearly two feet. and this morn
ing the government gauge here registered
twenty-five feet. which Is but one foot be-
low that in 1881.


Both streams continue to rise steadily
today and still further rise OF two feet
at this point Is expected within another
twenty-four hours. heavy rains having
fallen again last night for a mile around
Kansas CITY.

FIFrY.sIx bank robberies are reported to
have occurred in this country during the last
four months. Illinoise and Nebraska report
seven. Indiana FIVE Texas and Missouri four
each, Iowa, Kansas and Minnesota two each
and New Mexico one. These surprisingly
numerous crimes suggest a widespread bank
robbing organization, and recent events tend
to confirm the idea. Under the present ma
tional law, banks with small capital are multi
plying in towns and villages. Bank-robbing
gangs appear to have increased corresponding
ly. The situation suggests careful precautions
on the part of banks and vigilance in police
and detective circles. Banks in small COM
munities are valuable aids to the people and
the hunting down of bank robbers must be
pushed vigorously.

SAN JUAN, P. R.. March 25.-There was

evening. under the auspices OF the citizens
committee, in honor Of Miss Alice Roose-
welt. Following this was an elaborate dis

until 10 o'clock. and was witnessed by

mendous ovation from the people gathered
on the plaza and on the balconies AMI
roofs Of the houses. One OF the set pieces,
representing President Roosevelt, was
twenty-fiv feet, high.


The interior Of the theater was decorated
profusely and displayed the word ''Wcl-
come" formed of electric lights. Miss
Roosevelt spent two hours shaking hands
with the invited guests. She will leave
San Juan for the interior today, accom-
panied by Gov. Hunt, Mrs. Hunt, Miss
Elizabeth Hunt, Thomas Hunt, the gov
ernor's brother, and Mrs. Thomas Hunt:
Miss Beatrice Buck. the governors ward,
and Secretary Bliss. The party will be
away four days and win visit Cayey,
Ponce, Mayaguez and the intermediate
towns. as well as the principal sugar es-
tates. The Inhabitants of Ponce have
planned big reception for Miss Roosevelt.

Mrs. Lydia Terrell. sixty-seven years old,
committed suicide at her home, $40 10th
street southeast, about noon today by hang
ing herself to a bed post in her room. She
was found by her son, George Terrell. who
found 1t necessary to break the bed in Or
der to release the body. 1t had been only
about thirty minutes before the body was
discovered that Mrs. Terrell was about the
house conversing with members of her fam
lily. She had not been seen during the
time stated and search was made for her.
When the body was found, her son thought
there was "A possibility of saving her life.
but she was declared to be dead, and tie
coroner was summoned. The necessary
death certificate was given.


Mrs. Terrell was demented and her rela-
tives had kept close watch over her move
ments. Some days ago she Said she hoped
she would never do anything to herself in
the way of personal injury. Arrangements
for the funeral have not yet been made.
Mrs. Terrell used strips OF flag with
which to hang herself.

Five Bicycles.


Ulysses Briggs, colored, eighteen years
old, and his brother Campbell, fifteen years
of age, appeared in the Police Court yester-
day On five charges Of theft of bicycles.
They were arraigned several days ago, and
at that time demanded jury trial, but they
waived that right yesterday and withdrew
the demand. The evidence was against
them, and Judge Kimball directed that
Ulysses remain in jail for five months in
default Of fines amounting to $780, which
were imposed. Campbell, who is under age,
will remain under the control Of the board
of childrens guardians for two years unless
fines amounting to $40 are paid.


The light sentences were explained by the
fact that the defendants were youthful and
had never before been charged with crime.

WOODS HOLE, Mass. June 6-The

port. having on board large number of
passengers. the United States mail and a
heavy freight, collided with a fishing
schooner off Vineyard Haven in a dense
fog today and was badly damaged


One man was seriously injured and a
number of passengers were made uncon-
scious by the shock of the collision. The
damage to the steamer was all above the
water line and she succeeded in reaching
this port. The name of the fishing schooner
was not ascertained, owing to the fog She
lost her fore-riggng.


The collision occurred not long after the
steamer had left Vineyard Haven A
thick fog obscured the sound and the
Martha's Vineyard was hardly clear of the
harbor when she struck the schooner.


The vessels came together with great I
force The steamers bow struck the
schooner forward. the bowsprit of the fish
erman raked the steamer, carrying away
both the upper and the lower decks back
to the paddle box. The fore-rigging of the
vessel became entangled In the wreckage
and was carried away. Russell Hancock
of Chilmark, a passenger on the steamer,
was badly injured. and number of other
passengers, unable to escape the sweep
of the schooner's bowsprit, were knocked
insensible.


The vessels fell apart almost Immediately
after the collision and the schooner drifted
away in the fog before her name could be
learned. a hasty examination of the Mar
tha's Vineyard showed that she was not
leaking and 1t was decided to make for
this port She reached here at 9:30 O. clock.
Mr.. Hancock needed medical attention. The
others who had suffered in the collision
had recovered before arriving here.


The schooner, IL was learned later, was
the Gloucester fishing smack Senator Sauls-
bury. She lost her bowsprit but was not

Three boys were run over and killed

Bay Chester station, shortly after O'Clock

Chester crossing, says the three boys passed
him, walking westward. They were carry

Bay bridge

striking the boys. The three badly mangled
bodies We're found by freight hands who
were walking along the track some time
later. The police Of the West Chester sta
ton were notified and a patrol wagon
took the bodies to the station.


Late last night George Walz Of 1910
Home street, The Bronx, identified one

who the other two We're, but said he was told
that his brother had gone fishing with two
boys named Stader. who lived on Wesches-
ter avenue.

passenge train that ran over the boys.

CINCINNATI, Dec. s.-The United States
Court of Appeals delive red decision against
trusts to-day, giving to persons or corpora
tions obliged to pay excessive prices right
to recover damages for three times the
amount sustained.


The decision was handed down in the
appealed case of the City Of Atlanta against
the Chattanooga Pipe and Foundry Works
and the South Pittsburg Pipe Company.


The decision was based on the act OF Con-
gress relating to restriction Of Interstate
commerce. The city Of Atlanta advert ised
for bids for water pipes, and the testimony
in the Tennessee Federal Circuit Court
showed that the Pipe Trust arranged for its
Admission, Ala. establishment to get the
contract. This was done by having all other
neighboring mills bid above the market
price. The city Of Atlanta showed that
the Anniston mill paid money into the Pipe
Trust pool which was divided among
the various mills.


Suit was brought against the two Chatta-
nooga mills for their alleged share Of the
bonus. The Tennessee Federal Court had
instructed n dismissal of the suit on the
ground that the limitation Of three years
had expired. The Court of Appeals to-day
decided that the action was such as to force
Atlanta to buy from the Admission mills;
that the defendants were guilty OF inter-
fering with interstate commerce; that the
combine was illegally enhancing the price
of a commodity and restricted others from
competing 1t was held that under the
act of Congress the plaintiff had ten years
In which to sue and was entitled to triple
damages. The case was ordered back to
the Knoxville court for a new trial.

TACOMA, Wash, Jan. s.-The viceroy
of Canton, China, is taking severe meas
ures to stop piracy on the West River be-
tween Hongkong and Canton and along
the southeastern Chinese coast. The pi-
rates were getting so bold that they en-
dangered the commerce carried on by ma
tives. They sailed along the coast in
swift junks, overhauling and robbing the
slower and more heavily burdened mer-
chant junks. All who refused to land and
deliver were either knitted or thrown
overheard. On the West River passenger
junks were being stopped daily while the
pirates boarded them and relieved the
passengers of their valuabes.


The Canton Viceroy recently adopted a
plan of employing detectives to join the
pirate bands and give information as to
how they might be run to earth These
detectives were paid high salaries to pre-
vent their joining the pirates Their
work proved so successful that more than
ninety pirates were captured during No
vember and the early part of December
They were promptly executed at Canton,
being carried to their doom in sacks and
on the backs of stalwart Chinese Before
them walked the eXecutioner, who had
the sacks dumped on the ground wherever
he could find an open space The pirates
were made to kneel down with their
breasts forward and heads erect while the
eXecutioner clipped off their heads with
one blow of a rusty sword


The Chinese gunboat Kwong Yuen was
sent against the pirates after the attack
on junk in which Britisher was mur-
dered, and found pirate steam launch
towing two captured junks. The Kwong
Yuen sent her boats against the pirates,
who drove back the boats, killing three
men. The gunboat then opened fire with
her Gatling guns and two 3-pounders,
sinking both launch and junks. The pi-
rates tried to escape to shore by small
boats, but every one was sunk and the
pirates drowned. Three wounded pirates
were taken and instantly executed

large crowd Of military officers, civilians

Cabled advices were received from Lon

The syndicate handles the entire output

selling higher than they had been at any
time since the consolidation of the South

sensation among even the most conserva-
tive of the big diamond merchants in Mai
den lane. In two years the total advance

manifold, but the general feeling seems to
be that the enormous natural wealth of the
Kimberley diamond district is decreasing
rapidly, and that the board of life govern
ors, which is composed Of old men, is anx
ious to get the most possible for all that
the mines produce. One of the strongest
proofs of the correctness of this belief is
the great scarcity of rough diamonds.
The diamond market centerS abroad have
been almost depleted, and it is impossible
to obtain desirable goods in any but small
and irregular lots.


Immediately after the advance went into
effect several orders were placed at the new
price, thing never done before, because

the first to buy on advances. In spite of

London. July 17.-According to "The Daily
Chronicle" the action of America in annexing
the islands off Borneo raises exceedingly
delicate situation, and the British Foreign Office
has asked Washington for an explanation


The islands concerned, says the paper, are
group of seven which originally belonged to the
Sultan of Sulu. from whom they passed by
charter in 1881 to the control OF the British
North Borneo Company, whose officers confirm
that they are undoubtedly British territory.
They are insignificant in size, but Of the highest
strategic Importance, dominating Sandakan har-
Dor and Labukay. Their names are Taganae,
Baguan, Bakkungaan, Lihman, Sibaung, Beeaan
and Lankayan.


The American side of the question. as given
by the United States Embassy. says THE
Daily Chronicle" is that the islands are un-
doubtedly American by right Of conquest, hav-
ing belonged to the Philippines. and the Sui
tan of SuIu having confirmed and acknowl-
edged American supremacy over them. The
course taken was to demonstrate Americas
right and establish more clearly defined line
between the American possessions in the Phil
ippines and Sulu Sea. and the territories OF
the British Borneo Company.


The islands had never been occupied by any
European nation, and it is unknown whether
Spain ever recognized the trading treaty
which existed between the BOrneo Company
and the inhabitants of the Islands.

New York. Sept. 19.-According to the
story related by officers of the Occidental
and Oriental steamer Gaelic, while in

warmly commended the survivors of the
wrecked steamer vi Gloria and praised
them for the courage and bravery dis
played at the time that vessel met with
disaster on Little Bamboo Island. near
Chefoo.


These men. armed TO the teeth, were
compelled to defend their very lives
against a swarming horde of coast pirates,
who endeavored to take possession of the
Victoria after she had piled up on the
treacherous reefs surrounding the little
island.


Shortly after the vessel struck Chinese
pirates made a landing on the island and
were only prevented from Iooting the
wreck by the heroic resistance of the Off
GERS and crew. When the pirates hove in
sight, Captain Casey armed all hands, but
ordered them to retain their fire unless
shooting should become a necessity.


The pirates came on undismayed by the
show of arms. Iney had no firearms, but
cxhpited some ugly looking knives. Inc
shiPwrecked marines, barred their way,
and. when they refused to return to their
junks, Captain Casey and his men clubbed
rifles ana revOlvers and sailed into the
sea bandits in true sailor fashion.


After getting ashore the Victoria's peo-
pie underwent numerous hardships. Lit
tie Bamboo is a barren rock with precip-
itous sides. and it was with great diff
Guilty that the shipwrecked crew climbed
beyond reach of the angry breakers. Cap
tain Casey was accompanied by his wife,
who shared without complaining all the
trials which befell her shipmates.


The shipwrecked company, after spend
ing four days on the island. was taken
off by a passing war vessel.

miles for the better part of the run. The
steering gear being new and stiff made 1t
hard to keep to a straight course.


The two bow torpedo tubes are as yet
without their conical covers, and having
diameters of eighteen inches, their bluff
surface added considerably to the load
against the heavy seaway. The remark
able steadness of the vessel bears out all
that has been claimed for her sea boat.
Many of the mechansms were stiff and the
screws are not yet standardized, so the
speed performances are promising, indeed.


The Holland boats made about 81 knots
after two years preparation. The Pro-
tector, as recently described in The Star.
has a main cigar-shaped body, and above
and without this a light shp-shaped struc-
ture has been built to make the vessel sea-
worthy and stable. In this superstructure
are stored the air TASKS and the gasoline
tanks, thus completely removing all danger
from leaks and internal explosion.


The boat is sixty-five feet long. has a
maximum beam of II feet, and had today
displacement of 100 tons. Apart from
her surprising steadiness she is impressive
because of the compactness of all her ma
chinery and the available remaining space
Her cabin accommodation for crew Of
eight persons is quite double the space al
lotted crew of double that number on our
surface torpedo boats of the Thornton type.
NO submergence runs were attempted to-
day, but in few days, when the electrical
installation is complete, the boat will have
her subsurface and her bottom runs.

Clarendon, Ark. March 1.-THE steamer

south of st. Charles. about sixty-five miles

drowned in sixty feet of water. and his
body was not recovered. The people of st.
Charles are now looking for it.


Mann was IS years old. unmarried, and
lived in East st. Louis. Ill.

Three Englishmen and an Italian par
ticipated in confidence game in this city
yesterday. which recalled to the detectives
the days when bunco men operated in this
city on large scale. James Otterway
and Albert Stephens sightseers from Lon
don, were the victims, parting with 800.
They had but 81 left when they called on
the police several hours after they had
been buncoed.


The strangers arrived In the city two
days ago. and yesterday morning they
started on a visit to the bureau Of en-
craving and printing. Shortly after they
left their boarding house, at 418 Pennsyl-
vania avenue they met a fellow-country-
man, with whom they engaged in CONVEX
sation, after the latter had asked for a
match. The new acquaintance kindly con-
sented to go with them to the bureau.
Before reaching Uncle Sans money-mak-
ing establishment the man thought to be
an Italian was met.


On their way along the streets the sug-
gestion was made that the four men form
a common fund and travel about the coun-
try together. This arrangement proved
agreeable to Otterway and Stephens. as
they were to have possession Of the funds
and act as distributors. They accepted the
satchel containing the money. as they sup
posed, and went along believing that they
had the cash. There was no occasion for
them to spend any money until the Lon
doners wanted lunch.


You get your lunch" one of the alleged
confidence men remarked, land we'll wait
for you"


Entering the Twentieth Century lunch
room the men gave their order, and In a
few minutes they thought they would look
after the money. The satchel was opened,
but there was no money in it. The stran-
gers were directed to police headquarters,
where they saw Capt. Boardman and told
him their story. Descriptions of the men
were given, and Detectives Helan and Nc
Nance were assigned to search for the
missing men. The latter had several hours
in which to get away, and the police be-
lieve they left the city.

CHICAGO. March I0.-Dodging back
and forth between two cable trains. a
young woman fought blindly and madly
early last evening 20 evade the terrible
death that menaced her.


Trying to escape one train, she stepped
directly In front Of another. which
struck her and killed her instantly. The
tragedy was enacted at the corner OF
Goethe and North Clark Streets. Hun
dreds of people, spellbound. saw her
killed. She had started to cross Clark
Street from the west side. just after a
south bound train had passed. After
she reached the middle OF the tracks she
saw another train bearing down upon
her. The fender. instead OF picking her
up, passed over her.


Before the gripman could bring his
train to a stop she had been dragged
thirty feet or more under the car.


The body has not yet been identified
The woman was about thirty-two years
old. evidently a working woman.

Reports from Clinton Prison show that nearly
25 per cent of the convicts confined III that in
stitution are consumptives; that although one
entire tier has been set aside for these doubly
unfortunate creatures about one hundred must
be housed with men who are not afflicted with
pulmonary disease. The hospital accommoda-
tions are inadequate, and proper isolation OF
tubercular patients is impossible


These conditions have been brought to the
attention of the State authorities with view
to securing additional hospital room for the
consumpttve convicts, not only for their own
good. but for the protection OF those who are
confined with them and for the people with
whom they will come in contact when their
prison time has expired. The convict, deprived
of healthfuI exercise, confined for half the time
in close quarters and surrounded by depressing
and enervating conditions, is much more sus-
ceptibIe to the disease than the free man; and
since the punishment imposed on him does not
include continuous battle with contag1on, the
warning sent by the prison authorities should
be needed.


simultaneously with the request for more
room for consumptive convicts comes plea to
the public for fluids with which a home for
consumptives may he erected near New-York.
The Order of Brothers of Nazareth want to
add the home to the other charitable institCr
tons which they conduct at Priory Farm. This
farm is in Dutchess County. about one thou
sand feet above the level of the sea, "a place"
says the Superior of the brotherhood, where
''the life of consumptive can be prolonged

Jackson. KY. July N.-In a desperate
pistol duel at Cave Run schoolhouse, three
miles east of jackson, to-day. three persons
were severely hurt.


James and William Barrett and Jack
Howard and his I4-year-old son, were the
principals. A bullet from James Barretts
pistol lodged in the abdomen of James
Wires, u years old. who was sitting at his
desk in the schoolhouse. Jack Howard was
shot In the arm. and his elbow was shat
tered James Barrett was shot in the head
with buckshot and his skull was fractured


The civil authorities declined to take
action and two details of soldiers from here
were sent into the country to make ar
rests. Captain Foley's posse arrested the
Towards, and details under Lieutenant
Macleod overlook the Barretts several
miles from the scene of the shooting


Last night Howard and James Barrett
played poker in Jackson. and Barrett won
Towards money and accepted his pistol as
pawn for SO. Howard followed him TO
the scene of the shooting. in an attempt, he
says. to redeem the weapon.


Barrett claims the pistol was bought out
right. Howard borrowed a gun and his son
had a pistol. The Barretts had revolvers
and several shots were fired. The schoolboy
may recover, but the two men are fatally
wounded.

Philadelphia. June THE Working Com
mittee of the Central Textile Union, COM
posed of one delegate from each union on
strike, met at strike headquarters to-day
and considered the situation.


After five hours session the committee,
in conjunction with the Executive Board of
the textile workers, issued long statement
to the public. giving reasons for the strike
of over 1900 men. women and children.


The statement says that the strike was
ordered for sanitary reasons; that it was
necessary, because the health of the women
and children was at stake


The statement called attention to the
fact that children were compelled to work
ten and three-quarters hours a day in the
mills from Monday to Friday, and six and
one-quarter hours on Saturdays. The state
ment also declares that the textile industry.
as shown in statistics produced before the
Anthracite Coal Strike Commission. is dead
lier than the mining industry: that the
workers in the mills. where Is always dust
are subject to pulmonary diseases. The
statement also asks for the support Of the
public and reiterates the willingness of the
workers to meet their employees for con-
ference.

Marseilles Juno 7-More than a hun
dred persons, passengers and crew, were
drowned near Marseilles to-day in a COLI
sion between the Insulaire and the Iiban,
passenger steamers. belonging to the Frais-
senet Steamship Company Of Marseiles.
The Liban sank and seventy-seven passen-
gers were saved, while the remainder per-
ished.


The steamer Liban left Marseilles this
morning on her regular passenger trip to
BaStfa, Corsica, and was run down and sunk
by the Insulaire off the Marie Islands.
ATTEMPT TO RUN


STEAMER AGROUND.


The collision was witnessed from the
pilot-boat Blechanp, which was about two
miles distant. The Blechamp Immediately
repaired to the spot to render assistance.
The force Of the collision had cut a great
hole in the Libans side and 1t already was
making water rapidly.


The captain saw that the only chance was
to run the steamer aground, and the Liban
was headed full speed for the shore; but
within seventeen minutes after the collision
and while still in deep water the fore part of
the steamer plunged beneath the waves,
and few minutes later 1t had disappeared.


In the meantime the Blechamp, the
steamer Balkan, also belonging to the
Frassinet Company, and other vessels had
drawn near the sinking steamer and were
making desperate efforts to rescue those on
board. The Blechamp picked up forty per-
sons, many of whom were at the point of
exhaustion.


TERRIBLE SCENE


AS BOAT WENT DOWN.


Officers of the steamer Balkan describe
the scene just before the Liban disappeared
as a terrible one.


AS the vessel was sinking it was inclined
to such an angle that her masts struck the
water, causing an eddy, which made the
work of rescue most difficult.


A mass of human beings was clinging TO
the laundering vessel and uttering despair
ing cries as it went down.


At the same time the boilers exploded.
intensifying the horrors. For few mo-
ments the victims were seen struggling in
the sea, then the waves closed over them
and all was silent. Of about 200 passengers
who were aboard the Lban more than half
were drowned.


The Balkan launched three boats. and the
other vessels did all possible to save the
victims in the short time that elapsed be-
tween the time of the collision and the sink
ing of the Liban.


Up to o'clock this afternoon thirty bod
les had been recovered

ences Is that this important part Of the

Chicago, Nov. so.-Falling snow and
slippery rails caused a collision be-
tween Ogden avenue and Erie and
Sangamon street electric cars last
night in which thirteen persons were
injured. A police sergeant who risked
his life to save the passengers, was
among those badly hurt.


All the injured were on the Sanga-
mon street car, which was struck by
the heavier Ogden avenue car and
partly overturned. Police Sergeant
Thomas Meany was on the rear plat
form and saw the futile efforts of the
motorman of the Ogden avenue car to
apply the brakes.


The shout of the conductor aroused
the passengers to their danger and
they made rush for the rear plat
form. The police sergeant saw that
the car would be struck at that plat
form while the passengers were
crushed in the door, and he leaped in
side the car and forced the leaders
back.


Many were thrown to the floor by
the charge Of the policeman, but the
platform was clear when the collision
occurred.

CHARLESTON. S. G.. April 14.-There
was great indignation here today when
it became known that dispensary con
stables had invaded the Trenholm resi-
denee on wild hunt for blind tiger
liquor.


Mrs Trenholm is the widow of William
L. Trenholm. who was Comptroller Of the
Currency under President Cleveland.
She has a magnificent home at the head
of the aristocratic Battery. and she was
astounded when FIVE rough countrymen
called and said they had orders to search
the place. Protests and entreaties were
uEavailing. The officers pushed their
way in, frightened other women who
were calling, and went through every
room.


They opened wardTobes. scattered
clothing, and left without finding a sin
gle trace of whisky. Friends of the
family kept the wires hot today and
Governor Hayward was informed of the
outrage. The only explanation the con
stables could offer was that some griev-
Gus mistake had been made in the street
number and today the chief in this city
called on Mrs Trenholm with an apology.
1t was not accepted.


Feeling ran high for time and the
citizens recalled the fact that it was dis
pensary work OF this kind that precipi-
tated the Darlington war, when Senator
TiIlman was governor. Il was said to-
night that committee would be sent
to Columbia to file protests with Gov
ernor Hayward with the hope of pre-
venting similar outrages in the future

demented. Their clothing was torn and
when discovered they yelled like Indians,

ed for, and went out. but returned without

Regarding the sad death Of Louise Searle,
who sang in summer opera in Washington
for two or three years, the New York
World Of today says:


One need not be an old New Yorker to re-
member Louise Searle, the beautiful prima
donna of light opera, who died of starva-
ton soon after midnight on Saturday morn
ing. Her last hours were passed in miser-
able. cold, cherries lodging at 633 West
Houston street.


Louise Searle sang for several seasons in
grand opera with Emma Abbott's company.
She had an exquisite soprano voice, was an
accomplished actress, and her fresh blonde
beauty had hundreds Of warm admirers.


When Edward E. Rice was organizing the
company that made him and Evangeltne'
famous, he engaged Louise Searle to sing
the principal role Of Gabriel. Fay Temple
ton was Evangeline, but even her beauty,
Wit and velvety voice did not outshine the
attractions Of Louise Searle. The salary
Rice paid her was $500 a week-something
unheard of up to that time in comic opera.


Fortune Soon Melted Aawy.


When Rice produced "Adonis' at the
Bijou Theater, Louise Searle was still his
prima donna. During the long run of that
wonderfully successful musical hodge
podge, Miss Searle shared leading honors
with Harry Dixey.


Miss Searle became slightly lame ten
years ago from the effect of fall. She
retired from the stage, never to appear
again. She was married when very young
to William Franklin of Philadelphia, and
at the time of her retirement her sons VIII
liam and Harry were about to be graduated
from college She had saved several thou
sand dollars from her salary, and she be-
lieved that she was in comfortable cir
cumsances. Her husband died when the
boys were infants.


The prima donna's sons were not fortu-
nate. William tried literature and news
paper work, without making a success of
either. Harry was unable to earn much,
and he devoted his time to waiting upon his
mother, who became helpless invalid.


The prima donna's little fortune soon
melted away. Each year found the family
Of three poorer than they ever were before,
and at last they sold most Of their belong
ings and went to live in a lodging at 633
West Houston street. Just before Christ
mas William lost his employment, and the
existence of the family after that was. a
hopeless struggle with want.

The long dispute between the

cries are about half a mile apart and serve
almost the same territory. 1t was agreed
some time ago to consolidate, but each
state wanted the site. The patrons have
voted unanimously to locate the new

for it's use. The thing that weighed most

paid for Minnesota butter in the New
York market, a full cent higher than the
New York price.

Danbury. Conn, March 2.-With one arm

to his own courage and the speedy trotting
horse that brought him to this city and to a
surgeon.


Stevens was experimenting work on his
farm and when something went wrong with
feed cutter operated by horse power he
reached into the machine and his coat
sleeve was drawn into the choppers. In an
instant the sharp knives severed his left
arm between the wrist and elbow and the

bin.

that he would bleed to death unless he
could reach a surgeon quickly. With mar
velous nerve he directed his men to make
tourniquet out of rope halter and a
stick and told them how to twist 1t about
the stump of his arm to check the flow Of
blood


A fast horse was brought from the stable
and Stevens and his brother-n-law, Fred
erick Jewel. driver of trotting horses,
for the city, five miles away. The rough
tourniQuet had only partially stopped the
hemcrrhage, and Stevens life depended
upon the speed Of the horse. The FIVE miles
were covered at a three-minute pace Peo-
pie looked in establishment after buggy and
Its occupants as they dashed through the
city.

police station. where Doctor r. NJ English

When the tide goes out and the clouds pass by,
And the boats are beached on the sandy shore,
And the hotsam and jetsam idly lie


Cast up by the waves that are gone before;
When the roar has died from the surging sea,
And soothed in the calm is the breakers shout,
The driftwood remains, like a memory


When the tide goes out.
When the soul goes out and the life is DER,
And the days of our youth are passed away,
And our deeds cast up on the earthly shore
Are dull like the night, or bright as the day
Then the spirit of man, forever free


From the tempests wild in the seas Of doubt,
Leaves evil or good for eternity


When the tide goes out.

No fruit makes a more enjoyable sweet

Cover tightly and store in cool place.

eight hours, have cast an uncanny spell
about that particular train, which was
rendered all the more gloomy when a
third disaster was averted this morning
only by the quick action of Trackwalker
William Crane


While on his inspecting tour this morn

fallen through trestle in Niles Canyon,
between Niles and Sunol, and was hang
ing by its shoulders and fore feet when
the trackwalker met the obstruction.

Livermore was due within few minutes.

a very serious wreck.

as to become an obstruction. which would
easily have wrecked the train had the en-
CINE struck ii. After quarter hour s
work, in which the train men assisted,

sumed its run. Close behind the passen-
ger train was the wrecking outfit which
yesterday cleared the tracks of the de-
rallied and upset engine and cars that
were ditched near Pleasanton.


This mornings local left Livermore at
$50 o clock and arrived in Oakland a little
late but otherwise unijured.


The railroad officials are investigating
the cause of yesterdays derailment. but
have not reached decision. Because of
the reports that the rails had been tam
pered with the Southern Pacific Company
has had its detectives making a careful
inquiry along those lines.

somewhat abated the crew endeavored to make
temporary repairs. but the Menominee drifted
at the mercy of the sea for several days. it being
impossible to steer her. and she driven
back within 800 miles of the scilly Islands.
Temporary repairs at last effected, and
Captain Lucas decided to return to the nearest
port Tugs were sent from the Lizard to assist
the Menominee, hut she steamed to Falmouth
unassisted. 1t is reported that the passengers
all well.

speeches of the lawyers for the defence and Dis
trict Attorney Reese for the prosecution and
the charge 10 the jury. Judge Jones took nearly
two hours to charge the jury. He went
haustively into the facts of the case. and re-
viewed the history of peonage. He thor
oughly aroused and his earnestness impressed
every one.

witnesses Helms and Dunbar could be elm
mated by the jury and they still had the undis-
puted testimony that Turner bought the three
negroes, Helms, Williams and Johnson. paying
Dunbar $40 for them. He said that Turner had
no right TO work the men in bondage, though
they had made voluntary contracts, but when
the men asked to leave Turner they broke the
voluntary contract and they afterward
held involuntarily.

Turner There are street rumors TO the effect
that The jury polled eight for acquittal to four

officials were unable to realize fast enough
upon their best securities to meet the with
drawals.


The action of the bank officials in notify
ing the Comptroller was precipitated by
the rejection of draft upon the National
Bank of Redemption in Boston, the Packard
Banks correspondent

hastily called this afternoon and the loans

al know what you want. I'm accused

Capt. o. w. Ranney of WATERFOWL N. V
and his bride, who were making wedding
tour in luxuriously equipped steam launch
by the inland waterways, nearly persisted
in the Chesapeake bay in the terrific storm
yesterday.


They did not know the Chesapeake is like
the Atlantic in storm. Their frail craft
ran into the northeaster. Before they could
run to harbor the launch struck a reef and
sank off Hawkins Point.


For Ave hours the captain and his wife
chung to the top Of the pilot house, while
sea after sea washed over them Frank
Hancock and his brother sighted the wreck
from shore. They put out in a small boat
which was swamped twice before they
reached the nearly drowned couple.


The bride, unconscious, was first taken
ashore. Her husband. when rescued, was
exhausted and injured from his exertion to
save his wife.

NEW YORK, Aug. 29.-The stock mar
ket was extremely dull today, and in the
early dealings failed TO continue the
improvement which began yesterday un-
der the influence of Secretary Shaw's
monetary relief plan. Although London
prices showed rather general improve
ments, the opening here was only slight
ly higher For the first hour prices
sagged small fractions through the rail-
way list. but the dealings were wholly
devoid of significance.


When the bank statement was publish
ed. with the disappointing decrease in
surplus reserve, a slight selling move
ment took place, which put prices to the
lowest of the morning. 1t was not long.
however, before the market began To
gradually harden. until the general range
was established slightly above yester-
days final level. Atchison was a decided
feature in the recovery, rallying over a
point from the lowest price OF the day.
Similar recoveries were made by Union
Pacific. st. Paul Reading, and Penn
sylvania.


In the industrial list Amalgamated Cop
per continued to receive good support on
all concessions, and finished nearly d
point higher than yesterday. Anaconda
declined per cent from its opening
price. but later rallied and closed with
no net change. Tennessee Coal and Iron
and the United States Steel stocks were
stronger. Colorado Fuel and Iron, how
ever, after advancing a point, lost the
gain.


The market was almost entirely in the
hands of the professional element. ami
many issues received scarcely a single
quotation in the two hours OF the short
session. The general attitude of traders
was that OF indifference TO general news,
although there were no important de-
velopments over night, excepting the
correction of the original report of the
murder of one of our consular officers in
Syria. The closing was firm at about the
best prices.


Government bonds were unchanged.
Railroad bonds were very dull, but
strong.

From the Boston Advertiser.


Maine and New Hampshire do not yet
suffer from the tendency of the times
among millionaires to purchase the great
forest tracts and set them apart for their
private uses. However much this may be
SO In the Adirondacks and however much
1t may be becoming so in western Massa-
chusetts and Vermont, the two eastern
states have thus far escaped. And the
huntsmen and woodmen, who feel that they
have an inalienable right in a primitive
forest which holds good above legal title,
have reasons to be elated.


The experiment of Marshall Jewell, Gen.
Grants Postmaster General, in leasing a
one hundred thousand acre forest lot in the
Maine woods has never been repeated. For
time he and his associates made their re-
We're the only ones who were allowed a free
hunt IN the wilds No matter how big the
game might be or how tempting the chase
might prove, even the Maine guides who
mad roamed without restriction through the
great woods were forbidden to enter. This
stirred up hostile feelings throughout the
state. and eventually when the promoter
dled the vast tract again became the hunt
ing ground for Maine people themselves.


since then both state and individuals have
zeaiously guarded their interests against
any syndicate which would try to repeat
this experiment Hunting and fishing clubs
may control exclusively some of the ponds
and smaller lakes in the pine region. but
they have found it inexpedient to deny
others the hunting privileges which they
nave themselves enjoyed. The same stu
atlon mas been true in the main in New
Hampshire. the exception being in the case
OF the Corbin Park, which embraces parts
or two or three townships where there were
once villages and farms. But this is really
an animal reserve in which every citizen
feels a pride and interest, because hunting
is entirely secondary, the aim of the park
being to keep from determination some
animal species which would not survive
without protection.

VANCOUVER, Wash, Sept. 17.-Curt
and Grace Anderson of Lacenter made a
thirty-mile ride against death yesterday
from their home to this town. They
gained the race, but death finally won.
The stake was Glen Anderson, aged s
months.


Glen was suddenly seized with illness.
The parents thought there was one last
chance to save their child and. hastily
hitching two horses to the lightest wagon
they could find, they started on their long
ride to Vancouver. All the journey was
over rough and hilly country and scarcely
half the distance was passed before dark
ness fell upon the racing horses.


While the mother tenderly cared for the
child the father lashed the team in the
feeble last hope that all might still be
we'll The child was still breathing when
the weary horses dragged the wagon into
the CITY, but death had really won the
race for the baby died soon after it was
taken from the arms of the despairing
mother.


The body was prepared for burial last
night and to-day was shipped to La
center.

at different spot, and the men again swan
toward her The husband was nearest. but be
fore he could reach her she had gone down Tor

men and landed them at a nearby pier.

The little schooner Viking. which ar
rived yesterday, seventeen days from
Dutch Harbor, brought a large collec-
ton Of valuable furs gathered by hunt
ers and trappers in the far north. The
furs in their present condition are valued
at more than $4,000, and include the
skins Of many different species of ami
NAL. Probably the most valuable part Of
the consignment is a bundle of thirty
seven sea otter skins. Securing the furs
involved the sacrifice of many animal
lives, the victims ranging from cinnamon
bears to white rabbits There are skins
of mink, lynx, beaver, red and white fox
bears, black, white, cinnamon and griz-
zly, and otter. The Vikings cargo also
includes little ivory.


The Viking left here May with $4,000
worth Of supplies for the mission stations
located around Kushakwim Bay. A
scow. 40 feet long, 10 feet wide and feet
in depth, was taken up on the Viking
deck. During a heavy gale this scow
got loose from It's moorings and was
saved from going overheard with consid-
erable difficulty. While adrift the heavy
scow did considerable damage about the
schooner's deck


After discharging her. furs the Viking
will go to Grays Harbor to load lumber.

Philadelphia, June 6-After accidentally
setting fire to her home, little Ethel Ash
worth dashed upstairs, awakened a young
brother and sister. and, taking the latter. a
baby, into her arms. made her way through
smoke and fame to the street outside. The
boy was later rescued by a neighbor.


All this happened while the three children
were alone in the house. 1t was about ten
minutes before o'clock in the morning
and the father, Frederick Ashworth, had
gone to his work. Mrs. Ashworth about five
minutes previously had left the house to
go to the corner grocery and do some shop
ping.


The Ashworth home is two-story brick
structure. After her mother had departed
Ethel, who is years old, and the oldest
Of the children, came downstairs and went
into the dining-room. While there she be-
thought herself of kitten and. thinking
that 1t was asleep under couch, she struck
match to look for 1t.


The match flared up brightly. 1t threw a
light into the darkest corners underneath
the couch. The cat was not there. The
burning match came in contact with the
couch draperies, and instantly the latter
were ablaze.


The little girl tried to put out the incip-
lent fire, but to no avail and it spread fast
Then, believing that the house was doomed
and thinking only of her sleeping brother
and sister, she ran into the hal! and up the
stairway to their room. There she roughly
awakened Frank, 4-year-old youngster,
and told him to follow her.


The baby, years old, Ethel picked up in
her arms and then dashed out into the hail.
now thick with smoke. while below the
stairway the flames cracked angrily. Sne
was undaunted, however, and with her bur-
den CROPPED her way down the steps and to
the front door. This she threw open easily
and was soon out in the open air with her
little sister.


Not so with the Agar old toddling boy.
however. The smoke and fire had awakened
all his childish fears.


Besides, Frank had not had time to dress,
and the little fellow stoutly refused to leave
the house until he was suitably attired.
But there was no time for parleying. and
hastily grabbing UP a coat, Ethel wrapped
hand, she led him downstairs through the
smoke and out the front door to safety.
The boy Frank and the baby Lavina Ethel
took in the house of a neXt-door neighbor,
Mrs. Robert Lawrence.


In the meantime Mrs. Ashworth had re-
turned from the grocery store, and was al
most frantic until told that her three chill
dren were safe. On the pavement. blinking,
and perhaps wondering what all the ex-
element was about, was the little Maltese
kitten, which had been the indirect cause
of the fire. 1t had evidently followed Mrs.
Ashworth to the store when she had opened
the door.


When the firemen arrived the blaze was
quickly eStngutshed, but not before about
$500 damage had been done The furniture
on the lower floors was almost completely
ruined. The Ashworths loss will be about
$3.50, with no insurance.

From the Springfield Republican


The commercial growth of Maine has been
rapid during the past few years, more so
than most people realize. The country has
somewhat looked upon that state as one
vast forest, with every man north Of Au-
gusta lumberman, and nearly every man
south Of the capital sea captain. The
great pine forests are, of course. the center
of a great industry, especially at this time
Of the year. when the lumber jacks are
romping through the woods, whose stiffness
the mighty spruce trees. This is one Of
Names great industries, and another Is
granite quarrying. The people live largely
from the things produced on their own land,
and during the past few years they have
burrowed and blasted deep into 1t in search
of wealth, and great has been their reward
Maine is much more than the playground
Of the east, with Bar Harbor, the Range
leys and MOosehead lake as the social GEN.
tiers. Outsiders have seen the logging roads
in the wilderness. the scattering quarries on
the hills and near the coast, while along
every river they have heard the water rush
ing through the sideways or crashing
over the great dams. Few of them have
realized that Maine has taken her stand
along with the other great producing states,
IS utilizing her vast waterpower, is cutting
into her great forests more ruthlessly than
ever, Is seeing more cotton and pulp mills
built But still her little schooners go busily
dancing up and down the coast, directed by
the long gray bearded men who made the
state famous for her fishing and canning
industry, and now their quick nervous sons
are developing the vast interior into a COM
mercial power.
headline: Maine a Commercial Power.

Tired and dusty with their tramp of nearly
two hundred miles. about halfway across the
State. Elhu Root. jr.. son of the Secretary of
War, and his classmate. Frederick B. Bastian,
reached this city about o'clock last evening.
after two weeks the road. from Clinton.
Oneida County, where they had finished year
al Hamilton College. They undertook the long
walk in the spirit of a lark, and found it fine
fun" Although the trip in hot weather
most of the time. they covered distances worthy
of veterans some days, and the treatment Of
the farmers along the way gave them an op-
portunity to thoroughly appreciate the rural
beauties of the Empire State.


Leaving Clinton. their route lay in as straight
a line as possible toward this city, through
Madison. Chenango, Delaware, Orange and
Rockland counties, along the southwestern bor-
der of the State On Sunday night they reached
the little village of Suffern, near the Jersey
border, and about ten miles from the Hudson,
and the final stage yesterday was a short one,
although the rain delayed them a little. Cross
ing from the Jersey side early last evening.
they reached Secretary Roots home at No. %
East SiXty-ninth-St., and, wanting rest after
their long tramp, Immediately retired.

1t is not known just how long mosquitoes

longer than Is ordinarily supposed. Thou
sands of them live through winter hiber-
mating or asleep in dark places in barns

for shelter. they live through the winter in
hollow trees; and. even though the tenn

in the woods before the snow has wholly
left the ground.

cling one evening in his motor car and was
thrown out. his thigh bone being badly
broken. He was at once taken home and
passed many weeks of suffering. but was
cheerful and hopeful. and all seemed going
well. However. the weeks passed into
months, and they say the months will pass
into years. and he still walks with crutches
as the bone will not knit.


Puccinf was noted among Italians for his
love Of sport, especially shooting When
his fingers were not at the keyboard of the
piano they held a gun. the tramping and
physical fatigue being not the least of the
enjoyment That this man. almost a giant
In stature and strength. should become
chronic invalid must distress not only his
nearest and dearest. but also those who
know him only through his music Puccini
shows the marks of his suffering physical
and mental. He Is gaunt and pale with
an expression which causes the eyes of
those who know him to fill with tears since

SAN LUIS OBISPO, Dec. 20.-San
Luis Obispo County has derived very
little benefit from the rainfall so far
this season. There have been two or
three rains, aggregating about rs of an
inch, which has been general over the
county and sufficient to keep down any
serious alarm regarding coming crops.
The dairy and live stock interests have
suffered for the time being, but there
has not been scarcity of water in
wells and springs, as last years rains
were copious.


The ranchers are hopeful and are
pushing farming operations as fast as
possible under existing conditions. A
third of an inch Of rain has fallen gen
orally throughout the county within a
week. Sales of farming lands, which
have been many during the past year,
continue. Several notable farming and
seed growing enterprises have been
launched within the past few weeks.
