The announcement that the White Star
Line Steamship Brittanic is now on its last
voyage marks the passing of one of the
most famous Atlantic steamships. She has
just sailed from Belfast for Bremen. hav-
ing been sold to firm to be broken up.


The Brittanic was built in 1874, and soon
after being built reduced the time between
Queenstown and Sandy Hook to less than
eight days. She established a record for
the eastward voyage of seven days sixteen
hours.


The Brittanic was considered a wonder
in her day. not only for her speed but
for size and luxury. She has used the
engines and boilers which were nut into
her when she was built, never missing q
day through accident or disability


The Brittanic made better time after
years of continuous service than when first
put in service, making her 31Sth trip in
September. 1880 in seven days, six hours
and hfty-five minutes, breaking her pre-
vious record, made in 1888, of seven days
nine hours and thirty minutes, afterward
crossing in seven days, six hours and fifty
two minutes


Her bese westward record was made in
August, 1885, seven days. seven hours and
thirty minutes. Twenty-n!ne years of
service under her original engines and
boilers is record not likely to be an
to come.


The Brittanic between 1874 and 1899 made
some 2e0 voyages between New York and
Liverpool crossing the Atlantic more than
500 times. She Travelled about 100000
miles, or enough to take her more than
seventy times around the world. and car
ried more than 100000 passengers.


When the British Boer war broke out in
1899 the British government claimed the
Brittanic for use as transport In 1900
she was selected to convey the imperial
corps. which escorted the Prince OF Wales
on his tour of the colonies. making the
trip of $1,000 miles. This was the end of
her military service. and since then she
has been lying at Belfast.

ANNAPOLIS, Md. May 9.-The Yale
second crew won a decisive victory over
the crew OF the United States Naval
Academy today, crossing the line four
lengths ahead of the midshipmen, in
10 minutes and As seconds. The Yale
crew took the lead al the start and held
it throughout the race. For the first
half mile there was however, little ad-
vantage to the New Haven boys, but
slow recovery, soon began to tell. and
at the mile there was open water be-
tween the boats. From that point on.
though. the Cadets stuck to their work
doggedly and forced their stroke up to
thirty-six. The distance between the
boats constantly increased. The differ
ence between the two styles of rowing
was marked. the Yale crew pulling a
long stroke, getting their hands away
quickly, and slowing down their slides
and body swing as they came aft. while
the Annapolis crew were little shorter
in the water, got their hands away fast,
and recovered quickly. the idea being
to catch the water before the speed of
the boat could check it between strokes.
but the weight, rushing into the stern,
stopped the boat between strokes. Thus
Annapolis rowed thirty-five and thirty
six 10 the minute and even higher at
the start and finish. while Yale rowed
thirty-two, putting it at thirty-four at
start and finish. The difference in the
weights of the two crews was large
the college men averaging 169 and the
Midshipmen but 15S.


The day was ideal for a boat race.
There was scarcely a ripple on the water
and what wind and tide there was sit
ting with the crews. Promptly at 80
the crews took the water, and the ref
erees boat. the Manley, followed, it's
narrow deck crowded.


A few hundred yards from the float
the Manley stopped with jerk, throw
ing everyone suddenly forward. The pro-
peller had become entangled, and the
party had to be transferred to the tor
pedo boat Talbot. There was some de-
lay in starting the crews. and one false
start was made. They were called back.
When the final start was made the An
napolis crew was not ready, and the
Yale crew, catching the water first, gain
ed a slight advantage.


Mr. Timmins. the coach of the navy
crew, declared himself satisfied, how
ever. and the race was rowed to finish.

AURORA. Nc. July 1.-The failure OF
the wild strawberry crop this year has
brought trouble to many homes in eastern


Maine TO the city families who expected
to buy the fruit brought in from the country,


for mailing their winter preserves; TO the
country hoys and girls who hoped to secure


their circus money from selling what they


gathered in the fields, and to the hears,


who lay on he first coating Of fat for the
year by foraging among the rocky pastures
and gorging themselves upon the ripe
berries.


Owing to the great scarcity OF the fruit
the celebration on july was hollow


npckerv in many towns, the young FOLK
being unable TO buy fireworks for lack of
funds In the villages the nice old womf n


who give afternoon teas and invite the


minister in 10 sample their strawberry


preserves are In despair and do not know


which way to turn for a substitute.


But the suTerings endured by the human
race are az nothing to the hunger which


has afflicted the bears, who have grown


very audacious from their long fast and


are coming right up to the farmbouses
and taking whatever they can find in the


way Of food.


Early this week, while Mrs. Martha Jordan


WAS picking some strawberries in her gar


den, a bear climbed the stone wall at the


boundary line and amhled close up 10 her


side, picking the fruit from two adjoining


rows, apparently unconscious OF her pres
ence. As soon as che r, allied the character


Of the visitor she dropped her large tin pan


which was about half full of fruit. and ran
10 the house and locked the door.
Finding about four quarts OF ripe berries,
all picked and ready 10 eat, the bear nosed
about the pail for a moment, and. inserting


her head under the wire bail, began to fill
herself at leisure No sooner was the last
berry gone than the bear discovered that
she had made a mistake. The wire bail
had gone over her head and her neck with


great ease. but when she tried to remove
it she met with trouble.


She scratched and clawed at the pail and
tore the hair from her neck in trying to get
released and. finding that the pail remained
in place Ms firmly as ever, she staggered
over the wall and CROPPED her way toward
the West Branch of Union River, into which
she fell and swan across. in the hope OF
washing the pail away


On reaching the further bank she was
seen to reel away for the woods, falling
! down several times before she disappeared
in the bushes,


Meantime Mrs, Jordan had escaped from
her house by the front door and called the


neighbors TO her aid. They pursued the
bear with shotguns and dogs. They crossed
| the branch of the river on a bridge below
| the village, and, putting hounds on the track
| of the bear, soon overlook her.
| She was lying among bunch of ferns,
| and two lean cubs were SPRAYING across
| her body On coming nearer the hunters
saw that the bear was dead, having been
| drowned in about two gallons of water
which remained in the pail after her swim
| across the stream The taut wire fitted SO
| closely over her neck that her nose was
| forced to the bottom Of the pail and the
| water had done the rest.


The village blacksmith has adopted the
| two cubs. and Ia making them grow rapidly
| by feeding them all the new milk they can
drink.

FRANKFORT, Ky. April so.-The jury
In the case Of Jim Howard, on trial for the
third time for the murder of William Goebel,
returned verdict of guilty to-day and
fixed his punishment at life imprisonment.
The verdict was returned by the jury this
terday afternoon The jury stood eleven
for the death sentence and one for life inn
prisnment. The first ballot was unanimous
that the defendant was guilty. On the bal
loting fixing the punishment nine voted for
the death sentence and three for life impris-
onment Two OF the jury then joined the
majorityfor death. Juror Joseph Burke held
out for life imprisonment: explaining that
he was opposed to capital punishment.

change Of countenance. His wife sat by
him and was unaffected. He stoutly pro.
tests his innocence, and will make formal
motion for a new trial tomorrow, This
being overruled he will again go to the
Court Of Appeals.

Portland, Maine, Aug. 26.-Thru the
dense smoke and amid the tumult OF con-
tinuous firing Of cannon, the batueshlps
Kearsarge, Illinois and Alabama entered
this port early to-day, having stormed the
main entrance to the harbor, in connec
ton with the great war game which Is
going on this week In this vicinity The
firing continued from midnight, when the
scouts Of the hostile fleet were discovered
by the pockets Of the army, until daylight,
when the battleships came UP the channel.


The night was a sleepless one, not only
for all actually engaged In the maneuVers.
but for many In the city. 1t was nearly
midnight when the searchlights of the
forts disclosed two torpedo boat destroy
ers In the outer harbor. Firing began at
once and then ceased. An hour later the
presence Of a battleship was revealed by
the searchlights and several OF the forts
opened fire upon her. This vessel re-
turned the fire and after that the can
nonading became general.


A cutter and launch containing landing
parties were captured, and at 2:25 a. m.
all the outer forts were engaged in action
with the three big vessels which after
ward were recognized as the Kearsarge,
Illinois and Alabama. ,..


Attack Main Channel.


While two torpedo boat destroyers and
other small craft had been detailed to the





of the harbor, the movement against the
main channel had been reserved for the
little ships For more than an hour the
big vessels stood off the main entrance
the harbor- At O'Clock they began
the advance. With the Kearsarge leading
and the Illinois and Alabama close behind,
each belching broadsides at the forts, they
sailed slowly toward the city. Forts Will
liam, Preble and Bevell poured uninter
rupted fire toward the fleet. In turn each
ship seemed to concentrate fire on the
forts until the vessels reached the interior
harbor AS the vessels crept by the forts
the firing ceased and at o'clock the roar
of the guns at the eastern side of the
channel where small engagement was
taking place, was all that could be heard.


The battleships then maneuvered for a
time and then they went back toward
the outer harbor where they began cruis-
ing about among the islands. Early in
the forenoon the scene Of action shifted
to the passage into Husseys Sound be-
tween Peaks and Long Island. From this
vicinity great clouds of smoke were aris-
ing and the roar Of many guns was heard,
the Olympia leading a fleet against Fort
Mckinley. AS at the main entrance, they
came in slowly. The Olympia was closely
followed by the Baltimore. There were
four other vessels in this fleet. the prin-
cfpal one being the training ship New
port The others were the converted
yacht Vixen and the two torpedo boat
destroyers, Warden and Stewart.


The Action Ceases.


For time the firing was as violent as
that marking the passage of the battle
ships. Then the action ceased suddenly.


With the interval in the long continued
firing came chance to review the en-
tire movement from midnight to mid
forenoon. The land forces claimed that
tho the battleships had passed the forts
and entered the harbor they were not
able to take the city and had dropped
back to the outer harbor to signal for re-
Inducements. ..-

are short of provisions. One train. the further
from relief, has only two days food The relief
trains also blocked. One relief engine was
ditched yesterday, and most of the working
party of thirty men were frostbitten- The chief
trouble is that the relief parties are unable to
venture far from their own trains because of
the blizzard which has been raging during the
last week.


An expedition With dog sleds laden with food

to reach the distressed passengers. Snow banks
twenty feet high extend for miles. and the cuts
made by the engines fill again almost instantly.
Yesterday one train made only two miles The
whole railway service is paralyzed. The trains.
having consumed all their coal. now burn
ing the wood fences and trees alongside the
tracks No mail has come in gone out of the
colony for over a week

Joe Cans, the lightweight champion of
the world, defeated Dave Holly of Phila-
delphia in six fast rounds at the Washing
ton Sporting Club, Philadelphia, last night.


The champion started in to end matters
in the first round, and staggered Holly with
stiff rights to the jaw, and dropped him for
a count of seven Just before the bell
sounded.


The second round was almost a repetition
of the first, with Cans doing all the leading
and landing hard and often. Holly planted
two stiff rights under Cans heart. but was
sent to the floor with a left hook the
chin. Holly fought back hard. but could
not land an effective blow.


Holly was aggressive in the third round,
but did not appear to reach the champion
with any effect. He then tried mitigating,
but Cans had the better of the exchanges,
and the bell found both men hard at II.


Cans also did the better work in the fifth
round, but appeared to tire toward the end
and had visibly lost much of his speed
when the last round was called.


Holly improved in the final effort and put
three hard jabs to Cans face at the start.
The Philadelphia boxer then landed two
right swings on the champions jaw, and
Cans looked weary. Holly grew careless
and was staggered with hard left hook On
the jaw, but he came back with a hard left
to Cans nose, and both men were fighting g
hard when the bell rang.

TACOMA. Dec. 1S.-An earthquake
last Tuesday broke off the southeastern
peak of Mount Rainier. lying sixty
miles southwest of Tacoma. Hundreds
of acres of rocks and ice including
number Of glaciers, were broken loose
and hurled two miles down the noun
tain side into the valleys below


Mount Rainier is nearly fifteen thou
sand feet high, being surmounted with
three peaks. the highest of which has
been known for twenty years as Colum-
bias Crest. This peak stood on the
southeastern corner of the mountains
brow, being visible throughout Wash
ington, and on clear days from British
Columbia, Idaho and Oregon. The peak
contained a crater several hundred feet
in diameter, in which mountain-climb-
ers have usually spent the night on the
mountains top. Sulphurous fumes and
steam are always rising from this
crater, keeping it free from snow the
year round. Higher up the peak was
always covered with snow and ice The
mountain has glacial system compris-
ing fifteen distinct glaciers, several Of
them being located on its southeast
slope.


The earthquake was felt at several
points throughout Eastern Washington
Tuesday night. The breaking of Mount
Rainier's peak was witnessed by State
Senator Ruth of Olympia and George
E. Higgins, a wealthy stockman own
ing ranges around the southern base of
the mountain. They were startled
Tuesday morning by the earthquake
shock, followed by reports similar to
the firing of heavy artillery. These
gradually increased to a great roar.
Looking toward the mountain, they OBJ
served that the southeastern peak had
broken off and was tumbling down the
slope. Slides continued all day. In the
afternoon there was a broad black
streak of bare rock where before ice
and snow had been piled hundreds of
feet high.


Higgins and Ruth made public what
they witnessed to-day. Loud reports
were heard accompanying the earth
quake hundreds of miles away in East
ern Washington. They were undoubt-
edly caused by the tumbling Of the
peak.

Fosston, Mirln., May 5.-The Red Lake

Red Lake Indian reservation, as provided
in the bill passed at the last session of
congress.


Frank Kratka mayor of Thief River
Falls, has arrived from the council held
at Red Lake Agency between Major Nc
Iaughlin and the Indians. The council
commenced last Tuesday and closed Sat
urday night The bone of contention was
giving sections 16 and So to the state for
school purposes. The Indians objected to
that provision, but were almost persuaded.
Major Scott. acting Indian agent, was
sent for. and after his arrival word was
received from the acting secretary of the
interior that the consent of the Pembina
Chippewas on the White Earth reserva-
tons has to be secured. The Indians final
ly decided. Saturday evening, not to sign
the treaty and the council broke up.


Major Mclaughlin left for Washington
to-day. He told the Indians they would
reopen negotiations at any time before
the next session of congress should they
change their minds. 1t is believed they
will eventually sign.

and lovely flowers, more pleasing to many
people than more pretentious varieties.

NEW YORK, February 14.-The steam
ship Germanic arrived today from Liverpool
after what her commander, Capt. Smith,
said was not only the toughest trip since
the vessel went into commission, but the
stormiest voyage of his career as a seaman.


Almost from the day the vessel put to sea
the weather was stormy. AS the ship pro-
gressed the conditions became more and
more threatening, until early on Thursday
morning, week ago. the great waves were
breaking over the port side and rolling the
big steamer until sleep was impossible for
the passengers.


Immigrants Panic-Stricken.


The liner was making only five knots an
hour. The crew were called frequently to
allay the alarm Of the panicky passengers.


There were twenty-nine persons In the
first cabin, twice as many In the second and
one of the largest steerage lists on record.
The immigrants were panic-stricken.


Toward daylight the conditions became so
grave that Capt Smith ordered oil thrown
over the side Of the ship. The crew had to
move about the ship with ropes fastened to
their waists.


Tossed About in Every Direction.


Again on Friday morning the seas rose to
a great height and swept the steamship
from every direction. y


The captain ordered the engines to shut
down. and for three hours the Germanic
tossed about


Later in the day the weather cleared
slightly and the boat proceeded slowly. The
passengers expressed warm praise of the
captain and crew for theirGonduct through
out the voyage.

CHARLES Vandergrift, soldier attached
10 the Eighteenth Field Battery, lies in
precarious condition at the Post Hospital
az the Presidio, with two severe lacera-
lions Of the scalp and a possible fracture
or the skull, due to his horse falling with
him on Van Ness avenue, rising and drag
glng him for nearly block and kicking
him while his right foot was caught in
the stirrup.


At $3.50 o'clock yesterday morning the
young soldier, riding a spirited horse,
came UP Van Ness avenue from the Pre-
sidio at a hand gallop. AS he neared
Jackson street passing car caused his
horse to swerve and balk. With the ends
of the reins Vandergrift struck the shy
ing animal couple of sharp blows. The
horse broke into a brisk canter, but had
only gone few strides when the slippery
asphalt brought horse and rider heavily
to the ground. The horse fell its right
side, pinning the troopers leg under its
body. The man had barely recovered
from the shock when the horse started to
get on its feet As the weight of the ami
mails body was lifted from the man he
made frantic efforts to reach the stirrup
leather but failed. His right foot was
jammed in the stirrup. The horse, al
ready frightened by his fall, broke into
run, OTdSSlilS the unfortunate man dIlcI
him. The trooper kept his wits about
him wonderfully and made desperate ef-
forts to stop the animal, but the contin-
ued pounding on the unyielding asphalt
soon rendered him unconscious.


An effort was made TO stop the horse at
the corner of Washington street, but the
animal turned quickly down that street
and made for the pavement This turn
brought the mans body directly behind
the horses heels and he lashed out vi
ciously, kicking the unconscious form
again and again and dashing the body
with great force against telegraph post.
The foot came free at last from the stir
rup and the man lay limp on the grass
that edges the sidewalk, his limbs and
face twitching in agony. Blood poured
from wounds at the back of his head be-
low his right eye was cut and confusion.
his clothes were torn and his body
bruised.


DIR. T. L. Mahoney, who resides at 1903
Washington street, was quickly on the
spot and made rapid examination and
found two lacerated wounds of the scalp
and possible fracture of the skull The
doctor bound up the wounds and advised
that he be removed at once to the POST
Hospital at the Preside. This was done
The surgeons at the Post Hospital DO not
think the skull is fractured and stated
later in the afternoon that the man mad
a good fighting chance for life.

DOUBLING GAP,


WHITE SULPHUR SPRINGS, Pa,


July II, 1903.
The opening day of this old and famous
resort was one well worth remembering
by the many patrons who arrived here for
the season on July l. 1903.


For over one hundred years Doubling
Gap has been famous for its mineral
springs-sulphur, iron, magnesia and lthia
The resort had hotel as early as 1900
and from that time to the present. during
many changes and improvements. the Dor
tails of the Doubling Gap Springs Hotel
have never been closed during an entire
season.


At this time of the year. and, in fact
throughout the summer. the climate here
is always dry, cool and bracing and withaI
thoroughly delightful.


There has been lack of gayety since
the opening of the season and the great
number of incoming guests promises to
keep the wheels of social diversion rolling
and spinning gayly until the autumnal
tints appear on the mountain tops
Mountain climbing appears to be the fad
with the guests here this season, while
boating, tennis and bowling are not neg
lected by many who love milder recrea lions
including dancing, cards, pool and bill
lizards, concerts, private theatricals and
many other amusements offered by the
management entirely free Of charge to its
guests.

How many women doctors practice In

ago only seven women had taken their med
ical degree here. in the face, moreover, of

ganza. Nine. Perree has the same position

minority, most of the doctoresses who pass
in this country being Russians and Rouma-
mans. No woman physician has yet been
rewarded with the cross of the Legion of
Honor. but one midwife, Nine. Gross. holds

Medora, ILL.,. Dec. Miss Gertrude
Duckels. daughter Of Henry Duckels. a
wealthy farmer living near Chesterfield.
awoke to-day from a trance Of four days

had last Tuesday evening.


She and her brother were alone at
home when their uncle. Rollin Duckels.
telephoned as joke that tramp was
headed in their direction. never thinking
that the brother would take him seriously:


The boy was badly frightened and told
his sister. who swooned in her chair. The
brother had sufficient presence Of mind to
telephone his uncle what had happened
and to ask him to come before the tramp
arrived.


All efforts on the part Of the family and
of physicians failed to revive the girl,
who is of nervous temperament, until
this evening. when she awoke as from
sleep and asked for something to eat. She
was quite emaciated. During her trance
her body was rigid as iron.


The physician who attended her says

A special to the New York Times from
Omaha, Neb.. yesterday says: Nebraska,
Wyoming and South Dakota are suffering
from the results of the heaviest blizzard for
ten years, and grave fears OF large losses to
live stock are expressed by cattlemen. The
storm struck Nebraska early yesterday and
ragged all day. The wind reached veaoc-
ity of forty miles per hour. sAsssS


The snow has drifted deep In the small
valleys throughout the stock country. and
in many places is twenty to forty feet deep.
In other places the fierce wind has swept
the ground bare. Railroad traffic Is practi-
cally suspended, and freight service is
abandoned entirely.


Reports from all parts Of the state show
the storm to be lcentered over the stock
raising portions of the country, just where
the snow and cold will do the greatest
damage.


Telegrams from the Black Hills country
say many Of the canyons and gulches are
almost filled with snow. and prospecting
will be stopped for many days.

versal amnesty, releasing all political
prisoners from Jail, and welcoming back
to the republic all revolutionary eIiles.
There are probably more exiles from Nioara-
qua than from all the other Central Ameri-
can States.

part of the population, and many con-
spiracies have been formed against him
and revolutions started, the last Of which
was crushed only few weeks ago. The
proclamation of universal amnesty 10 made,
not only with view of conciliating all the
discontented factions but Of impressing
the United States with the genuinenees OF
the peace and order now existing in Mic
aragua. and 10 expected to have some
influence in canal matters, in view of the
hitch in the United States canal negotia-
tions with Colombia.


A telegram was received here to-day by
T. M. Solomon, fiscal agent Of the Republic
OF Nicaragua, from Seflor Ramircian,
Minister Of Foreign Affairs, announcing
the release of all political prisoners and
general and unconditional amnesty to all
political exiles and offenders.

tation of farm stuff, although mail and

paid. With the highest respect to Mr..

farmers are rich, most nf them. They
are not groaning under the weight OF
mortgages. They have got rich in the
last few years. Theirs is the garden
country" The potato blossom is their
favorite flower. Their miles Of potatoes
are wonder and gold mine This is
their first exclusively agricultural
electric railroad. Others are projected.

battle after suffering severe stings. To-
ward evening the bees disappeared, and
the factory was operated during the night
without any trouble. put again on Wednes-
day large swarms arrived, clearing out the
factory once more.


To-day. the third day OF the visitation,
the bees were much fewer in number and,
by keeping the doors and windows tightly
closed, employees were able to work. Places
about their heads. faces and arms showed
signs of many stings. The strange vista
ton is accounted for by the large acreage
of lowlands near the factory recently
opened for celery growing. Odors of the
large amount of fresh fruit and the smell
OF sirups radiating from the factory are
thought to have attracted the bees.

dispatch, from Kansas City, Mo-, last

train, which left the union station at 1890

siding at Rock Island junction, just out
side Of the Kansas City yards.


The smoker was thrown from the track,
turned over and smashed into kindling
wood, and the dozen or more persons in
side all sustained injuries, but no one was
killed. Two ether cars Immediately after
the smoker were derailed, but the Sleep
ers remained on the track. The Texas
train was on time and running rapidly and
the collision came with terrific force. Some
of the people in the deraled coaches were
injured, but neither their names nor the
extent of their injuries is yet known


The first news of the wreck was brought
by George Jacobs, a newsboy of the Col
orado train. He was in the smoker and
was thrown under the wreckage, but man
aged to crawl out and came to the city on
the mail car of an incoming train He was
badly bruised, but not seriously injured.
Jacobs, who came to the city for medical
attention, could give few details Of the
wreck, but said that it was impossible that
any OF the passengers in the smoker had
escaped injuries.

car Williams showed fight and struggle
ensued Williams attempted to throw him
from the car, the officer said, and when he
saw he could not do it, sunk his teeth into
the officers arm, holding on with the te-
nacity of a frenzied animal and not releas-
ing his hold until the officer struck him
with a blackjack the head.


Both officer and prisoner were sent to the
Casualty Hospital. where their injuries
were dressed.

posed fines on Williams amounting to $40

Grand Forks, N. D., Jan. 24.-Mrs. John
State, a widow, her son, II years of age,
and two daughters, 8 and 10 years Of age,
experienced the most thrilling escape from
death in a North Dakota blizzard that
has been recorded for many years.


After spending the day on their farm,
four miles from Hannah, they started for
town at 7 o'clock in the evening. They
had progressed but short distance when
! a whiffletree broke and the horses escaped
from the driver. ..'| ~.
The storm broke with terrific fury, and
in attempting to follow the team the
! sleigh and blankets were lost, though the
fur robe was retained. There was but
one avenue Of escape from perishing and
that was adopted. The boy scooped out
deep hole in snow drift and into this
! the four crawled and covered themselves
| with the robe.


The snow drifted over them and they


were nearly frozen to death, the mother


for eight seemingly interminable hours
fairly fighting to keep her children awake.


At o'clock in the morning the storm
abated somewhat and the mother dragged
the children from the snow bank and by
persuasion and threats urged them for
| ward toward Hannah, where two hours
| afterwards they staggered into a hotel,
completely exhausted, the boy with his


feet frozen and one of the girls with her
I face badly frozen, and all with their
fingers frost bitten.


The nerve of the mother is considered
| one of the most remarkable exhibitions


under trying circumstances ever recorded
Il in the history of North Dakota billiards..

Additional details have been received here
regarding the trying experience of the his
toric battle ship Oregon in typhoon she
encountered during her trip from Honolulu
to Yokohama several months ago.


The storm that the Oregon encountered
was the worst reported this winter from
Pacific waters. The steamship Gaelic was
in the same storm. and within $50 miles Of
where the Oregon was struggling with the
elements. The Gaelic was hove to for
nearly twenty-four hours, an occurrence
which Is very unusual with her, for she Is
one of the best sea boats


On the other hand the Oregon proved
very unwieldy in the storm, and was prac-
tically helpless. "All hands save the ship
was piped that night, and of the 500 and
some odd men aboard none thought that
the vessel would ever emerge safely from
the storm. But she did, and when she
went limping into Yokohama it was with
her superstructure dented and twisted, all
of her life boats smashed or swept away
and a quantity of other damage done to
her. The amount of this damage repre-
scented in the neighborhood of $50 900.


The Oregon was repaired at Yokohama
and again put into active service. She has
done considerable cruising since, and, so
far as the Navy Department is informed, is
in as good condition as ever.

Down under the guns of Fort Morgan lay
the Tennessee. She had been lightly
rammed by the Monongahela, and although
she had been struck possibly a hundred
times by heavy projectiles mainly from
the nine-inch broadsde guns Of the ships
she had suffered no material injury save
for few holes through the smokestack.
which could easily be repaired by her own
force. After careful inspection her officers
reported her otherwise to be in perfect con-
dition.


The Tennessee was a casemated broadside
ironclad 900 feet long. with a beam of
forty-eisht feet. She was armed with six
heavy Brook rifles, 100 Founders each in
round numbers, two in each broadside, one
pivoted forward and one aft; her ports of
which there were ten, were SO arranged that
the fore and after pivots could be fought
In either broadside She was entirely a
home production of the confederacy The
ship was built at Selma. the guns came
from Richmond, the iron plating was made
at Mobile from ore mined in Alabama. The
casemate a sort Of deckhouse with slanting
sides. was plated with iron armor varying
In thickness from four to six inches The
plating was carried in an unbroken slant
below the water line and then bent back
inward to the hull the buckle angle so
formed being filled with a solid wooden
packing, which was a great protection
against ramming. From the bows of the
tennessee a formidable iron spur projected
below the water line. No wooden ship that
hoated could have survived fairly deliv-
cred blow from that ram


There were two or three fatal defects In
her construction, however. Her engines
were taken from an Did iron river steamer
and were woefully weak and Inadequate.
the method for closing her gun ports was
faulty and the shutters working on pivots
were liable to jam; but the most serious
error of her designers had been in exposing
the rudder chains by which she was steered,
on the open deck without protection of any
sort In spite of these things, however she
was without doubt the most formidable YES

death.


Since her return from Nice several
months ago Miss Sanderson has been
seriously i'll with hardening of the liver

ones by her bedside.


Yesterday evening the watchers by

although she gave no evidence of con-

fill rapidly.

Hero, which suffered some damage.

the Victory and she was successfully docked.

MADRID, August 3.-The threatened gen.
eral strike began today in several centers
including Barcelona, Murcia. Cadiz. Ronda
and Alcoy the general unrest is largely
attributed to bad harvests, but the imme-
date motive for the strike is to reinforce
the demand for the release of numerous
workmen who have been thrown into pris-
on for offences in connection with recent
strikes. The leaders Of the movement are
exhorting the members Of the trades unions
not to return to work until all the impris-
oned men have been released.


The government has taken stringent
measures to cope with disturbances. The
military forces and the civil guards have
been reinforced wherever necessary, and
the troops have been confined to barracks
The instigators Of the strike are threatened
with severe penalties.


The residence of the mayor and num-
ber Of private houses at Alcala, province
Of CadZ have been attacked by strikers
who exchanged shots with the gendarmerie

In the Mount Katahdin region they
are giving the hunters some lively times.
and among the hill farms just east of
here they are going into the barnyards
after sheep. Three hunters on the upper
Kennebec had to fight for their lives
last week, when in the pursuit of deer
they fell In with hungry bears. One
took to tree and remained there sew

along and assured him that the bear
from whom he had fed and upon whom
he had wasted his last cartridge had
gone away. While in the tree the hun
ter was kept busy fighting off the bear

Within recent months, to a greater degree than

become familiar with the play of political influences
and the practical workings of politics. and the main
thing which recent events have tended to emphasize
in the public mind is the necessity for clean, intel
gent politics in the counties.


The weight of county influence upon the general
politics of the State has been conspicuously demon
srated in the legislative boodling disclosures Logic
ally and in the last instance the counties are to be
held accountable for the criminal operations of
Doodle combine for the sins of lobby for the barter

ence which there prevails. And upon the counties.
largely rests the burden Of renovang political con-
ditions


The better interests in the towns and counties are
opposed upon principle and upon self-interest to
Doodle politicians. Farming, mercantile, manufactur-
ing interests mining interests and every other repu-
table interest Identified with the counties of Missouri
hurt indirectly by Doodle Legislature; and some
are hurt directly since Doodle frequently involves
backmail or the consequences of a refusal to pay
tribute.


The cure for the political ills consists in ADEQUATE
representation. When the best men Of the counties
lay hold upon their local political situations weed
out unfit men from the organizations control nomna-
tons and work for the election Of good men with
part Of the zeal which is devoted to everyday business
there will be further legislative difficulties and no
further danger from the Doodle element The coming
campaign holds forth great opportunity to the best
people Of Missouri.

BOSTON, Dec. 1.-After hard
fought contest Marvin Hart of Louis
VILE was given the decision over Kid
Carter of Brooklyn in a fifteen-round
bout tonight at the Criterion Athletic
Club. The fight was stopped by Referee
Buckley within one minute Of the time
limit and when Carter was nearly out.


The first two rounds were slow. In
the third. Hart fioered Carter with
right, but the Kid, after taking the
count, got up and clinched. From that
time until the ninth both men fought
savagely, Hart having the best Of the
battle.


Carter was knocked down several
times, but Hart's blows seemed to lack
force and the Brooklyn boy always
arose before the ten seconds expired.


In the ninth Carter drove hard left
at Hart's face, making big cut over
the Kentuckian's left eye, which bled
freely. Hart was dazed, but managed
to continue the round. During the next
four rounds the men went at it hard
and fast, Hart scoring the most points,
Carter being knocked down repeatedly.
The Brooklyn boy boxed pluckily, oc-
casionally landing some terrific right
punches that made Hart stagger.


The fourteenth round was savage
one, Carter reopening Hart's eye and
the latter landing a wicked left on Car
ter's nose. Carter was groggy and was
finally knocked down, but the gong
rang before he could be counted out


In the fifteenth both contestants went
in to win. but Carter was outclassed
and the referee stopped the fight after
two minutes of savage boxing, during
which Carter was knocked down twice.

ing

Thu home life of the Doukhobortsi is quaint
bit of Old World, almost Oriental. life set down in
the midst of the breezy. hustling Western frontier
Their villages, framed In the wide stretching
praries of Eastern Assiniboia. are curious study
to the traveller in the Northwest.


Their cottages are ranged either side of an
open street. and are fairly Dutch in their inn
maculate neatness. They built Of unsawn
spruce, pastered inside and out with a clay MKT
ure and then painted with a wash of white mineral
clay Around the walls ornamental dado of
yellow clay $and the verandas neatly orna-
mented with woodwork, sometimes carved ana
scrolled.- Over the gates are ornamental arches,
relic of the Doukhobors' long residence in the
Caucasus which give an Oriental tinge to the
whole


The interiors are spotless with whtewash, and
floors and furniture fairly shine with the scrub
bling bestowed upon them by the Doukhobor house,
wives. Just inside the door of each living room is
the great clay oven five feet square. which radiat-
ing heat from its large surface. effects a great
economy of fuel. It is made with inches in the
outer surface, which serve to keep dish warm.
and the broad top. remote from the fire, makes a
comfortable cosey corner for the old grandmother.
There she sleeps with the youngest children. and
there cold days she sits and knits while beside
her swings the baby in his cradle hung from the
ceiling.


HER NEEDLECRAFT.


The Doukhobor woman is famous for her skill in
needlework. When she arrived in Canada three
years ago every shred upon her. from her quaint
peaked headdress of white quilted cotton to her
stout, sandal-like shoes. was the work of her own
hands, and the was true of her husbands
garb. with the exception of his boots. The old
spinning wheel still sits by the window, and she
still manufactures both linen thread and woollen
yarn. serviceable homespun and coarse Irvine. She
makes beautiful fancywork and weaves the finest
kind of baskets


The Canadat Womans Art Association organ
ICED for the promotion of the native industries OF
Canada. has shown many interesting specimens of
Doukhobor handicraft in it's annual exhibits, and
has furnished a profitable market for some Of
them In its handicrafts shop in Montreal. This
skill of the Doukhobor adds occasional
touch of actual elegance TO the plain pioneer
homes. One tablecloth of pure linen. with
pretty patterns woven in it, and knit linen lace
upon the edge. A dainty basket holds the house
wife's sewing, a richly embroidered handker-
chief peeps from the Sunday corsage.


The Doukhobor has very valuable ideas as
to cleanliness and sanitation. One Of the first
buildings erected when they reached their new
home worn, harassed i'll and poverty stricken,

Portland, Me, Aug. 26.-Daybreak this morn
ing witnessed the first conflict in the game
Skirmishes early in the evening were followed
by grand dash by the battleships Kearsarge,
Alabama and Illinois straight through the main
ship channel in the teeth OF the fire of the forts
and straight into the harbor. For two hours
the guns of the fleet and shore were booming,
and it was daylight before the last shots were
exchanged. The army says that great victory
has been won, alleging the destruction of the
fleet by mines and gunffre. The fleet will
say that the Searchlights, which guided the
shots of the army were destroyed by the sec
ondary batteries of the fleet. and that the fire
control station and headquarters were similarly
wiped out


The navy might also say, if it chose, that
General Chafee was dead, for ne faced the con-
centrated fire of a company of his own troops.
that is, Maine volunteers. for some time last
night.


Aside from the technical question last nights
conflict was most spectacular. From a senti-
mental point of view. the most striking thing
was the reappearance of Farragut's old flagship
the Hartford. in the battle line. When the
great modern battleships, headed by the Kear-
sarge, swept up the channel to destruction so
The army says. to victory, according to the
navy the shore searchIights fell upon the old
wooden ship, her decks cleared for action and
her men standing at quarters. her battle flag
aloft, just as she entered Mobile with Farragut
in the shrouds nearly forty years aeo--ss


Cease firing; spare Farraguts ship shout
ed Major Whistler, commanding the shore bat
teries. and the old craft passed on unscathed
by all the theoretical volleys that rained upon
her sisters.


TORPEDO BOATS DASH


The most daring feature of the fight was the
dash of the torpedo boat Truxton up Whitehead
passage, a dash that nearly succeeded and
would have resulted in cutting all the ca bIes
and fire control wires of the forts. Here also
was headquarters. and beneath a high cliff a
channel runs into the harbor.


1t was about o'clock when an astonished
sentry saw the fleet torpedo boat within a
stones throw of the commander in chiefs head
quarters, coolly scudding along at a twenty-five
knot clip His shout of dismay brought out a
dozen officers, and mighty rush of orders fol-
lowed Major Whistler, from the roof of a shack.
growing fairly purple with excitement the
little boat passed toward the cables. Then
the infantry turned out and wildly scrambling
down the rocks opened on the boat with rifles
second later FOUNDER on the shore
chmed in, and that ended the rush 1t
narrow call. and the daring Of the attempt drew
admiration from the army.


The affair with the torpedo boat and the little





searchlights at range of one hundred yards,
that essayed to come up the main channel at
ZIG o'clock were premnaries to the main fight.


FIRE ON THEIR GENERAL.


General ChaTee hastened to the scene of op-
erations on the Kanawha When the generals
yacht off Fort Levett volunteer patrol
suddenly sighted it and began blazing away
merriy at the commander.


Although theoretically hors du combat Gen
eraI Chaffee scrambled up the rocky shore and
hastened TO Whitehead. AS he climbed up the
cliff and looked out to sea the general beheld
the most remarkable spectacle Against a cloud
which reflected the searchlight. he saw the whole
fleet lying ten thousand yards away. This dis
cOvery at such range is regarded one of
the most wonderful results ever achieved with
a searchlght.


Even the general was watching them the
ships began to move, and soon loOmed up in the
gray of the dawn, with battle flags hoisted and
the flagship Kearsarge ahead.


Presently at extreme range the great mortars
at Fort Preble opened fire. shaking the windows
for miles around and sending people wonder
and so all along the line, from Forts Levett,
Williams and Prebe, the batteries opened. The
battleships busy also and through the
mists of the morning the flame of their volleys
could be plainly seen.


BATTLEsHIPS SUNK


Swiftly passing the lower forts, the ships head
ed into the narrow ship channel, sown with
mines Farragut's famous order, Damn the
torpedoes; go aheadr' Rear Admiral Bar
ker's sentiment. and in few moments the fleet
was over mine field. First the Kearsarge was
sunk by the explosion of mine beneath her,
then the Illinois ran afoul of contact mine, and
was also a wreck. The Alabama remained. and
she was quickly destroyed by the combined fire
of the forts.


Meantime the fleet was quite oblivious of its
destruction for il calmly sailed into the harbor
firing into the rear of the forts. Far into the
harbor the ships steamed and. when just abreast
of the breakwater. they turned in wide circle
and sailed out again. destroyed but undisturbed
This ended the nights conflict, and the fleet
withdrew to the north, taking shelter behind
the clusters Of islands

one TO the north at Long Island, and one to the
south at Two Lights. In both instances the

scope. Founded one hundred years

temporaneous with the most pregnant
period Of the nations history. Great
advances have been made in a hun
dred years, not only IN scientific
thought, In government, and in the
science of life, but also in religious
thought and methods. In all direc-
tons the human mind IS reaching out
for liberty, but many have mistaken
license for the thing they were seeking
for. With its intelligent and broad
minded pastors ever keeping abreast
of the advanced thought of the day,
this grand old church has stood for a
century bulwark Of old-fashioned
Christianity and mighty power for
good.

The question of an inland waterway from
Chesapeake bay into Albemarle and Pam
leo sounds, North Carolina, deep enough
to accommodate large vessels, is attracting
much attention from shipping masters here
and at places on the Atlantic coast. Dur
ing the past summer the United States
army engineers have been making surveys
Of the most practicable routes. and are now
computing their work before making report
to headquarters here.


There are several routes for an inland
waterway from Norfolk to Beaufort, N. c..
which could be made available for deep
draft vessels. One route is through the
present Albemarle and Chesapeake canal.
This channel runs from the Elizabeth river
into Currituck sound. and thence into either
the Roanoke or Crotan sound into Pamlico
sound, thence through the Clubfoot canal
to Beaufort.


Another route is through the Dismal
Swamp canal. By this route steam ves-
sells pass through the Elizabeth river from
into Albemarle sound, from there into the
Alligator river and by short canal into
Maltamusket lake and through another
small unnamed channel in Pamlico sound
and thence to Beaufort. These are the two
principal routes surveyed and on which re-
ports will be made.


A deep water canal. which would allow
large vessels to avoid the dangerous Cape
Hatteras and its Diamond shoals, would be
a boon that deep water sailors have long
prayed for. That section of the North Car
DINA coast Is the graveyard of hundreds
of vessels, and hardly a winter storm
passes that Is not followed by long story
of vessels lost and men drowned on the
dangerous shoals. This, inland waterway
would be the means Of saving many lives
and much money each winter. The present
gable only to vessels drawing less than
twelve feet OF water.

New-York and Norfolk express on the PhiIa

ran into a freight train on the outskirts of
this city this morning. Two Of the train crew.
the express messenger and five mail clerks
injured. The Norfolk express was pro-
ceeding at a rapid rate when Engineer Beckley
saw the lights of a freight train cross his path
The next instant his locomotive pIoughed
through the middle of the freight The force
Of the collision hurled the express locomotive
and tender over to the right and the mail coach
and baggage car to the left


Within few seconds after the coll SION flames
shot up from the cars, and crew and passengers
began saving the baggage and mail Assistance
was promptly sent from here By special train.
and two fire companies went to suppress the

PORTLAND, Me-, August 26.-ThrOugh
dense smoke and amid the tumult of con-
tinuous cannon fire. the battle ships Kear-
sarge. Illinois and Alabama entered this
port early today. having stormed the main
entrance to the harbor in connection with
the great war game which is going on this
week in this vicinity.


From midnight. when the scouts Of the
hostile fleet were discovered by the pickets
Of the army on shore. until daylight. when
the battle ships came up the channel, Port
land was treated to an experience very
much like actual war.


Entered the Inner Harbor.


This continued until after Z o'clock. the
battle ships entering the inner harbor in
spite Of the opposition of the fort batteries
and the guns behind the Notifications man.
ned by regulars in the vicinity of the city.


The warships apparently engaged in the
different defending points and after time
passed on. AS they did SO the forts one
after another ceased firing until only an
occasional gun was heard. The battle ships
sailed back and forth in the inner harbor.
At length they turned, and, passing toward
the entrance to the bay. began cruising
among the islands.


Where Victory Rests.


Where the victory. If any. rests is not ap-
parent. to shore observers.


The night was a sleepless one, not only
for all actually engaged in the maneuvers
but for many in the city. 1t was scarcely
midnight when the searchlights of the forts
disclosed two torpedo boat destroyers in the
outer harbor.


Firing began at once and then ceased
An hour later the presence Of a battle ship
was revealed by the searchlights and sew
eral Of the forts opened fire upon her.


Returned the Fire.


This vessel returned the fire, and after
that the cannonading became general. A
cutter and launch containing landing par
ties were captured and at 2:25 am. all the
outer forts were engaged in action with the
three big vessels, which afterward were
recognized as the Kearsarge. Illinois ard
Alabama.


While the torpedo boat destroyers and
other small craft had been detailed to the
duty of threatening the various passages
of the harbor. the movement against the
main channel had been reserved for the
battle ships.


Broadsides at Forts.


For more than an hour the big vessels
stood off the main entrance to the harbor.
At o'clock they began to advance.


With the Kearsarge leading and the Illi-
nois and Alabama close behind each pelch-
ing broadsides at the forts they sailed
slowly toward the city. Forts Williams,
Preble and Levett poured uninterrupted fire
toward the ships.


In turn each ship seemed to concentrate
fire on one fort after another until the yes
sells had reached the inner harbor. AS the
ships crept on past the forts the firing
ceased slowly, and by o'clock the echo
OF guns at the eastern side of the bay,
where minor WI
was all that could be heard


Maneuvered for a Time.


The battle ships then Unanswered for a
time, as IL making demonstration against
the city itself. but firing was not resumed.
Then they went back toward the outer har-
Dor. where they began cruising about
among the islands.


Early in the forenoon the scene of action
shifted to the passage into Hussey's sound,
between Peaks and Long Island. From this
vicinity great clouds of smoke were arising
and the roar of many guns was heard, and
the Olympia, Admiral Dewey's old flagship
appeared, leading fleet against the tire.
mendous strength of Fort Mckinley.


Came in Slowly.


AS at the main entrance, they came in
slowly. The Olympia was closely followed
by the famous Baltimore


There were four other vessels in this fleet,
the principal one being the training ship
Newport. The others were the converted
yacht Vixen. which has been seen in port
several times this summer, and two torpedo
boat destroyers, Werdon and Stewart.


For time the firing was as violent as
that marking the passage of the bottle
ships. Then the action ceased suddenly
and the Olympia and Baltimore came to
anchor just off Cow Island, in the direction
of Little Cheboague.


Hostilities Suspended


The Newport got further in back of Great
Diamond and we'll off Indian Cove; the
Vixen was anchored near at hand, only
little further in toward the city and the
two torpedo boat destroyers took positions
almost under Fort George.


Later the Kearsarge, Illinois and Ala
bama anchored not far from Fort George
and, for a time at least. hostilities were
suspended.

Ell Paso, Tex. Aug. ga fight between
a wild bull and big brown bear last
night, across the Rio Grande from FL Paso
on Mexican soil. was witnessed by large
and excited audience. The bull was the ag-
gressor throughout the contest.


The fight was exceedingly spirited, the
bear being hercer opponent to the bull
than the lion. which recently fought him.


Many Americans, including number Of
women. witnessed the fierce battle. which
lasted more than ten minutes. The signal
for its conclusion was when the bear. bleed
ing from wounds about the head, climbed
to the top Of the large cage and remained
there. II the tips of the bulls horns had
not been biunted. his adversary doubtless
would have been killed.


Once during the bulls fierce onslaughts,
the bear caught his enemy by the nose
and, with bulldog tenacity. held on for
more than minute. The bovine loudly bel
lowed in his agony. The bear was many
times fiercely gored and tossed and bat
tered against the side Of the cage. He will
survive, however.

LONDON, May 2o-A sudden outbreak
Of enteric fever on board the refornatory
ship Cornwall. lying of Purheet, has been
traced to infected blankets from the hos
pital camps in South Africa.


Further investigation revealed that many
thousands of these blankets had been sold
broadcast in the United Kingdom. How
they got on the market has not yet been
discovered, A regulation Of the War Office
is that all disused blankets be shredded, so
shat they will be available only for rags.


The War Office sold none and sent none
home. OF the many thousands issued in
South Africa the kaffirs used TO steal scores,
and the Beers captured quantities and ii is
suggested that they may thus have come
into the hands Of pedlers.


The Cornwall's blankets. which examina-
ton showed 10 be blood-stained and filthy,
and swarming with typhoid bacilli, have
been traced through their vendors to
Whtechapel firm, though which it was
learned that they were imported from
South Africa. These stores have been
seized and disinfec,ed. but large parcels
are known TO have been sold in the United
Kingdom. The sanitary authorities have
been warned. and the police are trying TO
trace the importers.

The dismasted British bark Olive
bank, which was sighted on Tuesday
off the Farallones, was towed into port
yesterday by the tug Sea King and
later taken by the Dauntless to the
quarantine station, where her ballast,
taken at Shanghai, will be fumigated.
The vessel will be released to-day,
when representatives of the under
writers will inspect the battered hull
and count the cost Of the Olivebank's
encounter with the elements.


The Olivebank left Shanghai October
IS, in ballast, for Royal Roads for or
ders. Everything went well until the
bark reached latitude s.02 north, lon
gitude 1924 east, which she did No
vember 9. a typhoon from the south
east struck the vessel on this day and
until late November 10 the Olivebank
had a wild time. While the typhoon
lasted the ship rolled heavily. From
port to starboard she wallowed. Down
on one side until the railtop almost
leveled with the seas surface, and then
back with a jerk and over on the other
side. AS she rolled steel yards swung
and tugged at their fastenings, masts
swayed and the rigging groaned and
creaked at the unwonted strain. The
topmast rigging started and when the
typhoon had passed the Olivcbank was
in need of considerable overhauling
aloft.


Such repairs as could be made were
effected as well as heavy weather
would permit. Under ordinary circum-
stances the bark might have made
Royal Roads with her spars intact, but
November p, when about 1900 miles
west-northwest Of San Francisco. or,
to be exact, in latitude Az 81 north and
/ longitude 14S.17 west, a heavy north
easter was encountered.


The gale found easy prey in the
Olivebank, with her slackened shrouds
and generally strained rigging. The
main topmast came down with a crash
at / a. m, bringing with it the main
topgallant mast and all the rigging.
The masts and most of the gear fell
overheard, but the main yard fell to
the deck, cutting a Jagged hole in the
port bulwarks The fore and mizzen
/ tops followed in rapid succession, and
within A few exciting moments the
Olivebank was lying helpless in a high
cross sea, dismasted, her decks piled


with junk stripped from aloft and the
wrecked steel spars still suspended bv
the dismantled rigging. beating with
fearful force against the vessels sides
All hands were on deck at the time
and that nobody was killed or even
hurt when that avalanche Of spars.
blocks and steel stays crashed from
aloft is strange.


1t took all hands five days to clear the
wreckage, and during the operation the
rolling Of the ship kept the swaying
Wreckage in constant motion. Axes
and cold chisels were piled with grim
industry. Sleep was at premium and
when the work was done the Olive
banks sailors were tired and dirty and
every man from skipper down bore on
hands and arms cruel scars and bruises
inflicted during the tussle by the jagged
edges of buckled spar and frayed steel
stay.


Fair weather fortunately fay ored the
dismasted bark and under jury rig she
made the last 1900 miles Of her voyage
! in good time.


Captain Henderson declined the ser
vices Of a towboat on Tuesday, but
( yesterday changed his mind, accepted
the services of tug and is now safely
anchored off the quarantine station.
where she viii remain until nr. Cum
mings. with the aid of scientifically
prepared fumes, succeeds in suffocating
such disease germs as might have

Rome, May Owing 10 landslide which oc-
CURED a short distance from this city, obstruct-
ing the railroad tracks, Emperor William
train was about an hour late in arriving here.
and some anxiety was felt for time by the
crowds waiting in the rain 10 receive him. Ih-
railroad officials who went 10 the scene OF the
landslide teIegraphed however. that there was

tiently in the downpour, as Emperor William is

zollerns regarding italian national suscepti-

The arrangements made for receiving him

King Edward. There were the same decora-

entwtned about the stand, and the chimes Of

royal anthems.


Shortly before the arrival OF the imperial
train King Victor Emmanuel and the Duke OF
Genoa drove in State carriages TO the railroad
station where had already assembled Premier
ZanardeIli the Cabinet ministers, those en-
titled TO wear the collar of the Annunziata, and
the chief court officials. In the distance the
HohenzoIIern flag could be seen floating from
the tower of the QuirinaL When the train was
signalled the guns at Monte Mario Fort
fired a salute, and before the train had fully
stopped Emperor William alighted, followed by
the Crown Prince and Prince Eitel Fred
erick. The Emperor greeted King Victor En-
manuel with a warm embrace, the soveregns
kissing each other four times. The Italian and
German princess then exchanged greetings
and Emperor William reviewed the guard OF
honor at the station the band playing d Ger
man air. The Emperor spoke to most Of the
officials present, without waiting for a formal
introduction, as ne knew most of them per-
sonally.


On the Piazza dele Terme. adjoining the rail-
road station. the quaint ceremony OF the Mayor
Prince Colonna and the municipal authorities
welcoming the Emperor 10 Rome was gone
through. The scene was mingling of ancient
and modern customs. On one side were the re-
Gently completed Esedra Palaces, forming
half circle with the new Via Nazionale begin
ming in its midst and separating the palaces.
On the other side were the ruins Of the Baths
of Diocletian, the soYereigns in modern car
riages. the Mayor and the municipal officers in
medieval coaches. The crowd was so great
that the soldiers and caribineers had difficulty
in maintaining order


The cortege passed down the Via Nazonale
and up the Via del Quirinale at trot and amid
continuous cheers. At the foot OF the grand
staircase in the palace their majesties were met

escorted the Emperor and the German princes
to the svizzeri Hall, where Queen Helena was
waiting with the ladies of her household. The
Emperor. after greeting her majesty, informed
her that the German Empress had desired him
to express her most sincere regret that she was
unable to accompany him to Rome. Queen
Helena said that It was she the King and the
people Of Rome who most deeply regretted that
the Empress was unable to visit Rome on this
occasion.


The Piazza del QArinaIe crowded and the
people continually called for the Emperor to
appear. His majesty appeared on the balcony
twice. with King Victor Emmanuel and Queen

The party was greeted each occasion with

went to the Pantheon to visit the toInbs Of King

roses from the wreaths to the Court Chaplain

talk

Ell Paso, Texas, Sept 19.-As the result
of his order restraining gamblers, bull
fighters and saloonkeepers, Governor Luis
Terrazas Of the state of Chihuahua, Mex
leo, was mobbed and narrowly escaped
with his life. r. ~ =-> 49,


Followed by a bowling mob that was
hurting stones and beating down all who
would check it, the governor fled from
the the plaza, where he had been making
a speech, and sought refuge in the palace,
which soon was stormed by the rioters.
Stones and bottles were thrown thru the
windows, until scarcely a whole pane of
glass was left.


In struggling with the crowd one police
man was beaten to death and another sus-
tanned fatal injuries. 1t was only when
soldiers from the military post were
called to the scene that any progress was
made against the mob. Bayonets and
dubbed guns were used and many Of the
rioters were beaten into insensibility. Two
hundred and forty rioters were arrested.
The mob was made up Of city and coun-
try people, who, angered by the gambling
order, and shouted for former governor
Apumada and cried, Down with Ter
razas." The government Of Chihuahua,
the state which borders on Texas, has
attempted to conceal details Of the affair.

Perhaps the most novel musical event on
record was the telephone band concert at
tended by all Hawaii a few weeks ago.
The Territorial Band, formerly the famous
Royal Hawaiian Band, leader Captain Ber-
ger, went to Hilo on its annual visit The
band ordinarily is stationed at Honolulu,
and was to return there in week The
Hawaiians were wild over the music, and
requests for the band poured in from all
over the island. A joking remark of an ac-
quaintance about playing into phono-
graph gave Captain Berger the idea Of the
telephone concert The telephone company
gave enthusiastic cooperation, getting their
instruments in shape, notifying subscribers,
ETC.. and from to o'clock Of a Sunday
afternoon business communication was sus-
pended through all its exchanges. Fully
eight hundred phones were included in the
system. The band played in the city of
Hilo, gigantic trumpet receiver connecting
with special switchboard being placed
close to the performers. The arrangement
worked perfectly. and not a complaint was
received. The concert was literally heard
all over the island

ALEDO, ILL.,, Jan. 2.-The case of Tona
Dunlap, charged with the murder of Allie
Dool. was submitted to the jury tonight.
The case, which has been on trial for
several weeks. is the outgrowth of a
tragedy that has excited the people of
this community since early last summer.


Allie Dool, clerk in a general store here.
died suddenly after eating chocolate
candy that had been given her by Tona
Dunlap. 1t was proved that she died of
stryehnine poisoning and charges were
made that the poison was administered
by Miss Dunlap. A Coroner 5 jury, how
ever, eXonerated Miss Dunlap, and thus
the matter was allowed to rest until late
in the fall, when Grand Jury indictment
was returned against Tona Dunlap. Her
trial followed.


The only motive alleged for the crime
charged was that Miss Dunlap hoped to
succeed Miss Dool in the store clerkship,
a position paying 50 a week. 1t was
proved that Tona Dunlap had purchased
strychnine from druggist. but the young
woman testified, and in this was corrobo-
rated by her mother, sister and brother,
that she had bought the poison and used
it as corn remedy.


The prosecution proved that the choco-
late candy contained poison and that
Miss Dunlap gave 1t to Miss Dool was
admitted.


The testimony also developed the fact
that Tona Dunlap and another young
woman had eaten candy taken from the
same paper bag and that neither suffered
injury.


Miss Dunlap has stoutly maintained her
innocence and her lawyers have tried to
establish case of accidental poisoning.

NEW YORK, March 5.-Several Atlantic
liners reached port today, all bringing re-
ports of an unusually rough crossing. The
big ship Kaiser Wilhelm der Crosse, which
arrived off the Hook last night, made her
way up to quarantine when the fog light
ened today, showing many evidences of her
battle with big waves. For the first five
days Of her voyage she experienced gales
Of hurricane force. The gale began from
the southwest, accompanied by hail squalls
which increased in violence. The Kaiser
Wilhelm bucked the big seas under reduced
speed for five days, her average on the
whole run being 1922 knots. Her tunnels
were crusted with salt and the seas were so
heavy that they boarded her decks and
smashed five lifeboats.


The Oceanic met equally as bad weather
She came into quarantine with a story Of
a voyage of high winds and tremendous
seas, and like the Kaiser Wilhelm, was
compelled to go under reduced speed for
five days.

A remarkable feat of snake surgery took
place recently in the New York Geological
Park under Curator Ditmars. Magma, a
splendid 10-foot king cobra had developed
an abscess next to one of her poison
fangs. and unless this were removed she
would die. To capture the dangerous rep
tile, to force her jaws apart, and to cut
the abscess, was the problem.


The curator had plan and he called
for an extra fat snake pill When the
stuffed snake appeared it was distended
to the bursting point. In more than a
month the cobra had not touched food.
Mr.. Ditmars summoned five keepers,
armed himself with surgeons pincers,
and proceeded to the attack. Through a
circular aperture, protected with a slide,
the snake pill was threaded. The hungry
snake took hold of it at once. Frequently
she stopped, in evident pain, but each time
she resumed until the long, black thing
was halfway down her throat


This was the moment to act. The door
was thrown open and before the cobra
could disgorge herself to fight, she was
seized by the head and throat. while other
hands g-asped her body and tail. Then
the mouth was forced wide apart, while
the pincers did their work, and the finest
specimen of cobra in captivity was thus
saved to the observation-disclosures

ing he was almost exhausted. He

The steamer saw the boat and bore down 10

The crew Of the Cambrian Prince num-
bered twenty men.

BELGRADE. June 26.-Affairs under
the new King seem to be progressing
calmly. Reports from the country say
that everything there is quiet and
peaceful and that the people are de-
lighted with the new government.


The King today received the heads
of the government departments. and the
officers of the various garrisons. The
national festivals close this afternoon.
His majesty attended a festival by
peasants and danced for a short time.
He expressed joy at the peoples merri-
ment


The Kaiser, who has been mentioned as
one OF those not in sympathy with the
new Servian government, has sent a
most cordial dispatch TO King Peter. II
was also announced this morning that
the Austrian minister has resumed dip
lomatic relations with the government.


The question OF what disposition will
be made OF the cases OF the officers who
participated in the assassination of the
late King and Queen still agitates all
circles. The newspapers today say that
the King has settled the question by
granting amnesty to all political offend
ers. under which head the conspirators
will doubtless come.

Washington, Sept. 5.-The general staff
of the army has ordered change in war
department regulations so that hereafter
food, fuel, forage and other garrison sup
plies shall be contracted for by the various
department commanders. This change has
been advocated by many able military
men in the past, but the beureaucrats
have been SO firmly intrenched in the
war department that nobody could accom-
plish the desired reform.


For years all army supplies have been
contracted for by the heads Of various
staff departments here, which has almost
invariably resulted in delay and in in
creased cost to the government. The gen.
eral staff thought that the officers COM
manding the several army department
scattered all over the United States were
In better position to purchase needed
supplies than department bureaucrats
hundreds Of miles away.

The forty-six German and Austrian
agriculturists, landowners and profess
sors who are studying farming and other

plimented the country and the climate
by donning American summer suits.
Some OF these distinguished travellers
stick to khaki; for instance. Count KN1sKY

But at Cincinnati the other day a re-

wore full summer togs, including belts. :"
IT'S the fatigue uniform OF American
sovereigns, and the distinguished travel
lers show both courtesy and adaptability
in wearing it.


The forty-six have inspected the
farms, the thoroughbreds and the Jer-
sey cattle OF the Kentucky Lexington,

genoe Of connoisseurs. But Lexington

art, the Kentucky mint julep. The

this masterpiece.

A remarkable feat of snake surgery took
place recently in the New York Zoological
Park under Curator Ditmars. Naigina, a
splendid ten-foot king cobra. had develop
ed an abscess next to one of her poison
fangs, and unless this were removed she
would die. To capture the dangerous rep
tile, to force her jaws apart. and to cut the
abscess. was the problem. The curator had
a plan and he called for an extra fat snake
pill. When the stuffed snake appeared it
was distended to the bursting point. In
more than month the cobra had not
touched food Mr.. Ditmars summoned five
keepers. armed himself with surgeons
pincers. and proceeded to the attack
Through circular aperture, protected with
a slide. the snake pill was threaded. The
hungry snake took hold of it at once. Fre-
quently she stopped, in evident pain but
each time she resumed until the long, black
thing was half way down her throat. This
was the moment to act. The door was
thrown open and before the cobra could
disgorge herself to fight. she was seized by
the head and throat while other hands
grasped her body and tail. Then the mouth
was forced wide apart while the pincers
did their work. and the finest specimen of
cobra in captivity was thus saved to the
collection.

LINCOLN, Neb.. April A.-Passengers on
Burlington passenger train were robbed
of $1,000 early this morning as the train
was leaving the Burlington union station
In Lincoln. This train has been robbed three
times, all within 100 miles of Lincoln The
robbery last fall netted $4,000 to the men
who did the work. and no trace of them
has ever been found


The work this morning was accomplished
mostly while the passengers from branch
and feeder lines of the Burlington were
In the depot awaiting the arrival of trans
continental trains. Many of the persons in
the depot were asleep and did not know
they had been robbed until the noise
aroused them as the train was pulling Into
the station.


The presence of the robbers was first
discovered by woman. She screamed and
the people in the waiting room gathered
around. Investigation proved majority
Of them had been robbed. The confusion
permitted the robbers to escape. -


Later the robbers made their presence
known on board an immigrant sleeper. The
conductor and porter, with the passengers,
were all herded into one end Of the car
and the search for valuables was made
by one man while the other held the crowd
back with guns. They left the train be-
tween Lincoln and Milford

Charles Hubert, Daniel Muller and Mich
olas Kellmeyer employees of the ice de-
partment of the Star Brewery at Belleviile.
narrowly escaped death yesterday by the
bursting of an ammonia cylinder.


Besides being almost suffocated when res
cued, the men were injured by flying pieces
of the cylinder.


Muller. who is machinist. was the most
seriously injured All were hurt about the
eyes by the ammonia.


The ammonia cylinder had not been work
ing properly, and Muller. with the other
men. attempted to repair It While work;
ing at it. the Cylinder exploded and covered
the men with the biting fluid. They were
unable to escape from the room and fell
fiat on their faces.


The noise of the explosion was heard bv
other employees and the machinery was
stopped. The ventilators and windows in
the room were opened. and a dozen men
soon rescued the trio. who were hurriedly
bathed. Several physicians were summoned
and attended their injuries, after which the
men We're taken to their homes.


Last evening all were resting easily, and
the doctors stated that their eyes would not
be permanently injured. Muller was struck
on the side by several fragments of the
cylinder.

away with them. Several of them

A young mother with her little three
year-old by her side was watching the
workmen putting down the cement
sidewalk which led from the garden TO
the rear of the new home. She was a
romantic young mother and as she
watched the care with which the work
men smoothed out each layer of the
soft stuff which was to remain endur-
ing for years, the familiar old quotation
from her schooldays ran through her
head:


Lives OF great mon all remind US,


We can make lives sublime,


And departing leave behind US


Footprints on the sands OF time


When the workmen had departed she
took off the baby shoes and stockings
of her little son and gently placed the
tinv warm feet on the soft cement. The
little fellow shivered and begged to be
taken away when he felt the Shiny cold
touch of the cement, but the fond
mother gently pressed the little feet
down into the stone, so that in years
to come the imprint of the childs foot
there on the cement would recall his
babyhood.


The cold touch of that cement
brought on pneumonia. The little tod
dler died. Now through all the weary
wears there are left only those two
baby footprints in the cement.

Ocean City, Md, has barely escaped obltt-

Of peril and anxiety. There was no sign of
storm early in the evening, although the
fishermen were on the lookout for blow


Shortly after II o'clock the wind, which

east. shifted to northeast, and gradually
increased in fury until the cottagers be-

made for escape to the mainland. By mid

two hours later a bowling hurricane was
sweeping over the city. A great deluge of

quickly made way with the electric light
poles. and the city was plunged into dark
ness.


With Hurricane Velocity.


The wind blew with increasing velocity
as the dawn approached, but at o'clock
had lulled. The storm broke with such fury

Washington had to find safety at a neigh
boris. Their trip from the house was thrill

rope. This was necessary, as the ocean
was sweeping alongside the cottage waist
deep. AS the members of the little party
were about to step into the water the back
porch. upon which they We're standing, was
swept away, and they were all precipitated
into the water. Four stout men dragged
the party through the surf which was then
running all over the island, to the Black
burn cottage, where dry clothes were pro-
vided and all made comfortable.


The flying sand cut the face. and the cot
tages occupied by the families Of Judge J.
Clements of the interstate commerce
ington were damaged to some extent. Sine
puxent bay joined the Atlantic, and they
swept everything in their path. Outhouses
were overturned and all the cottages suf-
fered more or less The cottage occupied
by Thomas E. Waggaman and family was
surrounded by water, ana the wind dam
aged the upper story. The cottage near
the northern end of the boardwalk occu-
ter, was somewhat injured about the
foundations.


Damaged Hotels.


The Mount Pleasant Hotel was also
among the severely damaged buildings. the
sun parlor on the second floor being COM
pletely demolished. The Plimhimmon and
the Atlantic escaped with slight damage.
The new Congress Hall had the entire front
blown in. and the Casino and the bath
houses in the old part of the city were bad
ly damaged. The fishermen were the great
est sufferers. many of them losing every
thing they had in the world. Some of the
sights were pathetic in the fishing village.
After the storm subsidized the fishermen hur-

fate of their boats. Dick Dublin lost all his
boats.

years." said Capt. Levi Bunting. land /

have been swept from the map and a great

Pointers came as plebes TO the picturesque
place. Old and inadequate as they are these
modest quarters have been an inspiration TO

loved them because they were old.


When the improvements have all been made,
when new buildings have been erected and old
buildings extended and improved. the old bar
racks, improved as to the interior, will still re-
main, and on that account and because the
West Point improvements will not wipe out
the old school. with its pictures dear TO every
American soldier the army and the nation are
to be graduated.

The recent Russian military maneuvers
near Kursk are described in a report just
received by Adjt. Gen. Corbin. From a
military standpoint the maneuvers were
very satisfactory and taught the Russians
many lessons In the rapid assembling of
large bodies of troops.


Automobiles were tried for heavy trans
portation and for the rapid movements of
officers. For the former use they failed,
owing to the very bad state of the Russian
roads. The light automobiles gave some
satisfaction in dry weather and ran from
nine to. eighteen miles hour. but when
the rain began the dust was transformed
into slippery mud, and their progress was
slow and somewhat dangerous. Side slips
were frequent. and the engineer in charge
was often unable, to control the motion of
the vehicle. Hill climbing was often difti-
cult, and it was the general conclusion tina t
automobiles are not well adapted for mil
itary service in Russia.
