The first open air concert ever given by
the United German Singing Societies OF
New York was held in Central Park yester-
day afternoon. with the usual Sunday
concert by the Seventh Regiment Band.
Probably $1,000 persons gathered to listen,
despite the threatening weather.


Before the concert was over the storm
burst and the crowd had to scatter for
such shelter as was obtainable. But ex-
cept for the unfortunate ending, the con-
cert was great success. The singing
society opened its performance with
Kreutzers Shepherds Sunday Song. |"
Then followed Die Lorelei," Mendelssohn's
Hunters Farewell to tho Woods" and
Forgotten" by Reuter-. The closing num-
Der, and that which possibly won most
applause, was our old familiar plantation
melody, MY Old Kentucky Home" sung
in German, and arranged by Van der
Stucken.


The chorus, numbering about $50 voices,
all men, was seated on a special platform
built on to the band stand in the Mall Carl
Helm, the conductor, stood on a small plat
form facing the singers. Seated in the
rows Of benches surrounding and stand
ing in solid masses behind these the crowd
listened eagerly as the chorus rose and
swelled and died away among the trees
The setting seemed particularly appro-
pirate to the Hunters FAREWELL which
was greeted with applause lasting several
minutes. Nor was the scene less fitting
when sDie Lorelei" was sung. for the lake
was just at hand and the splashing Of the
fountain could be heard in the intervals
of the song.


1t was very evident from the enthusiastio
way in which each number was received
that the music pleased the listeners greatly,
and President Theodore Henninger said
afterward that the society will be glad to
sing in the park again If the park authori-
ties consent.


The union Of the German singing so
cieties was formed in 1850. At present
there are twenty-five of the societies
Their combined membership Is over 1000
and their full chorus nearly ] 900. About
half the chorus sang yesterday.

PHILADELPHIA, November 7.-Pennsyl-
vania and Harvard will meet on Franklin
Field this afternoon in their annual foot
ball contest The day dawned hazy, but
just cold enough for ideal foot ball weather.
While neither Harvard nor Pennsylvania
has shown consistent form this fall, the
game should prove exceedingly close and
exciting, with but little to choose between
the two teams Harvard averages ten
pounds more to the man than the Quakers,
but the latter have shown more speed than
the Cambridge boys.


Coach Williams and Captain MetZger of
Pennsylvania are hopeful, but not over
confident of victory, while Assistant Coach
Lewis and Captain Marshall of the crimson
eleven do not hesitate to say that Pennsyl-
vania must play better foot ball than she
has shown this fall to win today's game.
Play will begin at o'clock. William H.
Edwards of Princeton will act as referee
Matthew McClung of Lehigh, umpire, and
E. A. Whiting of Cornell, lineman.

BERLIN, Sept. 2S.-Dr. Karl Ballod
read a paper to-day before the Interna-
tional Statistical Conference on the NOR
tality in large cities, contending that
cities having population of a million in
Western Europe were healthier than
smaller cities, because the latter's sani-
tary precautions were far inferior to those
of the larger cities.


Berlin, he said, was the more healthfuI
and London and Vienna came next. Paris
was the worst of all. Country populations
were the least healthy, but country peo-
pie going to the cities were healthier than
town-bred people. While the rural popu-
lations were stationary in Germany since
1871, the cities had doubled their popu-
lations and the country was increasing
in population by nearly a million a year.

Manuel Olivari, an italian fisherman.

Richmond by the capsizing of his boat.

about for an hour by the tug Sea Rover.
Olivari leaves a wife and three children.

day morning for the fishing grounds in
San Pablo Bay. They were off Point
Richmond about o'clock, when series

right herself. The third squal. however

hour, when the tugboat Sea Rover, bound

street about o'clock, when the tugboat

United States battleship Massachusetts, yester-

Details of the explosion we're obtained when
the Massachusetts arrived here to-day. The
plosion occurred in the starboard after S-inch
turret shortly before noon yesterday, and was
due 10 the accidental discharge of a percussion
primer. while the breech of the gun was open.
The full charge exploded in the turret and killed
injured all the crew of the gun. numbering
nine men. Ensign Ward K. Workman who
was in charge of the turret, escaped all injury,
although he standing near the scene of the
explosion.


Magnificent discipline was Immediately shown

withdrew the charge from the other gun. whose
breech was OPEN The survivors of the guns
crew when rescued were burned. mutiated and
nearly dead. One man whose clothing was on
fire jumped overheard.


The last words of all the men taken from the
turret in dying condition were practically the
same:


Il did my duty. Love to home.


The coolness and discipline of the officers and
men were credit to the navy In less than a
minute three streams of water were pouring
into the turret. preventing the charge in the
other S-inch gun from exploding

VICTORIA, B. c., July 10-The steamer
Miowera brings details of many shipping
disasters which occurred off the Australian
coast and in South sea, as result of tre-
mendous gales in June. Brief facts have
been cabled of the loss Of the German bark
Eoith, with Captain Ertell and eleven men.
en- route from Puget sound to Port Pirie
with lumber, and of the dismastiIg of the
German bark c. H. Watjen. Both vessels
were long overdue.


The Edith struck a reef Off New Gale
donia and her crew left in two boats, one
with Capt. Ertell and eleven men and the
other with the mate and eight men. The
captains boat was not seen after they
left the vessel. 1t was provsioned for
fourteen days.


The other boat was at sea for eight days,
and the shipwrecked men suffered great
privatiops On the eighth day they sighted
the Watjen, from New York to Yokohama.


The vessel had been caught in a furious
cyclone, which rendered her almost COM
plete wreck. Twenty thousand cases of
kerosene had been jettisoned I'm order to
relieve her. For seventy-six days the Wat
jen partly drifted and partly sailed, with
the assistance of jury masts, finally reach
ing Yale Island, off the coast of New
Guinea, whence the Edith's crew was taken
to Australia, while the Watjen's people
remained with their vessel, hoping to get
her to Australia for repairs. The Edith
broke in halves after striking the reef.
The Norwegian bark Lotus ran on a reef
in the Fiji group and was total loss.
The crew was saved.


The steam collier Illaroot was wrecked on
the Australian coast, after losing her pro-
peller. The crew was saved.


The French bark Admiral Cecille, which
was damaged on reef off New Caledonia,
and was cast adrift by the steamer st.
Louis, which ran short of fuel after towing
her 1000 miles, was found in disabled
condition eighty miles off Sydney and
towed to the port.


Other vessels damaged during the storm
were the German bark Mowana, wheat
laden from Buenos Ayres to Sydney; the
West Lothian, from Tacoma for Sydney
with cargo of wheat and -four; the Cas-
tor, from Portland, Ore; the James Drum
mond, from Fair Haven, and the Swedish
bark Tropic.


The American bark Abbey Palmer was
long overdue from Sydney for New Castle
and it was feared she had been lost, but
she was sighted all well after the gales.


The schooner Elliston of Sydney was
wrecked, but the crew ESCAPED.
